statement: Software testing is best understood as the process of applying a few precise, general-purpose criteria to a structure or model of the software under test.
Test coverage criteria are based on only four kinds of software structures - input space, graphs, logic, and syntax - and this classification is the key organizing principle for designing tests.
A test organization is not ready to apply test criteria successfully until it has first automated its tests.
The RIPR model (Reachability, Infection, Propagation, Revealability) orders the four coverage-criteria families so each imposes successively stronger requirements on a test.
Input space partitioning requires neither reachability, infection, nor propagation of a fault.
Graph coverage criteria require reachability - execution reaching a location in the artifact - but not infection or propagation.
Logic coverage criteria require that a predicate be reached and exercised so that one clause affects the predicate's result, meaning the predicate must be infected.

Syntax-based (mutation) coverage requires that the mutated location be reached, that the mutated program state differ from the original (infection), and that the difference be visible in output after execution (propagation).

A test reveals a failure only when the automated test oracle examines the part of the software output that carries the incorrect value; this revealability requirement extends the older RIP model to RIPR.
condition: only when the oracle inspects the output location holding the erroneous value

statement: Test design should be treated as an abstract activity that is independent of the specific software artifact used to derive the tests.
A software fault is a static defect in the software.
A software error is an incorrect internal program state that is the manifestation of some fault.
A software failure is external, incorrect behavior with respect to the requirements or another description of the expected behavior.
Software faults are design mistakes that result from human decisions; they do not appear spontaneously through physical degradation.
Because no foolproof way exists to catch arbitrary human mistakes, all faults can never be eliminated from software.
A program state during execution is the current value of all live variables together with the current location given by the program counter.
A program state is in error if it differs from the expected state, even when every individual variable value would be acceptable in isolation.
Executing a faulty statement can produce an error state that does not propagate to the output, in which case no failure is observed even though the fault was reached.
condition: when the erroneous state does not propagate to an observable output

statement: Verification is the process of determining whether the products of a development phase fulfill the requirements established during the previous phase.
Validation is the process of evaluating software at the end of development to ensure compliance with its intended usage.
Verification is a technical activity that relies on knowledge of the software artifacts, requirements, and specifications, whereas validation relies on domain knowledge of the application.
Validation exposes flaws in specifications: an implementation can pass verification against its specification yet fail validation when that specification does not reflect users' true needs.
Independent Verification and Validation (IV&V) is evaluation performed by people who are not the developers, sometimes internal to the project and sometimes an entirely external entity.
A fault that is extremely hard to find during system testing may be trivial to catch at the unit level: almost any unit-level coverage criterion would have detected the Pentium division-table fault.

A reused component that was correct in its original context must be re-analyzed and re-tested for the new operating context, because unchanged code can fail under different conditions (the Ariane 5 reused an Ariane 4 guidance function that was never re-analyzed for the new trajectory).
condition: when reusing a component in a different operating context

statement: Integration faults arise when separately built modules disagree on an interface assumption such as units of measure, so integration testing must check the assumptions modules make about each other (the 1999 Mars lander loss came from one module sending English-unit data to a module expecting metric units).
Testing is the primary way industry evaluates software during development, even though other factors such as careful design and sound process management also affect reliability.

Designing tests on abstract models (input-domain characterizations, graphs, logical expressions, syntactic descriptions) and then implementing them concretely is more efficient and effective than designing tests directly on concrete artifacts such as source code or requirements.
At test-maturity Level 0 an organization treats testing as identical to debugging, failing to distinguish a program's incorrect behavior from the mistake that causes it.

At test-maturity Level 1 the purpose of testing is taken to be showing correctness, but correctness is virtually impossible to achieve or demonstrate for any non-trivial program, so testers are left with no real stopping rule.
At test-maturity Level 2 the purpose of testing is to show failures; this goal is valid but negative and tends to put testers and developers into an adversarial relationship.
At test-maturity Level 3 the team accepts that testing shows the presence but not the absence of failures, so testers and developers work together to reduce the risk of using the software.

At test-maturity Level 4 testing is treated as a mental discipline whose purpose is to improve developers' ability to produce high-quality software, with testers acting as quality experts who help train developers.
Every individual test should have a known purpose - a specific fact it is trying to verify - because a test whose rationale is unknown will not be very helpful.
Test objectives and test requirements, including the planned coverage levels, should be documented so that the team can state how much testing is enough and when testing will be complete.

The relative cost of finding and fixing a fault rises steeply the later it is detected: about one unit cost during requirements, design, and unit testing, roughly five times as much during integration testing, ten times during system testing, and fifty times after deployment.

Faults are introduced mostly in the earlier phases (roughly 10% in requirements, 40% in design, 50% in implementation) yet a large share are not detected until system testing, which is why late detection is so expensive.
The practical goal of testing is to eliminate faults as early as possible, because every fault removed during unit testing or earlier saves money.

Completely correct software is an unreachable goal, so engineers should evaluate whether the software's behavior is acceptable across factors such as reliability, safety, maintainability, security, and efficiency rather than seeking correctness.

Model-Driven Test Design breaks testing into a series of small tasks and designs test values at a higher level of abstraction, independently of the details of software or design artifacts, test automation, and test execution.
Test case design can be the primary determining factor in whether tests successfully find failures in software.
Tests can be designed either with a human-based approach that uses domain knowledge and experience or to satisfy well-defined engineering goals such as coverage criteria.
Testing can show only the presence of failures, not their absence; more precisely, the problem of finding all failures in a program is undecidable.
Testing is defined as evaluating software by observing its execution.
A test failure is the execution of a test that results in a software failure.
Debugging is the process of finding a fault given a failure, and is distinct from testing.

For a failure to be observed, all four conditions of the fault/failure (RIPR) model must hold: the test reaches the faulty location (Reachability), the resulting state becomes incorrect (Infection), the infection propagates to an incorrect output or final state (Propagation), and the tester observes the incorrect portion of the output (Revealability).
condition: all four conditions must hold simultaneously

statement: A failure is not revealed if the tester observes only the correct portions of the final program state, even when the infected state has propagated to output.
condition: when the oracle inspects only correct parts of the output

statement: The RIPR model applies even to faults of omission (missing code), because when execution passes the point where the missing code should be, the program counter that is part of the program state necessarily has the wrong value.
A formal coverage criterion is one of a test engineer's most powerful tools: it decides which test inputs to use and provides an objective stopping rule for testing.
Each software artifact should have an associated set of test cases, and the person often best positioned to define them is the designer of that artifact.
Test design and construction are the most time-consuming parts of testing, so test activities can and should be carried out throughout development rather than only after the software is implemented.

Testing levels map to development activities: acceptance testing assesses software against requirements and user needs, system testing against architectural design and overall behavior, integration testing against subsystem design, module testing against detailed design, and unit testing against the implementation.

Tests should be designed concurrently with each development activity, even before the software is executable, because the act of designing tests identifies defects in design decisions that otherwise appear reasonable.
Early identification of defects is by far the best way to reduce their ultimate cost.
Acceptance testing must involve users or other individuals who have strong domain knowledge.
Integration testing assesses whether the interfaces between modules make consistent assumptions and communicate correctly, and it assumes the individual modules already work correctly.
Regression testing is performed after changes are made to software to help ensure the updated software still possesses the functionality it had before the changes.

Faults originating in requirements or high-level design become visible only through testing months or years later, are dispersed across components, and are hard to locate and expensive to correct, so test planning should proceed concurrently with requirements analysis and design rather than being deferred.

The distinction that matters most among testing levels is not when they are applied but the type of faults being sought, which depends on the artifact under test and the artifact the tests are derived from.
The input space of even a small program is for practical purposes infinite, so exhaustive testing is impossible and the test designer's goal is to find the fewest tests that reveal the most problems.
Testing poses two key problems - how to search the input space and when to stop - and coverage criteria provide a structured, practical way to answer both.
Satisfying a coverage criterion gives a tester confidence that the tests have examined many corners of the input space and have a fairly low amount of overlap.
Coverage criteria provide traceability from software artifacts to tests, which supports regression testing by making it easier to decide which tests to reuse, modify, or delete.
A test requirement is a specific element of a software artifact that a test case must satisfy or cover, and a coverage criterion is a rule or collection of rules that yields test requirements.

Many differently-named coverage criteria in the literature turn out to be identical once their artifacts are abstracted to a common mathematical model, as with switch cover, two-trip, and transition-pair, which are all edge-pair coverage on a graph.
All test coverage criteria reduce to a few dozen criteria defined on just four mathematical structures: input domains, graphs, logic expressions, and syntax descriptions (grammars).

Asking whether a coverage criterion is black-box or white-box is the wrong question; because the underlying structures can be extracted from any artifact, one should instead ask from what level of abstraction the structure is drawn.

The belief that white-box testing is used for system testing and black-box testing for unit testing is false: any white-box technique can be used at the system level and any black-box technique on individual units.

The work of testing divides into four distinct tasks - test design, test automation, test execution, and test evaluation - each requiring different skills, so assigning one person to all of them wastes resources.

Criteria-based test design creates test values that satisfy engineering goals such as coverage criteria, while human-based test design creates test values from domain knowledge and testing experience; the two are complementary and both are needed to fully test software.

Human-based test design deliberately targets stress tests - very large or very small values, boundary values, invalid values, and unusual user actions - and can catch special-situation problems that criteria-based tests may be blind to.
Test automation is the process of embedding test values into executable scripts, and it is necessary for efficient and frequent execution of tests.

Software with low controllability or observability, such as embedded, real-time, or web software, makes test automation harder and requires extra software to access hardware, simulate conditions, or otherwise control the environment.
condition: when the software under test has low controllability or observability

statement: When tests are well automated, most test evaluation can and should be embedded in the test scripts, for example as assertions.
With a well-planned division of labor, a single criteria-based test designer can support a fairly large number of test automators, executors, and evaluators.

In the MDTD process a software artifact is modeled as an abstract structure (input domain, graph, logic expression, or syntax description), a coverage criterion is applied to produce test requirements, those are refined into test specifications, concrete input values are derived and augmented with values to reach the target, display output, and terminate, and the tests are then automated, run, and evaluated, with execution results fed back into test design.

The abstract structures used in MDTD represent behavior rather than specify it and can be created by the tester after the software is implemented, distinguishing the approach from model-based testing that relies on a model built during design.
Test automation is a prerequisite for unit testing and criteria-based testing.

Test automation is the use of software to control the execution of tests, compare actual outcomes to predicted outcomes, set up test preconditions, and perform other test control and reporting functions.

An important goal of testing is to automate as much as possible, because automation reduces cost, reduces human error, and makes regression testing easier by letting a test be rerun repeatedly at the push of a button.

Excise tasks that are necessary but contribute nothing to behavior - such as maintaining test scripts, rerunning tests, and comparing expected to actual results - are the candidates for automation, whereas revenue tasks such as test design usually are not.

Automating excise tasks removes drudgery, frees engineers for revenue tasks like test design, lets the same test run thousands of times, eliminates errors of omission, and reduces variance in test quality caused by differences in individual ability.
Software testability estimates how likely testing is to reveal a fault if one exists, and is largely determined by controllability and observability.
Software observability is how easy it is to observe the behavior of a program in terms of its outputs, effects on the environment, and other hardware and software components.
Software controllability is how easy it is to provide a program with the needed inputs in terms of values, operations, and behaviors.

Low observability and controllability, common in embedded, component-based, distributed, and web software, can be mitigated with simulation - extra software built to bypass the hardware or components that interfere with testing.
condition: when the software under test has low observability or controllability

statement: Test case values are the input values necessary to complete an execution of the software under test, and they largely determine the quality of the testing.
Prefix values are the inputs necessary to put the software into the appropriate state to receive the test case values.

Postfix values are inputs sent after the test case values, and divide into verification values needed to see the results and exit values needed to terminate the program or return it to a stable state.
Expected results are the results a test case should produce if the software behaves as expected, and a test oracle uses them to decide whether the test passed or failed.
A test case is composed of the test case values, prefix values, postfix values, and expected results necessary for a complete execution and evaluation of the software under test.
Coverage is a property of a test set (a set of test cases), not a property of a single test case.

The parts of a test case are concrete realizations of the RIPR model: prefix values achieve reachability, test case values achieve infection, postfix values achieve propagation, and expected results reveal the failure.

Because expected results usually cannot cover the entire output state, a well-designed test case should check the portion of the output state that is relevant to the input values and the purpose of the test.
Test engineers should automate as many test activities as possible; the only time not to automate is when the cost of automation outweighs its benefits.
exception: when the test will be used only once, or automation requires knowledge or skills the test engineer does not have

statement: A test framework is a set of assumptions, concepts, and tools that support test automation, providing a standard design for test scripts and a test driver that runs each test, compares actual results to expected results, and reports the outcome.
JUnit and similar xUnit frameworks are designed primarily for unit and integration testing, not system testing.
A JUnit test fixture uses a @Before method to set up prefix state and an @After method to reset postfix state so that each test runs independently of the others without sharing state.

State-based testing compares values produced by the unit under test to known reference values, while its complement, interaction-based testing, defines success by how objects communicate with each other.

Tests for exceptional returns are better implemented with the framework's expected-exception mechanism (such as annotating @Test with the expected exception class) than with manual try/catch, because identifying the exception by class avoids mistakes arising from the exception inheritance hierarchy.

Exceptional behavior is notoriously harder to program correctly than happy-path behavior and inexperienced testers tend to test few exceptional conditions, so when evaluating a test set one of the first things to check is how thoroughly exceptional behavior is exercised.
If a condition is possible in the software, the test engineer should write a test for it.
Well-written specifications such as JavaDoc that document both normal and exceptional returns let testers write high-quality tests directly from them.

Each of the four structures in Part II adds one RIPR condition: input-domain criteria satisfy none of the RIPR conditions, graph criteria require reachability, logic criteria additionally require infection, and grammar-based (syntax) criteria additionally require propagation to external behavior.

When the same test logic must run with different inputs and expected outputs, use data-driven testing - write the test once and supply the values in a table - rather than copying and editing the test method, which yields unmaintainable test code and many chances for mistakes.

Data-driven testing can suffer a combinatorial explosion because the number of tests is the cross-product of the possible values for each parameter, so testers must watch for it and adjust when the framework generates more tests than can be practically run.
condition: when there are large sets of data values or test methods with many parameters

statement: A parameterized (theory-style) test expresses a universally quantified assertion in a Precondition-Action-Postcondition form: the engineer hypothesizes that for all parameter combinations satisfying the precondition the postcondition holds, and leaves it to the test engine to find a counterexample.
When a test theory's precondition is not satisfied for a given combination of values, its postcondition is not evaluated for that combination.
Test automation frameworks are not silver bullets: they do not solve the core technical problem of testing, which is deciding what test values to use - that is the subject of test design.
Testability can also be defined probabilistically as the likelihood that a piece of software will fail on its next execution during testing if the software contains a fault.
Information hiding reduces controllability and thereby makes testing harder.

Both controllability and observability are needed to trust a test result: if inputs cannot be controlled one cannot be sure what caused an output, and if outputs cannot be observed one cannot be sure the execution was correct.

Type-safety violations that raise ClassCastException are possible even in code that properly uses Java generics, so it is often necessary to write tests for type-safety violations in addition to relying on the generics mechanism.
condition: because generics guarantee type safety only if no raw types are used anywhere in the system

statement: It is always better to identify a problem at compile time than to wait for a failing test case or, worse, a field failure.

If high-quality testing is not centrally and deeply embedded in the development process, the project is at high risk of failure, whether technical (losing control of what the code does) or business (competitors shipping better functionality faster).

Effort spent revealing failures early delivers an enormous return on investment, and the key cost variable is the lag between when a change should ideally be made and when the need for it is recognized.

The cost of a change climbs ever more steeply the longer the interval between the original decision and its revision, primarily because later work built on that decision must also be revised, and secondarily because the root cause of failures gets harder to find as the software grows.

Traditional software engineering rests on two assumptions - that modeling and analysis can identify problems and changes early, and that the resulting savings justify their cost - both of which presume the requirements stay complete and current.
The traditional up-front-modeling assumptions hold only if humans are perfectionists, whereas people are good at approximate solutions and bad at precise ones, so requirements inevitably change.

Agile methods argue the traditional assumptions often fail because engineers are poor prognosticators (anticipating unneeded changes while missing needed ones), business value is hard to predict, and non-executable artifacts diverge from the running system as it changes.
A model's value in aiding system understanding should be separated from the practice of archiving models as documentation, which tends to become misleading as the system evolves away from the model.
A test harness is not just the automated tests but the process by which the execution of the tests is managed so that developers obtain critical feedback as quickly as possible.

Knowing the correct behavior on a particular test is far more restricted and simpler than knowing correctness of the software in general, and this is what makes the agile view of correctness workable.

Agile methods measure correctness existentially through test cases rather than universally through specifications: the software is considered correct if it passes a particular set of automated tests that include their expected results, and otherwise the build is broken.
Test automation is a prerequisite for test-driven development.
In TDD, when someone believes the system should behave differently, the constructive response is to write or modify a test case, because test cases serve as the de facto specification of the system.
TDD orders the work as writing tests first, implementing functionality second, and applying good design principles third; good design still matters but occupies a later niche in the cycle.
A non-executable document that correctly describes an artifact is helpful, but one that incorrectly describes it is a liability because it is potentially misleading.
Making agile methods work requires high-quality test cases and efficient test processes; use of test automation is necessary but not sufficient.

In continuous integration a developer pulls source and tests into a clean environment, builds, verifies the test set, and after a verified change pushes back so the CI server rebuilds and re-verifies, which catches a developer's mistakes quickly and makes the whole team immediately aware of divergent design decisions.

Continuous integration builds should include verification steps beyond compiling - running test sets, checking code coverage, and monitoring static-analysis results - with dashboards and notifications giving near-real-time status.

A continuous-integration test set must be engineered to run to completion within minutes to at most hours, so that rework is flagged while the problem is still in developers' short-term memory; tests must be not only good but fast.

Agile system tests are designed from user stories - short sentences in the end user's language describing what a user does or needs - which are smaller and less detailed than use cases and are discarded, while the tests derived from them are archived.

In agile TDD a user story becomes one or more acceptance tests that fail on the current software, and each failing acceptance test drives a sequence of TDD tests that force the developer to implement more functionality until the acceptance test passes.
Acceptance tests come from users and represent users' needs; they sit at the same abstraction level as traditional system tests but differ in intent.
Because tests define software behavior in agile methods, high-quality tests are of central importance to whether agile projects succeed.

Freezing an untested legacy system to avoid the consequences of change is not necessarily safe, since leaving unneeded code unchanged caused the Ariane 5 loss, where the fault lay in reused code that was not needed for the new system.
Rather than halting all new work to build a full test suite, test cases should be introduced incrementally so the system moves over time toward both new functionality and tests that verify it.
Refactoring is modifying the structure of existing code without changing its behavior, and it cannot be done safely without tests that check the behavior has not changed.
To refactor legacy code safely, first write and pass test cases for just the section being refactored, then refactor with those tests catching mistakes, and confirm all tests still pass at the end.

To change functionality or repair a fault in legacy code, write tests for the affected section first so some fail, make the change, and confirm all tests - including the previously failing ones - then pass.
Under TDD, code implementing new functionality should be written only in response to a failing test, so every added behavior is motivated by at least one test case.
TDD tests primarily define behavior rather than evaluate whether the behavior is correct, so they tend to score weakly on even basic coverage measures such as statement coverage.

Agile and TDD tests tend to focus on happy paths and are less likely to exercise confused-user, creative-user, or malicious-user paths, so applying coverage criteria to design tests is needed to improve the quality of software evaluation.
Terms like complete testing, exhaustive testing, and full coverage are poorly defined because the number of potential inputs for most programs is effectively infinite.
The rationale of coverage criteria is to divide up the input space so as to maximize the number of faults found per test case, and to provide practical rules for when to stop testing.
A coverage criterion is a rule or collection of rules that impose test requirements on a test set.
A test set T satisfies a coverage criterion C if and only if for every test requirement in the requirement set TR at least one test in T satisfies that requirement.

Satisfying a test requirement with more than one test introduces unneeded redundancy, and because each test has a cost, redundancy should generally be avoided; a test set with no such redundancy is called minimal.

A minimal test set loses full satisfaction if any single test is removed, whereas a minimum test set is one for which no smaller satisfying set exists; making a set minimal is easy, but finding a minimum test set is generally undecidable.
The coverage level of a test set is the ratio of the number of test requirements it satisfies to the total number of test requirements.

An infeasible test requirement is one that no test case values can satisfy, such as one implied by dead code; detecting infeasibility is undecidable for most criteria, so 100% coverage is impossible in practice and infeasible requirements are often dropped or replaced with less stringent ones.

Coverage criteria are used either to directly generate test values that satisfy the criterion or to measure externally-generated tests against it; the measurement use is common in industry but can mislead, because there is no principled meaning for how much worse 99%, 90%, or 75% coverage is than 100%.

Recognizing whether a test set satisfies a criterion is possible far more often than generating a satisfying test set, and both are undecidable in general only because of infeasible test requirements; without infeasible requirements the recognition problem becomes decidable.

The set of test requirements depends on the specific artifact under test: combining a criterion with a particular artifact yields the concrete requirement set, so a requirement like execute statement 42 only makes sense if the program has a statement 42.

Coverage criterion C1 subsumes criterion C2 if and only if every test set that satisfies C1 also satisfies C2 - for every test set, not just some - and for example branch coverage subsumes statement coverage.
Abstraction should be used to handle complexity, not to ignore it.

When a criterion C1's test requirements include infeasible ones, C1 may fail to subsume C2; subsumption can be restored by replacing each infeasible C1 requirement with the corresponding requirement from C2, and criteria should be defined to remain robust to subsumption in the face of infeasible requirements.

Coverage criteria can yield fewer tests than human-based approaches yet be more effective at finding faults, because dividing the input space produces a comprehensive test set with minimal overlap in fault-revealing capability.

Because coverage criteria are derived from specific artifacts they give built-in traceability that answers the why for each test and supports regression testing, and they provide stopping rules that let testing cost and completion be estimated in advance.

Empirical research indicates that satisfying coverage helps testers find faults and that satisfying stronger coverage criteria helps find more faults, so coverage is a valid proxy for fault detection.

No definitive answer exists for what makes a coverage criterion good, but three issues govern its use: the difficulty of computing its test requirements, the difficulty of generating tests to satisfy it, and how well the resulting tests reveal faults.

Subsumption is at best a rough way to compare criteria: there is no theoretical guarantee that a subsuming criterion reveals more faults and experimental results have been mixed, so testers must choose criteria by their cost/benefit tradeoff for the software under test.
Effective tests must not only reach the faulty code but also force something interesting to happen downstream, an empirical confirmation of the RIPR model.
All testing is fundamentally about choosing elements from the input space of the software being tested.

The input domain is defined by the possible values of the input parameters, which may be method parameters and non-local variables in unit testing, objects representing current state in class or integration testing, or user-level inputs in system testing.

Input space partitioning divides the input domain into blocks (equivalence classes) that must be complete (cover the entire domain) and pairwise disjoint (no element in more than one block), and selects values from each block.
The underlying assumption of partition coverage is that any test drawn from a block is as good as any other in that block for testing purposes.

Input space partitioning is easy to start because it needs no automation and little training, the tester does not need to understand the implementation (only a description of the inputs), and it is simple to tune for more or fewer tests.

Each characteristic should address only one property, because lumping several properties into one characteristic (such as ascending versus descending order) produces overlapping, non-disjoint blocks; splitting them into separate characteristics fixes it.

Input-domain testing has two distinct tasks - modeling the input domain (choosing characteristics and partitions) and combining partitions into tests (choosing a coverage criterion) - that must be kept separate, because an IDM that prematurely encodes combination decisions is unnecessarily complex and yields tests that do not reflect the coverage criterion.

Verifying the completeness and disjointness of partitions guides the engineer and keeps modeling separate from combination, since mixing the two tasks is the most common cause of incomplete or overlapping partitions.

Identifying testable functions is the first input-domain-modeling step; each public method is typically a testable function tested individually, but because characteristics are often shared across a class's methods it helps to build a common set of characteristics for the class and then specific tests per method.

When identifying the parameters that affect a testable function, the object's state must be included as a parameter for stateful methods, because behavior can depend on it, as when TreeSet.add behaves differently depending on whether the element is already present.
condition: for methods that have state

statement: A test input is a tuple of values, one per parameter, using exactly one block from each characteristic; adding a characteristic with n blocks multiplies the number of combinations by n, so controlling the total number of combinations is essential and is the job of the coverage criterion.
Once an input domain model and its values are built, some value combinations may be invalid, so the IDM must include constraint information to identify and avoid or remove invalid sub-combinations.

The interface-based IDM approach analyzes each parameter separately: it is almost mechanical, makes characteristics easy to identify and translate to executable tests, but may leave the model incomplete and miss sub-combinations that depend on several parameters together.

The functionality-based IDM approach derives characteristics from the intended behavior and so incorporates domain semantics, which can yield better tests and can start before implementation from requirements, but identifying characteristics is harder and they often do not map to single interface parameters, making test generation harder.

Preconditions are excellent sources for functionality-based characteristics because they separate defined normal behavior from undefined exceptional behavior, and postconditions are also good sources.

When designing characteristics the engineer should look for relationships between variables such as aliasing (two object parameters pointing to the same or logically equal objects, a form of stress testing) and for missing factors that affect execution but have no associated IDM parameter.

It is often better to have many characteristics with few blocks each than few characteristics with many blocks, because characteristics with few blocks are more likely to satisfy the disjointness and completeness properties.

Characteristics should preferably be developed from specifications or documentation rather than program code so the tester uses domain knowledge instead of the implementation, though in practice the code may be all that is available; the more semantic information incorporated, the better the resulting test set.
Different testers produce different input domain models depending on creativity and experience, creating variance in test quality that a structured modeling method can reduce.

Choosing how many blocks to partition a characteristic into is a tuning decision: more blocks mean more tests and possibly more faults found at higher cost, while fewer blocks mean fewer tests at lower cost but possibly reduced effectiveness.
Values at or close to boundaries often cause problems, so boundary values should be included as a form of stress testing.
Every partition must include all values, valid and invalid, in order to satisfy the completeness property.
For each characteristic the tester must check that the union of its blocks covers the whole input space (no missing blocks) and that no value belongs to more than one block (no overlap).
Special values deserve their own blocks: null for a Java reference variable, and empty versus non-empty for a container such as a Set or List.
Identifying candidate values for each block early helps the engineer reason concretely about the predicate that defines the block, even though those values may be refined later.

When two categories overlap, such as equilateral triangles also being isosceles, breaking the characteristic into separate boolean characteristics plus a constraint invariably satisfies the disjointness and completeness properties.

The input domain model should be checked by asking whether any information about how the function behaves is left out of the characteristics, and by explicitly verifying completeness and disjointness for each characteristic.

All Combinations Coverage (ACoC) requires every combination of blocks across characteristics, so its test count equals the product of the blocks per characteristic and becomes impractical beyond two or three partitions.
Combination-strategy criteria assume that different value choices from the same block are equivalent from a testing perspective, so only one value per block is needed.

Each Choice Coverage (ECC) requires one value from each block of each characteristic in at least one test, and is a relatively weak criterion because it does not require values to be combined with other values.
Pair-Wise Coverage (PWC) requires each block value of every characteristic to be combined with each block value of every other characteristic.

T-Wise Coverage generalizes pair-wise to groups of t characteristics and equals all-combinations when t is the number of partitions; it is expensive, and experience suggests that going beyond pair-wise (t equal to 2) does not help much.
Pair-wise and t-wise criteria combine values blindly, without regard for which values are being combined.

Base Choice Coverage (BCC) picks a base-choice block for each characteristic, forms a base test from those choices, and then holds all but one base choice constant while using each non-base block, giving one base test plus one test per remaining non-base block.

The base choice in BCC can be the simplest, smallest, first-in-ordering, or most likely block from an end-user viewpoint, and choosing the base blocks is a crucial design step that greatly affects the resulting tests.
Combining more than one invalid value in a single test is usually not useful, because the software often recognizes one invalid value and masks the negative effects of the others.

Making the base choice valid and most non-base choices invalid turns BCC into an easy way to achieve stress testing, and the base-choice strategy should be documented so regression testers can re-evaluate those decisions.
Multiple Base Choice Coverage (MBCC) allows more than one base choice per characteristic and can produce duplicate tests, which should be eliminated.

Some block combinations are infeasible and must be documented in the IDM as constraints, which relate blocks from different characteristics either by forbidding a combination or by requiring a specific one.

How constraints are handled depends on the coverage criterion: for ACoC, PWC, and TWC the only option is to drop the infeasible combinations, whereas for BCC and MBCC the base case can be changed to make a conflicting requirement feasible.
If an input domain model has too many constraints, it probably has a structural problem and should be redesigned.

Input domain modeling is an excellent way to analyze a JavaDoc API to design test cases, and if the API is not clear enough to identify what is testable and what the parameters are, the problem is deeper and the software designer should be consulted.

To derive tests from an API, first determine characteristics iteratively (functional units, parameters, return types and values, exceptional behavior), then define test requirements (choose a criterion and base cases and mark infeasible requirements), then refine each feasible requirement into one automated test.
When a method has no return value, its effect creates an observability problem that can be solved by checking state through observer methods on the underlying object.
A precondition describing undefined behavior can be converted into defined behavior (a postcondition) through the exception-handling mechanism, as design-by-contract prescribes.
A tester should worry about what happens when preconditions are violated, because violated preconditions are a prime weapon in a security attacker's toolkit.

A specification saying behavior is unspecified does not excuse testing it, because a correct implementation may do anything - silently ignore the call, corrupt the data structure, return arbitrary values, or fail to terminate - and many implementations instead convert the violated precondition into a defined exception.
Systematic input-domain testing derived from an API can reveal genuine defects, such as the inconsistency where hasNext() returns true yet an immediate next() throws ConcurrentModificationException.
Adding a new characteristic that applies to every testable method affects every existing test requirement and adds new ones.

The specific implementation chosen has a major impact on the feasibility of implementing tests, because behaviors differ by implementation - for example, null values are possible in ArrayList but not in TreeSet.

Partition-testing methods - equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, category partition, and domain testing - all divide the input space into subsets under the assumption that all inputs in a subset cause similar behavior.
Empirical studies of large real projects found that pair-wise coverage is nearly as effective at finding faults as testing all combinations, supporting the practice of not going beyond pair-wise.
Continually monitoring code coverage helps improve the input domain model; in one study, refining IDMs against coverage raised decision coverage from about 50% under ad hoc testing to 84%.
Base Choice Coverage has been found to detect as many faults as more expensive strategies such as AETG and orthogonal arrays despite using fewer test cases.
Applying input space partitioning has been shown to both increase the number of faults detected during testing and significantly reduce the cost of testing.
Pair-wise configuration testing can save more than 60% in both cost and time compared to quasi-exhaustive testing.
Graph coverage criteria begin the RIPR progression by ensuring that tests reach certain locations in a graph model of the artifact under test.

Directed graphs underlie many coverage criteria and can be extracted from many artifacts - control flow graphs, design structures, finite state machines, statecharts, use cases - with graph criteria requiring the tester to cover the graph by traversing portions of it.
The graph extracted from an artifact is not the same as the artifact and usually omits details, and the same artifact can have several useful but different graph abstractions.

A graph consists of a set of nodes, a non-empty set of initial nodes, a non-empty set of final nodes, and a set of edges, and it is useful for generating tests only if each of these contains at least one element.
Every test starts in an initial node and ends in a final node; some criteria require a particular final node while others accept any node as final.

A node or edge is syntactically reachable if a path to it exists in the graph and semantically reachable if some input can execute a path to it; testing restricts attention to graphs where every node and edge is syntactically reachable from an initial node.
A test path is a path from an initial node to a final node; a single test path may correspond to a very large number of test cases, or to zero test cases if it is infeasible.
Because testing is carried out with test cases and a test path is only a model of a test case in the graph abstraction, the goal is usually the fewest test paths that satisfy the test requirements.
Graph coverage criteria divide into structural (control-flow) criteria and data-flow criteria, both defined by identifying test requirements in terms of graph structures.
Node Coverage requires the test set to visit every reachable node in the graph and corresponds to the classic notion of statement coverage.
Edge Coverage requires every reachable path of length up to 1 and corresponds to branch coverage; the up-to phrasing ensures Edge Coverage subsumes Node Coverage even for a node with no edges.
Edge-Pair Coverage requires every reachable path of length up to 2 in the graph.
A simple path has no node appearing more than once except that its first and last nodes may be identical (so it has no internal loops), and any path can be composed from simple paths.
A prime path is a maximal-length simple path - a simple path that is not a proper subpath of any other simple path - and Prime Path Coverage requires every prime path in the graph.

Prime Path Coverage keeps the number of test requirements low, but an infeasible prime path may contain many feasible simple paths, so an infeasible prime path should be replaced with its relevant feasible subpaths.

Complete Path Coverage requires all paths and is useless when the graph has a cycle because a cycle yields infinitely many paths; Specified Path Coverage instead covers a supplied set of paths such as customer usage scenarios.
It is important to distinguish the path that specifies a test requirement from the portion of the test path that meets it, and this separation is what enables infeasible requirements to be handled.

A strict tour requires the subpath's nodes and edges in exact order, a tour with sidetrips requires every edge of the subpath in order while allowing departure and return at the same node, and a tour with detours requires every node in order while allowing an edge to be skipped.

Detours can drastically change the behavior of the intended test because the bypassing edge may exercise different behavior, so this book allows sidetrips (practical for infeasibility) but excludes detours.

Best Effort Touring meets each test requirement first with a strict tour and only then allows a sidetrip for requirements that cannot be toured directly, meeting as many requirements as possible while meeting each in the strictest possible way.
If a test requirement can be met without a sidetrip, meeting it directly may be superior to meeting it with a sidetrip.

Round-trip criteria, where a round trip is a nonzero-length prime path that starts and ends at the same node, are special cases of prime path coverage, and in practice it is usually better to simply adopt prime path coverage.
All prime paths in a graph can be found automatically by extending simple paths from length 0 upward and filtering, and test paths that tour them can be constructed automatically.
Prime paths are computed by taking all simple paths and eliminating any that is a proper subpath of another simple path.
The prime-path computation is guaranteed to terminate because the longest possible prime path has length equal to the number of nodes in the graph.
A graph typically has far more simple paths than are needed to tour all prime paths, so prime paths can usually be covered with a much smaller set of test paths.

To derive test paths by hand, start with the longest prime paths and extend them backward and forward to the graph's initial and final nodes, since one such test path can tour several prime paths at once.
condition: when computing test paths manually rather than with a tool

statement: A test path can be eliminated from a test set when the prime paths it tours are a subset of those toured by another test path, yielding a smaller test set.
condition: when a smaller test set is desired

statement: In data flow testing a def is a location where a value is stored into memory for a variable and a use is a location where a variable's value is accessed; the criteria exercise def-use pairs by ensuring values flow correctly from defs to uses.
A def of a variable reaches a use only along a def-clear path, one on which no intervening node or edge redefines that variable between the def and the use.
A du-path for a variable is required to be a simple, def-clear path from a def of that variable to a use of it, and requiring simplicity is what keeps the number of du-paths reasonably small.
All-Defs coverage requires that at least one du-path from each def-path set be toured, i.e. each definition reaches at least one use.
All-Uses coverage requires that at least one du-path from each def-pair set be toured, i.e. each definition reaches every one of its possible uses.
All-du-Paths coverage requires that every du-path in each def-pair set be toured, differing from All-Uses only in changing the quantifier from 'at least one' to 'every' du-path to each use.

The authors recommend Best Effort Touring (allowing def-clear sidetrips where necessary) for data flow criteria because it yields the intended subsumption relationships even when some test requirements are infeasible.

Edge Coverage subsumes Node Coverage, and Edge Coverage is defined to include paths of length up to 1 (length 0 for all nodes and length 1 for all edges) so that nodes with no incident edges are still covered.
Node Coverage does not subsume Edge Coverage: a test set can visit every node without traversing every edge.
Prime Path Coverage subsumes Edge-Pair Coverage only when the graph has no self-loops; a self-loop creates edge-pairs such as [m,n,n], [n,n,o], and [n,n,n] that are not prime paths.
condition: assuming the graph has no self-loops
exception: when a node has a self-loop

statement: Among data flow criteria, All-Uses subsumes All-Defs, All-du-Paths subsumes All-Uses, and All-Uses subsumes Edge Coverage because each edge rests on a predicate and therefore carries at least one use.

Prime Path Coverage subsumes All-du-Paths Coverage because every du-path is also a simple path, which is significant because computing prime paths is considerably simpler than analyzing data flow relationships.

The data flow subsumption results hold only under three assumptions: every use is preceded by a def, every def reaches at least one use, and at every node with multiple out-edges at least one variable is used on each out-edge and the same variables are used on each.
Prime Path Coverage subsumes all the data flow criteria and is simpler to understand and compute, so a testing course may omit data flow entirely.
For source code the most common graph is a control flow graph whose nodes are basic blocks (maximal statement sequences with a single entry and exit) and whose edges represent branches.
On source-code control flow graphs, Node Coverage is commonly called Statement or Basic Block Coverage and Edge Coverage is commonly called Branch Coverage.

When building a control flow graph for a while loop, the loop's iteration edge must return to a dummy decision node rather than to the initialization node, otherwise the graph would wrongly re-run the initialization on each iteration.

The standard du-path definitions work for uses on edges but break down for definitions on edges, because such a du-path need no longer be simple (it can share a common first and last edge rather than node).
exception: when the graph has definitions on edges

statement: The coverage criterion based on def-path (All-Defs) groupings tends to be quite weak.

In source code a def of variable x occurs when x is on the left of an assignment, is an actual parameter whose value the method changes, is a formal parameter (an implicit def at method entry), or is an input to the program.

In source code a use of variable x occurs when x is on the right of an assignment, appears in a conditional test (which is always associated with at least two edges), is an actual parameter, is a program output, or is returned by a method.
When a variable has multiple definitions within a single basic block, only the last definition is relevant to data flow analysis.

Data flow analysis considers only global uses, not local uses: a local use is preceded within the same basic block by a def that overwrites any definition from other blocks, so no def-clear path from another def can reach it.
A du-path that is a prefix of a longer du-path is necessarily toured by any test that tours the longer path, so the prefix need not be separately covered.
exception: when the extended du-path is infeasible even though the prefix is feasible

statement: Deriving du-paths and data flow information by hand is extremely tedious and error-prone, so the analysis is best done automatically by a tool.
When drawing a control flow graph by hand, a good habit is to draw it first with the program statements and then redraw it with the def and use sets marked.
condition: when constructing CFGs manually

statement: Programming-language features such as array element versus whole-array defs, object versus instance-variable defs, and aliasing greatly complicate the otherwise simple notion of a def.
All-du-paths coverage can often be satisfied by a relatively small test set, and some du-paths may be infeasible so that no test path can cover them.

Graph coverage for design elements is based on couplings between software components, where coupling measures the dependency between two units and reflects that a fault in one unit may affect a coupled unit.
The most common graph for structural design coverage is the call graph, in which nodes represent methods (or units) and edges represent method calls.

On a call graph, Node Coverage (called Method Coverage) requires each method be called at least once, and Edge Coverage (called Call Coverage) requires each call be executed at least once, so a method called from two sites must be exercised from each.

Within a module such as a class the units may not all call each other, producing several disconnected call graphs; when there are no calls between units, call-graph module testing is inappropriate and techniques based on sequences of calls are needed instead.
exception: when units do not call each other

statement: Classes cannot be tested directly because they are not executable, and edges in an inheritance hierarchy represent inheritance dependencies rather than execution flow, so applying coverage first requires instantiating objects for the classes.

OO Call Coverage requires that Call Coverage be satisfied on at least one object per class, while the stronger All Object Call criterion requires Call Coverage for every object instantiated for every class.
Requiring merely that one object be created for each class is a weak interpretation of Node Coverage for inheritance hierarchies because it says nothing about execution.

Control connections among design elements are simple and tests based on them are probably not very effective at finding faults, whereas data flow connections are complex and difficult to analyze and are therefore a rich source of software faults.
During unit testing the defs and uses of a variable are in the same unit, whereas during integration testing they are in different units, which is what makes data flow testing of interfaces relevant.

The premise of coupling data flow testing is that confidence in integrated interfaces requires ensuring variables defined in caller units are appropriately used in callee units, which can be restricted to last-defs before calls and returns and first-uses after them.

There are three types of data flow coupling: parameter coupling (parameters passed in calls), shared data coupling (two units access the same global or non-local object), and external device coupling (two units access the same external medium such as a file); a coupling variable is one defined in one unit and used in another.

A last-def is a node that defines a variable for which there is a def-clear path through the call site to a use in the other unit; if the function has no return statement, an implicit return is assumed at the last statement.

A first-use is a node with a use of a variable reachable by a path that is both def-clear and use-clear from the entry point (if the use is in the callee) or the call site (if the use is in the caller); a coupling du-path is a path from a last-def to a first-use.

Applied to coupling graphs, All-Coupling-Def coverage requires a path from every last-def to at least one first-use, All-Coupling-Use requires a path from every last-def to every first-use, and All-Coupling-du-Paths requires touring every simple path from every last-def to every first-use.
In coupling data flow only variables that are used or defined in the callee are considered, because last-defs with no corresponding first-use are not useful for testing.

Coupling data flow analysis must account for implicit initialization of class and global variables, which in languages like Java and C receive default values that can be modeled as defs at the beginning of the main method or constructors.

Coupling data flow analysis deliberately ignores transitive du-pairs (if A calls B and B calls C, last-defs in A are not tracked to first-uses in C) because such analysis is prohibitively expensive with current technology and of questionable value.

Because identifying individual array element references is undecidable in general and expensive in finite cases, data flow testing traditionally treats a reference to one element of an array as a reference to the entire array.

For a direct object-oriented du-pair, the defining method and the using method must be called through the same instance context (object reference), otherwise the def and use apply to different instances of the variable.
condition: when the def and use are class or instance variables reached through method calls

statement: Analysis of indirect du-pairs, where the def and use lie in methods reached through intermediate calls, is considerably more complicated than for direct du-pairs, and du-pairs in distributed software are harder still.
A sequencing constraint is a rule that restricts the order in which certain methods of a class may be called, such as requiring initialization before use or a push before a pop.

Sequencing constraints may be expressed explicitly, implicitly, or not at all, so a responsible tester must look for formal relationships even when they are not stated and use formal specifications when they are available.

Sequencing constraints abstract only certain key aspects of behavior and do not capture everything (for example enQueue-before-deQueue does not capture emptying the queue), so richer relationships must be handled by state-behavior techniques.
In stating constraints, 'must' means a violation of the constraint is a fault, whereas 'should' means a violation is a potential fault but the software will not necessarily fail.

Sequencing constraints can be checked both statically, by testing whether prohibited or required paths exist in the client's control flow graph, and dynamically, by generating test requirements that attempt to violate each constraint.

Because deciding whether a particular path through a program can actually be taken is formally undecidable, some potential sequencing-constraint violations can be confirmed only by executing the program.

Test requirements generated to violate sequencing constraints will be infeasible in well-written programs, but any tests created from those requirements will almost certainly reveal a fault if one exists.

In a finite state machine, nodes are states defined by specific values of a set of variables and edges are transitions that occur in zero time and change variable values, moving the software from a transition's pre-state to its post-state; guards define values required to enable a transition and triggering events cause it to be taken.

On an FSM, Node Coverage is called State Coverage, Edge Coverage is called Transition Coverage, and Edge-Pair Coverage (which was originally defined for FSMs) is also called transition-pair or two-trip.

FSMs do not necessarily have final nodes because they often model devices that run indefinitely, but a test graph abstracting an FSM needs designated initial and final nodes so that test paths can be derived.

Data flow criteria are troublesome for FSMs because states usually carry no defs or uses, defs of triggering variables immediately reach uses, and defs are hard to find, so All-Defs and All-Uses can only be applied meaningfully to variables involved in guards.
A test engineer who derives an FSM to describe existing software will almost certainly detect design flaws in the process.

Deriving an FSM by combining the control flow graphs of methods is not effective or recommended, because the nodes are not true states, it builds in nondeterminism, it requires a finished implementation (defeating early test preparation), and it does not scale to large software.

Deriving an FSM by mapping methods to states using the software structure is subjective, so different testers produce different graphs and introduce inconsistency, and it also requires in-depth knowledge, waits on detailed design, and scales poorly.

A more mechanical way to derive an FSM is to model the program's state variables: identify the state variables, keep the relevant ones such as global and class variables, and omit constants that do not define state.

Because each combination of state-variable values theoretically defines a distinct state, the raw state space is often huge or infinite, so values must be grouped into semantically similar ranges to keep the FSM model tractable.
Choosing between a smaller nondeterministic FSM model and a larger deterministic one is an important test design decision, and the modeled nondeterminism need not be reflected in the implementation.

Modeling state variables is appealing because different testers tend to derive similar FSMs and it needs the design rather than finished software, but it cannot be fully automated because transitions are hard to determine from source and choosing which variables to model requires judgment.
FSMs derived from explicit requirements or formal specifications are usually cleaner and easier to understand, and for well-designed software should carry the same information as UML statecharts.
Because UML use cases are developed early in software development, they let the tester begin testing activities early.

A use-case actor diagram is too coarse for useful testing beyond 'try each use case once' (Node Coverage); useful tests require the elaborated textual description of each use case, including its alternatives.
Following Beizer's admonition, testers should first find a graph and then cover it, extracting a graph structure that is latent in artifacts such as a use case's textual description.

To model a use case as a graph, treat the numbered description steps (inputs to or outputs from the software) as action-state nodes and treat the alternatives (decisions) as sequential-branch nodes in an activity diagram.
Activity diagrams built from use cases usually have few loops and any loops are tightly bounded or determinate, so Complete Path Coverage is often feasible and sometimes reasonable for them.

Use case predicates rarely contain multiple clauses because the use case is expressed in user terms, so logic coverage criteria are usually not useful, and use cases have no obvious def-use pairs so data flow criteria do not apply.
The two coverage criteria most obviously applicable to use-case graphs are Node Coverage and Edge Coverage, with test values derived by interpreting nodes and predicates as inputs to the software.

A use case scenario is a complete path through a use case that makes semantic sense to users, and Specified Path Coverage with the set of all scenarios is the appropriate coverage criterion for use-case graphs.

Specified Path Coverage is not guaranteed to subsume Edge or Node Coverage because scenarios are chosen by people using domain knowledge, so a chosen scenario set could omit some edges, though doing so would probably be a mistake.

Despite their names, All-Defs and All-Uses treat definitions and uses differently: All-Defs focuses on definitions while All-Uses focuses on def-use pairs, so All-Uses is not obtained by substituting 'use' for 'def' in All-Defs.

The claim that Prime Path Coverage subsumes All-du-Paths Coverage is a slight overstatement because of infeasibility involving sidetrips, but in most situations it is reasonable for the test engineer to ignore this special case and proceed with Prime Path Coverage.
exception: when a du-path can only be toured via a sidetrip that is not def-clear

statement: Logic coverage advances the RIPR model by ensuring that tests not only reach a location but also infect the internal state, by trying multiple combinations of truth assignments to the expressions.

The semantic approach to logic coverage yields the same tests regardless of how a predicate is formulated, whereas the syntactic approach tailors tests to the specific formulation and thereby targets the ways an engineer might incorrectly formulate a logic expression.

Studies have found that the syntactic approach to logic coverage usually detects more faults than the semantic approach, but its criteria are relatively complicated and can be expensive, though recent research has reduced the number of syntactic tests to be competitive with the semantic approach.

A predicate is an expression that evaluates to a boolean value, and a clause is a predicate that contains no logical operators; a relational expression, a boolean variable, and a boolean-valued function call are each clauses.

A predicate can be written in many logically equivalent forms, and because logic coverage treats predicates by their semantic meaning rather than their syntax, a semantic criterion yields the same test requirements no matter which equivalent form is used.

Logical expressions for logic coverage can be derived from several sources, including source-code conditions, transitions (guards and events) in finite state machines, and preconditions in specifications.

Predicate Coverage (also called decision coverage) requires each predicate to evaluate to both true and false, and for control flow graphs whose predicates are the branch conditions it is the same as Edge Coverage.

An obvious weakness of Predicate Coverage is that the individual clauses of a predicate are not always exercised, since the predicate's true and false values can be reached while some clauses never change value.
Clause Coverage (also called condition coverage) requires each clause to evaluate to both true and false.
Clause Coverage does not subsume Predicate Coverage and Predicate Coverage does not subsume Clause Coverage; neither criterion subsumes the other.

Combinatorial Coverage (multiple condition coverage) requires clauses to take every combination of truth values, but a predicate with n independent clauses has 2^n assignments, so it is impractical for predicates with more than a few clauses.

The active-clause family of logic criteria captures the effect of each clause in a reasonable number of tests by checking that varying a clause in a situation where it should affect the predicate does affect it, and complementarily that varying it where it should not affect the predicate does not.
A major clause c_i determines a predicate p when the minor clauses have values such that flipping the truth value of c_i changes the truth value of p.

The definition of determination does not require the major clause and the predicate to have the same value, because requiring them to match is not practical (for example when the predicate is the negation of the clause, p = not a).

Each clause should be tested under circumstances where it determines the predicate, because otherwise there is no evidence that the clause is used correctly, and test sets that satisfy Clause and Predicate Coverage can still fail to exercise any clause effectively.

Active Clause Coverage requires that, for each predicate and each of its major clauses, the minor clauses be chosen so the major clause determines the predicate, with two requirements per major clause: it evaluates to true and to false.
A predicate with n clauses needs at least n and at most 2n tests to satisfy Active Clause Coverage, because test requirements for different major clauses often overlap.

Active Clause Coverage is a framework that generalizes the several variants of modified condition/decision coverage (MCDC), and the ambiguity over whether minor clauses must hold the same values when the major clause is true as when it is false yields three distinct flavors.

General Active Clause Coverage (GACC) lets the minor clauses take different values when the major clause is true than when it is false, and as a result GACC does not subsume Predicate Coverage (for example for p = a equivalence b or when exclusive-or is used).

Correlated Active Clause Coverage (CACC) requires the minor clauses to make the predicate true for one value of the major clause and false for the other, which guarantees that CACC subsumes Predicate Coverage.
Restricted Active Clause Coverage (RACC) requires the minor clauses to hold the same values when the major clause is true as when it is false.

Some logic expressions are fully satisfiable under CACC yet have infeasible test requirements under RACC, but this only occurs when dependency relationships among the clauses prohibit some combinations of values, which happens often in real programs because variables depend on one another.
condition: when constraints among clauses prohibit some truth-value combinations

statement: Inactive Clause Coverage requires choosing minor clauses so that the major clause does NOT determine the predicate, with four requirements per major clause (the clause true and false, each with the predicate true and false), verifying that a clause which should not affect the predicate does not.

Inactive Clause Coverage has only two flavors, General (GICC) and Restricted (RICC), because correlation is irrelevant when the major clause does not determine the predicate, and Predicate Coverage is guaranteed in all flavors subject to feasibility.

Inactive Clause Coverage is valuable because a reasonable implementation mistake is to account for a clause in modes where it should be irrelevant, so a skeptical tester should test both settings of a clause that the specification says should not affect the outcome.

Infeasibility is the most vexing issue for the Active Clause Coverage criteria, arising because clauses are sometimes related so that choosing a truth value for one constrains another, as with a short-circuit guard such as i < n and a[i] != 0.
Recognizing whether a test requirement is truly infeasible is a formally undecidable problem.

The simplest way to handle infeasible test requirements is to ignore them, which usually does not affect test quality, though the difficulty is distinguishing a truly infeasible requirement from one that is merely hard to satisfy.

A better way to handle some infeasible requirements is to replace them with the feasible counterparts from a subsumed criterion, for example substituting feasible CACC requirements when RACC is infeasible, analogous to Best Effort Touring in graph coverage.
The Inactive Clause Coverage criteria do not subsume any of the Active Clause Coverage criteria, and vice versa.

Because General Active Clause Coverage does not force Predicate Coverage on each clause's test pair, it may under-test; it is easy to construct predicates where GACC holds but PC does not for one- or two-term predicates, but difficult with three or more terms.

The restrictive nature of Restricted Active Clause Coverage can make it hard or infeasible to satisfy when some combinations of clause values are infeasible, and there is no evidence that RACC yields more or better tests than CACC.
Correlated Active Clause Coverage is often the most practical flavor of Active Clause Coverage.

Semantic logic coverage criteria test the software's logic regardless of how predicates are written, which is an advantage but can produce tests blind to certain fault types, whereas syntactic (DNF) criteria are stronger but more complicated to understand and use.

Disjunctive Normal Form is a common way to express logic expressions because it captures complex situations in small independent chunks that track the specifier's mental model, which motivates approaching logic coverage from a syntactic perspective focused on the representation.

In DNF terminology a literal is a clause or its negation, a term is a set of literals connected by ANDs, and a DNF predicate is a set of terms connected by ORs; terms are called implicants because if one term is true the whole predicate is true, and the DNF representation of a predicate is not unique.
Every result for DNF has an equivalent result for the dual Conjunctive Normal Form, but CNF is used less in both practice and the research literature.
Implicant Coverage requires, given DNF representations of a predicate and its negation, that each implicant of both evaluate to true, using the negation's DNF to test the false case.

Implicant Coverage subsumes Predicate Coverage but does not subsume any Active Clause Coverage criterion, and it is fairly weak because a single test can satisfy multiple implicants and because the DNF chosen for the negation is arbitrary.

A prime implicant is an implicant no proper subterm of which is also an implicant of the same predicate, a redundant implicant is one that can be omitted without changing the predicate, and a DNF representation is minimal when every implicant is prime and none is redundant.
Because non-prime implicants impose unnecessary constraints and redundant implicants are by definition unnecessary, a software engineer has good reason to refactor DNF predicates into minimal form.

A unique true point for the ith implicant is an assignment where that implicant is true and all others false (impossibility implies the implicant is redundant), and a near false point for a clause c in implicant i is an assignment where the predicate is false but negating only c makes i and the predicate true.

The nine syntactic DNF fault classes capture the typical single-mistake ways of mis-expressing a predicate and are regarded as reasonably complete; stuck-at faults are omitted because detecting the included faults also detects them.
In the DNF fault hierarchy, a test set guaranteed to detect a given fault type is also guaranteed to detect the fault types downstream from it, and any test detects Expression Negation Faults.

Multiple Unique True Points coverage chooses, for each implicant, unique true points such that clauses not in the implicant take on both true and false values, and when feasible it detects all Literal Insertion Faults and hence seven of the nine fault classes.
condition: when unique true points exist that let literals not in each implicant take both truth values

statement: MUTP cannot detect Literal Omission Faults or the And-to-Or Operator Reference Fault because those require false points and MUTP generates only true points, and it also has blind spots wherever it is infeasible.

CUTPNFP pairs, for each literal in each implicant, a unique true point and a near false point differing only in that literal, so it detects Literal Omission Faults when feasible and subsumes RACC, but does not guarantee detection of Literal Insertion Faults and therefore cannot replace MUTP.
Multiple Near False Point coverage chooses, for each literal in each implicant, near false points such that clauses not in the implicant take on both true and false values.

MUMCUT applies MUTP, CUTPNFP, and MNFP together and detects the entire DNF fault hierarchy even when some individual test requirements are infeasible, because feasible requirements from one criterion compensate for infeasible ones in another.

MUMCUT is quite expensive in number of tests compared to a semantic criterion such as RACC, and although less expensive MUMCUT variants exist they still require more tests than the semantic ACC criteria.

RACC is theoretically guaranteed to detect only TNF and ENF faults, and researchers have found that RACC tests detect only about one-third of the faults in the DNF fault hierarchy, so MUMCUT should be considered for applications where the consequences of failure are especially severe.
When refining abstract truth assignments into concrete tests, the program-variable values need not match across tests as long as each clause is set to the required truth value.

A Karnaugh map is a tabular representation of a predicate in which groupings of adjacent cells correspond to simple DNF representations, and it is useful for predicates of up to four or five clauses but becomes cumbersome beyond that.

In a Karnaugh map any pair of adjacent cells differs in the truth value of exactly one clause, and the map's edges wrap so that the top and bottom rows are adjacent and the left and right columns are adjacent.

A minimal DNF expression is read from a Karnaugh map by grouping adjacent cells into rectangles of size 2^k (overlaps allowed), where each maximal rectangle yields a prime implicant, and then dropping any implicant whose cells are all covered by others as redundant.
