A DNF representation of a predicate's negation can be read off a Karnaugh map by swapping the blank and filled entries and then grouping the result.
On a Karnaugh map a unique true point is a true point covered by a single rectangle, and the near false points for a given true point are the false points immediately adjacent to it.

Determination can be computed from a Karnaugh map by finding all pairs of adjacent cells where both the variable in question and the predicate change value, and for deriving RACC tests it does not matter whether the paired true points are unique.

Logic coverage applies to programs by deriving predicates from decision statements such as if, case/switch, for, while, and do-until, and when a predicate has only one clause all logic coverage criteria collapse to Predicate Coverage.

The vast majority of predicates in real programs have only one clause and programmers tend to write predicates with at most two or three clauses, so the higher-end criteria such as active clause coverage are most useful only as the number of clauses grows.

The primary complexity of applying logic coverage to programs lies in reachability rather than in the criteria: obtaining input values that reach the decision statement can be far harder than satisfying the requirement once there, and those reachability values are prefix values in the test case.

Because logic test requirements are expressed in program variables that may be internal or local while a test can only set program inputs, internal variables must be resolved as functions of the inputs, and this internal variable problem is formally undecidable.

The controllability problem of working backward from a decision to inputs that force an internal value is a major reason why program-level logic coverage criteria are usually limited to unit and module testing.

To control an internal variable, prefer setting program state so the real call returns the desired value rather than replacing the call with a direct assignment, because the direct-assignment hack requires recompiling before each test and means testing a different method than the one to be deployed.
Automated logic testing implicitly requires that the test team include programmers who understand the software well enough to write the calls needed to set program state for each test.

Predicate Coverage on programs is simply another formulation of the Edge Coverage criterion, so it is not necessary to draw a graph for the logic criteria, though the control flow graph can be used to find values for reachability.

Selection of values for don't-care inputs should be postponed until reachability is determined, because an input that is don't-care for the test requirement may need a specific value to reach the decision, and choosing too early can make reachability difficult or impossible.

Satisfying Clause Coverage with one all-true and one all-false test collapses Clause Coverage into Predicate Coverage, and under short-circuit evaluation it leaves some clauses never evaluated, so it is a poor way to satisfy CC.

Rewriting a program to eliminate multi-clause predicates in order to reduce ACC to branch testing is explicitly advised against, because the rewrite may have far more complicated control structure with repeated statements that endanger reliability and maintainability, and its tests may not be equivalent to ACC on the original.

Predicate Coverage on a program transformed to split a multi-clause predicate into branches does not subsume CACC, and CACC does not subsume that Predicate Coverage, so branch-splitting does not reliably reproduce ACC.

When a predicate contains the same clause twice and an intervening clause has a side effect that changes that clause's value, controlling the two values of the clause is a very difficult controllability problem for which neither the logic-testing nor the test-automation literature gives a clear answer.

The best remedy for a predicate with a side-effecting duplicated clause is social rather than technical: ask the programmer whether the construct is really intended, since the predicate can often be replaced with a simpler logically equivalent one.

Software specifications, formal or informal, almost invariably include logical expressions, so logic coverage criteria can be applied to them, and preconditions in particular are common and rich sources of predicates, as are postconditions and invariants.
A tester may develop the preconditions of a method specifically as part of the testing process when preconditions do not already exist.
condition: when preconditions are absent from the specification

statement: Transforming preconditions into exceptions is common practice for reasons including defensive programming and security.

For a predicate in disjunctive normal form, making each clause determine the predicate is simple: set every minor clause true and then make each other clause false in turn, so CACC, RACC, and GACC coincide for such predicates.

When satisfying Clause Coverage, some clauses are related and cannot be false at the same time (for example month cannot be both less than 1 and greater than 12), so a naive two-test all-true/all-false approach is not always achievable and extra tests are needed to make each clause false.

The most common way to apply logic coverage criteria to a finite state machine is to treat the logical expression on each transition (its trigger and guards) as a predicate and apply the logic criteria to it.

Guards on FSM transitions are conjuncts in effect even when they are not explicitly written as conjuncts, so they must be combined with the trigger using the AND operator when forming the transition predicate.

In the SCR specification language a triggering event means the resulting expression must explicitly change value, which implies both a before-value and an after-value and is modeled by introducing a new primed variable so the predicate has two parts.

The requirement that two events occur simultaneously, or the timing of near-simultaneous events, cannot be represented by the logical-expression mathematics used for logic coverage, so such events are merely ANDed together and the timing must be addressed as a real-time software problem.

Reachability for FSM logic tests requires prefix values to reach the transition's pre-state, usually found by a depth-first search path from an initial state with the transition predicates solved for inputs, and exit states similarly require postfix values.

When the initial state of an FSM cannot be controlled, a practical technique is to begin every test with a prefix of inputs that forces the system into a single known state regardless of which state it started in.

A major advantage of FSM-based testing is that the expected output is easy to determine: it is the transition's post-state for test values that make the transition predicate true and the pre-state for values that make it false, so the system should remain in the current state.
exception: when a false predicate coincidentally satisfies another transition (then the expected output is that transition's post-state) or when the transition is a self-loop

statement: Converting an FSM test's predicate variable assignments into executable inputs is the mapping problem, analogous to the internal variable problem, and it can range from a simple renaming to turning a single model-level input into long sequences of inputs or method calls, so no general solution exists.

Unique-cause MCDC corresponds to Restricted Active Clause Coverage and masking MCDC corresponds to Correlated Active Clause Coverage, and the FAA has come to accept masking MCDC, in which the minor clauses may differ between the two values of the major clause.

MCDC and the RACC criteria need at least n+1 tests and always fewer than 2n tests for a predicate with n clauses, and n+1 tests suffice when n is less than 4 because of overlap, with the number approaching 2n as n grows.

An empirical count of 400,811 predicates in 63 open-source Java programs found that about 88% had only one clause, roughly 10% had two clauses, and under 2% had three or more, confirming that most real-program predicates are single-clause.

Syntax-based testing uses a syntactic description such as a grammar or BNF directly as the model and creates tests from that syntax, and it is the source of test criteria that can require propagation, the fourth condition of the RIPR model.

Syntax structures can be used to generate either valid artifacts (correct syntax) or invalid artifacts (incorrect syntax), and the generated structures may serve as test cases themselves or as aids to designing test cases.
A grammar can be used as a recognizer that decides whether a given string is in the grammar or as a generator that derives strings of terminals to serve as test inputs.

Terminal Symbol Coverage requires a test requirement for each terminal symbol in the grammar, Production Coverage requires one for each production, and Production Coverage subsumes Terminal Symbol Coverage.
Terminal Symbol Coverage and Production Coverage can be rewritten to be equivalent to Node Coverage and Edge Coverage on the graph that represents the grammar.

Derivation Coverage requires every string derivable from the grammar, but the number of derivations is generally infinite (or astronomically large) so DC is impractical, warranting skepticism toward any claim of achieving full string or full path coverage.
A program's rejection of malformed inputs should be tested explicitly, because requiring a program to reject invalid inputs is easy for programmers to forget or get wrong.

In syntax-based testing a mutation operator is a rule specifying syntactic variations of strings generated from a grammar, a ground string is a string in the grammar, and a mutant is the result of one application of a mutation operator, producing either an invalid string or a valid string from a different derivation.

The design of the mutation operator set is critically important because a well-designed set produces powerful tests while a poorly designed set produces ineffective ones; for example a tool that only changes predicates to true and false is merely an expensive way to implement branch coverage.

Strong experimental and theoretical evidence indicates that in program-based mutation only one element should be mutated at a time (one mutation operator per mutant), the exception being occasionally useful subsuming higher-order mutants.
exception: when subsuming higher-order mutants are useful

statement: Program-based mutation usually applies every possible application of each mutation operator to the ground string, because program-based mutation subsumes several other test criteria and that subsumption is lost if the operators are not applied comprehensively.
exception: when the ground string does not matter, as in invalid-input testing

statement: A test kills a mutant m for a derivation D if and only if the output of the test on D differs from the output of the test on m, and Mutation Coverage requires exactly one requirement per mutant: to kill it.

The mutation score is the ratio of mutants killed to all mutants, and when a grammar is mutated to produce invalid strings the mutation operators themselves become the test requirements (Mutation Operator Coverage and Mutation Production Coverage).

Mutation usually yields more test requirements than any other coverage criterion, is hard to apply by hand and to automate, and is widely regarded as a high-end criterion that is more effective but more expensive, so it is often used as a gold standard for comparatively evaluating other test criteria.
Mutation operators have been designed for several programming languages, formal specification languages, BNF grammars, and at least one data definition language (XML).
The primary purpose of BNF grammar testing for languages has been to generate test sets for compilers.

Program-based mutation applies operators defined over a programming language's grammar to a ground-string program, and because the mutants must be compilable it creates valid strings that are not themselves tests but are used to help design tests.
A mutation-adequate test set is one that distinguishes the program under test from a set of its syntactic variations (mutants).

For most operator sets the number of program-based mutants is roughly proportional to the number of variable references times the number of declared variables, and selective mutation reduces this to being proportional to the number of variable references alone.

Mutation operators are designed to meet one of two goals: to mimic typical programmer mistakes (such as changing a relational operator or a variable reference) or to force the tester to create tests known to be effective (such as failOnZero forcing a zero value or a bomb operator forcing statement coverage).

Stillborn mutants, which are syntactically illegal and would be caught by the compiler, should either not be generated or be discarded immediately, and a trivial mutant is one that almost any test case kills.
An equivalent mutant always produces the same output as the original program, so no test case can kill it, and equivalent mutants therefore represent infeasible test requirements.

Detecting equivalent mutants, like detecting infeasible paths, is an undecidable problem in general, though strategies such as algebraic manipulation and program slicing can detect some equivalent mutants.

To strongly kill a mutant a test must satisfy reachability, infection, and propagation (the RIPR model), whereas weak mutation relaxes killing to only reachability and infection by checking the program's internal state immediately after the mutated component executes.

Strong mutation may require more tests to satisfy coverage than weak mutation because an incorrect internal state does not always propagate to the output, but experimentation has shown the difference is very small in most cases.
Tests that kill mutants can be found by intuition, or when more rigor is needed by analyzing the reachability, infection, and propagation conditions under which the mutant will be killed.

In the mutation analysis process a test case that does not strongly kill at least one mutant is considered ineffective and eliminated, even if it weakly kills mutants, because strong-kill coverage requires the output rather than the internal state to differ.

The mutation score is the ratio of dead mutants to the total number of non-equivalent mutants; a test set that kills all of them is adequate, but a score of 1.00 is usually impractical, so the tester sets a threshold as the minimum acceptable score and iterates test generation against live mutants until it is reached.
The fundamental premise of mutation testing is that if the software contains a fault, there will usually be a set of mutants that can only be killed by a test case that also detects that fault.

When designing mutation operators for a new language it is reasonable to start inclusive, but this yields many operators and even more mutants, so the two common ways to reduce mutants are randomly sampling from all mutants and using only particularly effective operators (selective mutation).
A set of mutation operators is effective if tests created specifically to kill its mutants also kill, with very high probability, the mutants created by all remaining mutation operators.
Researchers have concluded that a collection of mutation operators that insert unary operators and that modify unary and binary operators forms an effective operator set.

Mutation operators must be chosen per language and, though they overlap, differ according to language features; operators have been designed for many programming languages (Fortran, COBOL, C, Lisp, Ada, Java), the specification language SMV, and XML messages.

Mutation is widely considered the strongest coverage criterion for finding faults but also the most expensive; a mutation operator yields a criterion when its mutants can be killed only by tests satisfying that criterion's requirements, and if a criterion is yielded then mutation subsumes it.

Subsumption of other coverage criteria by mutation must be based on weak mutation rather than strong mutation, because mutation's global propagation requirement means a test set satisfying a criterion may fail to strongly kill the associated mutants, whereas weak mutation imposes only the local requirement and so preserves subsumption.

The statement-replacement 'bomb' operator yields Node Coverage by forcing each basic block to be reached, and the ROR operator that replaces a predicate with both true and false yields Edge Coverage by forcing both branches to be taken.

The ROR, COR, and LOR mutation operators together replace each clause in each predicate with both true and false, so they yield Clause Coverage; more generally the operator that replaces a clause with true and false yields clause coverage.

Mutation cannot subsume Combinatorial Coverage, because Combinatorial Coverage has 2^N requirements for a predicate with N clauses and no single or combination of mutation operators produces 2^N mutants.

Mutation subsumes General Active Clause Coverage because killing the clause-to-true and clause-to-false mutants requires the clause to determine the predicate, but mutation does not subsume Correlated or Restricted Active Clause Coverage because those require properties of pairs of tests while each mutant is killed by a single test.

Mutation subsumes All-defs data flow coverage via the statement-deletion operator, but this argument uniquely requires strong mutation, and while an operator to subsume all-uses is possible it has never been published or used in any tool; whether mutation subsumes the inactive clause coverage criteria is undetermined.

Integration testing tests the connections among separate program units such as classes, packages, and components, and it is where object-oriented features specifically inheritance, polymorphism, and dynamic binding are tested.

Faults in the integration between two components usually depend on a mismatch of assumptions (as when the Mars lander sent English units while the recipient assumed metric), and whether to fix the caller, the callee, or both depends on the design specification and pragmatic factors such as which is easier to change.

Integration (interface) mutation works by mutating the connections between components, with most mutants placed around method calls and both the calling and called method considered, mutating the values sent, the call itself, the values entering and leaving the callee, and the return statements.
Java's four access levels (private, package/default, protected, public) are poorly understood by many programmers and often not considered during design, making them a rich source of faults.

Object-oriented features such as method overriding, variable hiding, and explicit parent-constructor calls via super are powerful but are potential sources of error, and mutation operators are defined for them to verify the programmer is using them correctly.
A particular concern about the use of object-oriented language features is that many programmers learned them on the job without studying the rules for using them appropriately.

Overloading is the use of the same name for different methods or constructors in the same class distinguished by signature, and it is easily confused with overriding, which occurs between a class and one of its descendants.

A finite state machine can be described compactly by declaring variables with limited ranges (the state space being the Cartesian product of the ranges), limiting ranges to define initial states, and rules characterizing each transition's source and target, which is typically far smaller than the explicit graph.

Finite state descriptions capture system behavior at a high level suitable for communicating with the end user, which makes FSMs incredibly useful for the hardest part of testing, namely system testing.

The verification community has built powerful, highly automated FSM analysis tools that produce counterexamples for properties that do not hold, and because those counterexamples can be interpreted as test cases, test generation from finite state machines is easier to automate than from program source.

Mutating a state-machine description is much like mutating program source, and a test that kills an FSM mutant is a sequence of states allowed by the original machine's transition relation but not by the mutated machine.
Higher order mutants, in which more than one change is made at the same time, can be very helpful, primarily when the two changes interact but do not cancel each other out.

Finding a test to kill a mutant of an SMV finite state machine can be automated with a model checker, which takes a finite state machine and a temporal-logic property and returns a state sequence witnessing where the property fails.

For SMV finite state machines the equivalent-mutant problem is decidable, unlike for program code, because the model checker works in a finite domain, so if the model checker produces no counterexample the mutant is provably equivalent.

A grammar or regular expression can formally define a program's input space, and a regular-expression input description corresponds to a finite automaton to which the graph coverage criteria such as all-nodes and all-edges apply directly.

When only an informal description of the input syntax exists, the engineering task of formally describing that syntax is extremely valuable because it exposes ambiguities and omissions in the requirements and software, and it should be carried out early, before implementation and preferably before design.
XML schemas serve as grammars for XML messages, so the grammar coverage criteria such as Production Coverage can be used to derive XML messages that serve as test inputs.
A program's rejection of malformed inputs should definitely be tested as a form of stress testing, because it is the kind of thing that slips past programmers who are focused on the happy paths.

Invalid inputs matter in practice because unhandled invalid inputs often represent security vulnerabilities, such as buffer overflow attacks that supply input too long for the buffer or web attacks that supply malicious HTML, JavaScript, or SQL, so software should behave reasonably on invalid inputs.
When mutating input grammars the mutants are themselves the tests, both valid and invalid strings are created, and because no ground string is used the notion of killing mutants does not apply.

Grammar mutation operators include nonterminal replacement, terminal replacement, terminal-and-nonterminal deletion, and terminal-and-nonterminal duplication (the stutter operator), and some replacements are inappropriate and should be avoided based on the grammar's type or syntactic rules, analogous to avoiding compiler errors in program-based mutation.

Grammar mutation operators can be applied either by mutating the grammar and then generating inputs, or by applying one mutation to the production used during each derivation, and applying them during production is preferred because the resulting inputs stay closer to valid inputs.

Some strings produced by a mutated grammar rule are still valid ('equivalent'), so to generate invalid inputs exclusively they must be screened out by a recognizer built from the grammar, and unlike the program equivalence problem this one is solvable.

When a program is supposed to accept only a subset of a larger language, the tester has two grammars (the full language and the allowed subset), and tests that are valid in the full grammar but not in the subset are good tests because they can represent an attack.

XML schema constraining facets (such as fractionDigits, minInclusive, and minOccurs) restrict the range of datatype values, which suggests mutation operators that modify facet values to produce a rich collection of tests for software that consumes XML inputs.

There is significantly more experience with program-based mutation operators than with grammar-based mutation operators, so the list of grammar mutation operators should be treated as much less definitive.

The coupling effect holds that complex faults are coupled to simple faults in such a way that test data detecting all simple faults will detect most complex faults, and it has been supported empirically for programs and shown to hold probabilistically for large classes of programs.

The competent programmer hypothesis, on which mutation testing rests, assumes that programmers write programs close to correct, so faults are small syntactic deviations captured by mutants in the program's neighborhood.

Postponing testing to the end of development compromises it, because insufficient time and budget remain, earlier-stage problems have been solved by consuming testing resources, and there is no time to plan; quality cannot be tested in and must be built in from the beginning.

Testing should be integrated with development, beginning as soon as development begins and carried out in parallel with every lifecycle stage, so that faults can be detected and prevented throughout the software development process.

Projects that begin test activities only after implementation is complete often produce very unreliable software, whereas integrating testing into all parts of development makes dramatic improvements in the effectiveness and efficiency of testing.

Testing should not be isolated into separate stages but should run on a parallel track that affects all stages, with testing embedded within every aspect of development and testers embedded within all teams.

At most lifecycle stages testing activities fall into three categories: test actions (testing the artifacts created at that stage), test design (using that stage's artifacts to prepare to test the final software), and test influence (using artifacts to influence future development stages).

Each requirement should be evaluated to ensure it is correct, testable, and that the requirements together are complete, and this should be done before design starts, because developing test scenarios during requirements analysis often exposes ambiguous and inconsistent specifications.

During system and software design the tester should verify the mapping between the requirements specification and the design, keep specifications traceable and testable, and prepare acceptance and usability test plans as well as coverage criteria for later unit and integration testing.

Many problems in large software systems arise from component interface mismatches, so intermediate design should aim to avoid interface mismatches and decide the order in which components will be integrated and tested early, because that decision materially affects detailed design.

Integrating classes in whatever order they happen to pass unit testing is a convenient default but can create significantly more integration work (like maintenance debt), so it is better to decide the most efficient integration order ahead of time and have developers complete in that order.
Integration testing is concerned with finding errors that result from unexpected interactions among components.

System testing validates the software against its original functional and non-functional requirements, acceptance testing ensures the complete system satisfies the customers' needs and should involve the customer, and usability testing evaluates the user interface and should involve users.

When software is changed during operation and maintenance it must be regression tested to ensure it still possesses the functionality it had before the change as well as the new or modified functionality.

A key factor in instilling quality is professional ethics: put quality first, refuse to build what cannot be tested, begin test activities early, and resist shortcuts by documenting objections even at the cost of conflict.

Test artifacts (test design documents, tests, test results, and automated support) must be placed under version control, kept available and updated, and their criteria-based source tracked, so that when the source changes it is possible to identify which tests must change.

Putting too much focus on test-plan documentation can produce many meaningless reports while nothing useful is done, so a test plan should emphasize content (how and why the tests were created and how they will be run) rather than form.

The IEEE 829 standard defines two major test-plan types: a Master Test Plan that provides overall planning and management across multiple levels of test or projects, and a Level Test Plan that describes the scope, approach, resources, and schedule of testing at one particular level.

A Level Test Plan should include a test traceability matrix documenting the origin of each test (requirements, test coverage requirements, or design elements) so that testers and managers can look up why each test was included and what it tests.

A test plan should explicitly list both the features to be tested and the features not to be tested (explaining why not), and should define item pass/fail criteria and suspension/resumption criteria for when testing should stop and await fixes.

Developers want tests to become executable as early as possible so they benefit from immediate feedback on failures, which requires that all code compile, that tests cause no collateral damage, that the process be repeatable, and that it complete in a timely manner.

Integration testing is the testing of incompatibilities and interfaces between otherwise correctly working components and is emphatically not the same as testing an already integrated component, and it is often carried out on an incomplete system.

A component, broadly defined, is any piece of a program that can be tested independently of the complete program, including classes, modules, methods, packages, code fragments, and even non-executable artifacts such as XML files, XML schemas, and databases.

The class integration test order (CITO) problem is to integrate and test classes in the order that requires the least scaffolding, because creating test doubles is a major cost of integration testing.

If the dependency graph among classes has no cycles, integration order is a topological sort: classes that depend on no others are tested first, then classes that depend only on already-tested classes, and so on.
condition: when the dependency graph is acyclic

statement: When the dependency graph has cycles, the integration tester must break each cycle by choosing one class in it to test first, ideally the class that results in the least extra stubbing work.
condition: when the dependency graph contains cycles

statement: Although design textbooks strongly recommend against cycles in class diagrams, cycles commonly creep in as design progresses (for example to improve performance or maintainability), so practical testers still have to solve the CITO problem.

A test double is a software component that implements partial functionality and is used in place of the real component during testing, and it often helps solve problems of controllability or testability.

The four common reasons to use a test double are that a needed component is not yet implemented, that a component performs an unrecoverable action that must be avoided during test (such as sending email or executing a financial trade), that a component depends on an unreliable or unpredictable resource such as a network, and that a test would otherwise run too slowly (such as accessing an external database).

A test stub is a skeletal or special-purpose implementation of a component that replaces a called component, most basically by assigning constant values to its outputs, with more sophisticated returns coming from hand-crafted constants, table lookups, random values, or user entry.

A mock is a special-purpose class that includes behavior verification to check that the class under test made the correct calls to it, and mocking tools let the test engineer specify rather than program its limited behavior, which is a key enabler for interaction-based testing.

Interaction-based testing defines success by how objects communicate (whether an object was asked to do its job) rather than by what the objects do (state-based testing), and it is needed when the real action must not actually occur, such as verifying that a send call was made rather than actually sending an email.

The model for interaction-based unit testing is to obtain the necessary test doubles (possibly with a mocking tool), specify the expected sequence of interactions with them, carry out the action under test, and then verify that the expected interactions actually occurred.

Building a separate version of the system in which test doubles replace dependencies scales poorly and forces the test engineer to synchronize multiple versions that will eventually diverge, so instead there should be a way to efficiently switch the system's behavior from operational mode to test mode.

A seam is a variable defined so that a test can change the program's behavior without changing the component that contains it, and it requires an enabling point, a place where the variable can be set from outside the component such as from a JUnit test.

A setter method can provide a seam's enabling point so a test can inject a test double via dependency injection, whereas a static factory method is not an enabling point because the connection is too tight to change dynamically.

Making a seam variable public creates maintenance debt and a potential security hole, reflecting the general tension that information hiding aids design and maintenance but reduces controllability and hinders test automation, so restricting seam access to package-friendly with tests in the same package addresses the security concern.

Regression testing is the process of re-testing software that has been modified, and it constitutes the vast majority of testing effort in commercial software development and is an essential part of any viable process.
Small changes to one part of a system often cause problems in distant parts of the system, which is exactly what regression testing is used to find.
Regression tests must be automated, to the point that unautomated regression testing is equivalent to no regression testing, and it is often incorporated into a continuous integration service.

Choosing the regression test set is a Goldilocks problem: too large a set cannot be run as often as the software changes and disrupts development, while too small a set covers functionality poorly and passes too many faults to users.

Regression tests must finish in a timely manner (traditionally overnight, and much sooner for agile processes), and while it is worth spending extra computational resources to run them, at some point the marginal value of an added test is not worth the resources needed to execute it.

A good regression policy is that for each field problem report there exists a regression test that would detect that problem, because customers tolerate new problems better than the same problem repeatedly, and this supports traceability by giving each test a concrete rationale.

Coverage criteria provide an excellent basis for evaluating regression test sets; for example if method-call coverage shows some methods are never invoked, the team should either declare them dead code for that application or add a test that calls them.

When a regression test fails the first step is to determine whether the change to the software is faulty or the regression test set itself is broken, and even when no tests fail a test set adequate for one version is not necessarily adequate for a later version.

Corrective, perfective, adaptive, and preventive changes all require regression testing, and even when the external functionality is unchanged the regression test set must be re-analyzed for adequacy, because structure-derived tests may no longer cover an internally restructured implementation.

Adding a few tests to a regression set has small marginal cost but cumulatively makes the set unwieldy, while removing tests risks a field fault that a removed test would have caught; the same criteria that guide constructing a regression set apply to updating it.

A regression test can be safely omitted if its execution visits nothing that was modified, and regression-selection techniques are characterized by inclusiveness (including modification-revealing tests; unsafe if under 100%), precision (omitting non-revealing tests), efficiency, and generality.

A test oracle encodes the expected results of a test, and an automated test must encode that knowledge as an explicit check such as a JUnit assertion, rather than leaving the judgment to a human at run time.

A test oracle must strike a balance in revealability between checking too much (unnecessary cost) and checking too little (failing to reveal failures), and it must also solve observability problems to obtain values not readily available to the test script.
An oracle strategy is characterized by precision (how much of the output state is checked) and frequency (when and how often the output state is checked).

The null oracle strategy of only checking whether the software crashes or throws a runtime exception is extremely wasteful, because only about 25% to 56% of software failures result in a crash, so the remaining 44% to 75% of such tests are wasted.

A good test oracle checks the right outputs, those directly affected by the test's goal, whereas a poor oracle checks outputs that are unrelated or only peripherally related, such as the first element of a collection instead of the whole collection or an output value instead of the state reached.

Which outputs are affected depends on the testing level: at the unit level checking method return values and returned parameter values is almost always enough, and at the system level checking the directly visible output such as to the screen is usually sufficient.
exception: when the test's primary purpose is to evaluate something visible only in a file, database, or sensor, which must then be checked

statement: Low precision is acceptable for a test oracle: researchers have found that once the right outputs are checked, checking additional outputs increases revealability very little.

Low frequency is acceptable for a test oracle: the vast majority of failures are revealed if the final output state is checked once, and checking multiple times during execution increases revealability very little.

Automating direct verification of output against a specification is one of the best methods of checking program behavior, but writing output checkers can be hard and direct verification is often impossible because specifications are hard to write and rare, and sometimes the correct answer is unknown.

Redundant computation, comparing the program against a trustworthy gold version or a different algorithm, is a useful oracle alternative, but the two can share faults giving identical wrong outputs, and independent development is hard and unlikely to yield independent failures because some inputs are inherently harder and cause common failures above the independence rate.

In industry the redundant-computation oracle is most often implemented as regression testing, where the executable specification is simply the previous release of the software, and testing one implementation against another is an effective practical technique for the oracle problem.

Consistency checks verify output plausibility (for example a probability outside zero to one is wrong) and can be internal: checking invariant relations on internal structures, such as a container never holding duplicates, is an extremely effective way to find faults and can detect faults with only reachability and infection, without requiring propagation to the output.

Metamorphic testing evaluates correctness by relating a program's behavior on one input to its behavior on other inputs through a metamorphic relation; it is most powerful for well-behaved mathematical problems with identities and applicable wherever the input space has continuity so that nearby inputs should yield nearby outputs, and the relation need only sometimes detect a failure to be useful.
The test oracle problem has been summarized into four broad categories of approach: specified oracles, derived oracles, implicit oracles, and no test oracle.

Comprehensive empirical studies that defined ten test oracle strategies found the null oracle strategy very ineffective, high precision relatively unhelpful, and high frequency relatively unhelpful, and that work extended the RIP fault-and-failure model to RIPR by adding revealability.

Multiversion software works better for testing than for fault tolerance, because if two versions of a program behave differently on the same inputs then a good test has been found and at least one version is wrong, and regression testing can itself be viewed as a multiversion testing arrangement.

The key difference between program checking and metamorphic testing (or data diversity) is that program checking requires relationships between outputs strong enough to guarantee probable correctness, whereas metamorphic testing and data diversity remain useful even when the relationship between outputs is weaker.
When a specification S is under-determined, the correctness constraint is not that S(t) equals P(t) but that the program produces one of the allowed outputs, that is P(t) is a member of the set S(t).

Testing the business logic inside the system under test through its user interface is inadvisable, because even minor interface changes can make the tests fail even when the underlying behavior is unchanged.
Test automation built with commercial record-and-playback or robot-user tools tends to incur high test-maintenance cost because such tests fail for trivial reasons (the fragile test problem).

Fragile tests arise from four sensitivities: behavior sensitivity, interface sensitivity, data sensitivity, and context sensitivity, and these sensitivities exist regardless of the automation technology used.
Tests whose outcome depends on external context such as the system clock, devices, or other applications cannot be repeated deterministically unless the test gains control over that context.
exception: when the test gains control over the external context (clock, devices, other applications)

statement: A test fixture defined in terms of data already present in the system makes the test data-sensitive: if that data changes, the test may fail.
exception: when great effort has been expended to make the tests insensitive to the data used

statement: The core value of automated unit tests is that they pin down the existing functionality of the system under test so that it cannot be changed accidentally when new code is added.

Feedback about software is more valuable the sooner it arrives, so testing done only after the software is complete has greatly diminished value compared with testing that gives developers feedback earlier.
When practicing test-driven development, write the test and verify that it fails as expected before writing the production code that makes it pass.
condition: when practicing test-driven development

statement: Refactoring changes the design of code without changing its behavior, and it depends on the safety net of automated tests to prove that nothing was broken during the redesign.
When refactoring test code, prefer conservative safe refactorings that minimize the chance of changing the test's behavior, because there are no automated tests covering the test code itself.
A test with a large number of lines is an Obscure Test: the sheer number of lines makes the big picture of what the test verifies hard to see.
Replace an obtuse assertion such as assertTrue(false) or an if/else that ends in a failure with a direct call to fail() carrying a descriptive message.

Do not repeat assertions that verify fields already covered by another unit test (for example fields set by a constructor that has its own test), because the duplication just creates more test code to maintain when the logic changes.
Replace one-assertion-per-field result verification with a single assertion on an Expected Object that is constructed to look exactly like the expected result.

Avoid Conditional Test Logic (if statements) in a test because multiple paths make it unclear which path actually ran; replace an if/else-fail construct with a Guard Assertion that halts the test when the precondition is not met.
Extract verbose or repeated verification logic into an intent-revealing Custom Assertion to make the test shorter and to state explicitly what it is verifying.

Put cleanup in a finally block or the tearDown method so it runs whether the test passes or fails; because a failed assertion throws an exception handled by the framework, this avoids having to catch and rethrow.
Writing per-object teardown as deeply nested try/finally blocks is unworkable (a Complex Teardown): it can roughly double the length of the test and the teardown code is itself untestable.
Do not avoid teardown by switching to a Shared Fixture that is never torn down, because interactions through the shared fixture lead to Unrepeatable Test, Interacting Tests, and Mystery Guest smells.
Prefer a Fresh Fixture combined with automatic cleanup, such as an in-memory fixture that is garbage-collected, so you do not have to write teardown code for every test.
exception: when the created objects are persistent, for example saved in a database

statement: Construct the system architecture so that most tests can run without a database, while accepting that a few tests will still need one.
For persistent test objects, extend the Test Automation Framework so each created object is registered when created and then deleted automatically during teardown (Automated Teardown).
condition: when the objects created by the test are persistent

statement: Extract object construction in tests into Creation Methods; they encapsulate the SUT's construction API so that when a constructor changes you modify one place rather than every test.
Avoid Hard-Coded Test Data when the SUT persists the objects it creates and any field must be unique, because it can cause Unrepeatable Test, Interacting Test, or Test Run War.
condition: when the SUT persists created objects and one or more fields must be unique

statement: Generate a unique value on each test run and use it to seed the attributes of the objects the test creates, so the test creates different objects every time it runs.

Hide fixture values that do not affect the outcome inside Creation Methods and pass in only the values the SUT's expected behavior actually depends on, so the test makes clear which values matter to what is being verified.
Replace magic numbers in test code with symbolic constants that have role-describing names.
Show the derivation of an expected value in the test using an explaining variable rather than a bare literal, and if the value came from a reference system, state that in the test.
A library of Test Utility Methods forms a higher-level language for testing the application, after which writing additional tests becomes much simpler and faster.
Factor shared fixture setup into a setUp method only when many tests need the same fixture configuration; otherwise it is not worthwhile.
condition: when many tests need the same fixture configuration

statement: Writing tests before writing the software provides an agreed-upon definition of what success looks like.

For new development, first automate a suite of customer tests that verify the application's functionality, then augment them with unit tests that verify all code paths not already covered by the customer tests.
Use code coverage tools to discover which code is not being exercised, then retrofit unit tests to cover the untested code.
Organize unit tests and customer tests into separate test suites so that each set can be run independently of the other.
Unit tests should always pass before they are checked in, an idea captured by the phrase keep the bar green.
Ensure unit tests are run frequently by including them in the smoke tests that run as part of the integration build.

Keep unit tests for business logic minimally dependent on the database; doing test-driven development helps concentrate the business logic needing verification into well-defined objects that can be tested independently of the database.
Enumerate the customer tests before beginning development, whether or not they are automated, because doing so helps the development team understand what the customer really wants.
Recorded Tests tend to be Fragile Tests, so they are usually discarded once other tests have been developed that cover the same functionality.
Long tests are often Obscure Tests and tend to give poor Defect Localization when they fail partway through.
To keep tests simple, bypass the user interface by performing subcutaneous testing against one or more Service Facades that encapsulate the business logic.
Have each test set up its own starting point (a Fresh Fixture) each time it runs so that tests do not depend on anything they did not set up themselves, which avoids Interacting Tests.
Avoid a Shared Fixture unless it is an Immutable Shared Fixture, to avoid starting down the slippery slope to Erratic Tests.
exception: when the Shared Fixture is immutable

statement: When tests run too slowly because of database access or other slow components, replace those components with functionally equivalent Fake Objects to speed up the tests and encourage developers to run them more regularly.
Avoid Chained Tests wherever possible because they are the Interacting Tests smell in disguise.
Each unit test should be a Fully Automated Test that does a round-trip test against a class through its public interface.
Aim for Defect Localization by making each test a Single-Condition Test that exercises a single method or object in a single scenario.
Write each test so that each part of the Four-Phase Test (setup, exercise, verify, teardown) is easily recognizable, which enables using the tests as documentation.

Make tests self-checking by expressing the expected outcome as one or more Expected Objects and comparing them with the actual objects returned by the SUT using built-in equality assertions or Custom Assertions that implement test-specific equality.

Use a Test Stub to gain control of the SUT's indirect inputs when a code path cannot otherwise be executed, and use a Mock Object to intercept and verify the SUT's indirect outputs when its behavior is not observable through its public interface.
Adopt a Layered Architecture that separates business logic from the database and the user interface, so the business logic can be tested easily using subcutaneous tests or service-layer tests.
Do most or all testing using in-memory objects to minimize dependence on a database, which lets the runtime provide Garbage-Collected Teardown automatically and avoids Slow Tests caused by disk I/O.

Keep complex GUI logic out of the visual classes by using a Humble Dialog that delegates decision making to nonvisual classes, so the GUI logic can be unit-tested without instantiating the graphical objects or their framework.
condition: when building a GUI

statement: When a Testcase Class ends up with too many Test Methods, split it based either on the features verified (Testcase Class per Feature) or on the tests' fixture needs (Testcase Class per Fixture).
A test smell is a symptom of a problem, not necessarily its cause; a single smell may originate from any of several causes, and one cause may reveal itself through several smells.

Decide which test smells to eliminate by weighing cost against benefit, eradicating first the smells that cause the most grief; many smells can be avoided outright by choosing a sound test automation strategy and good coding standards.
When a project, behavior, or code smell appears, find the underlying root cause (for example with the Five Whys) instead of solving the symptom at one level without understanding what causes it.
Include every test in the AllTests suite used at check-in and by the automated build, because Lost Tests that exist but are not in the suite let bugs through.
Any one change to the SUT should break only a few tests; if many or most tests break from a single change, that is itself a sign of a test-design problem, not merely expected behavior sensitivity.

A Fragile Fixture, where a change to a commonly used test fixture breaks multiple existing tests, has poor test design as its root cause and discourages good coverage by raising the cost of extending the Standard Fixture.
Assertion Roulette makes it hard to determine how and why tests failed in the integration build because the failure log lacks enough information to identify which assertion failed.

Erratic Tests fail for no apparent reason even though neither the tests nor the production code was changed, and their many causes include Interacting Tests, Test Run Wars, and Unrepeatable Tests, most of which stem from using a Shared Fixture.

Interacting Tests arise when several tests use a Shared Fixture; they make it hard to run tests individually and can cause cascading failures where one test leaves the shared fixture in a state that fails many others.

Frequent Debugging is a sign that unit tests lack coverage or test too much functionality at once; good automated unit tests should make a debugger unnecessary in all but rare cases because the set of failing tests makes the cause obvious.
Eliminate Manual Intervention from tests, because tests that require it are run less frequently, which increases the cost of finding the defects introduced since the tests were last run.

Keep test suites fast: when tests take more than roughly 30 seconds to run, developers stop running them after every code change and wait for a logical break, which loses flow and delays defect feedback.
Treat a Shared Fixture as the solution of last resort for Slow Tests, because although it is the most frequently used fix it causes many behavior smells.
Tests should be simple, linear sequences of statements; when a test has multiple execution paths (Conditional Test Logic) you cannot be sure exactly how it will execute in a given case.

Hard-Coded Test Data makes tests harder to understand and, when the SUT includes a database, can cause Erratic Tests (when tests use the same database key) or Fragile Fixtures (when the values refer to database records that have changed).

Factor commonly used sequences of statements into reusable Test Utility Methods to cut Test Code Duplication, but reuse test logic rather than whole Test Methods, because reusing Test Methods produces Conditional Test Logic (Flexible Tests).

Keep test logic out of production code, because there is no way to ensure it will not run accidentally, it makes the production code larger and more complicated, and it may pull other components or libraries into the executable.
Keep each test as simple as possible so that it can easily be seen to be correct.
Write unit tests for any Test Utility Method to which the test methods delegate a complex algorithm, even though writing tests for the tests themselves is generally not practical.
The primary purpose of automated testing is to prevent (repel) bugs through regression coverage, not merely to find them.

Small unit tests that each verify a single behavior give Defect Localization: the failing test pinpoints the bug, so unit tests tell you why something broke whereas customer tests only tell you that something broke.
A customer test that fails while no unit test fails indicates a Missing Unit Test.

Keep test-specific hooks out of the production SUT: it is fine to design for testability, but any test-specific code should be plugged in by the test and exist only in the test environment, never remaining in the SUT in production.
Do not modify the SUT: be clear about which SUT you are testing and avoid replacing the parts you are actually testing with test-specific logic.
Replacing too much of the SUT with a Test Double is a common beginner mistake that gives false confidence that code is reliable because it was thoroughly tested when in fact it was not.

Tests that are easy to run must be Fully Automated (need no manual intervention), Self-Checking (detect and report errors without manual inspection), and Repeatable (same result every run), and ideally each should be an Independent Test runnable by itself.
A Self-Checking Test encodes within it everything needed to verify the expected outcome, so a clean run requires zero manual effort and the Test Runner reports only the tests that did not pass.

Because test code is optional and does not directly satisfy the customer, there is a strong temptation to abandon it when maintenance becomes hard; but giving up on keeping the bar green loses much of the value of the automated tests, so reduce test maintenance cost instead of abandoning tests.

Aim to make test automation pay for itself: the added cost of building and maintaining automated tests should be offset by savings from reduced manual testing, debugging, and remediation of defects that would otherwise surface late, so automation does not raise the total cost of development.

Make tests repeatable so they produce the same results every run without human intervention; unrepeatable or nondeterministic tests erode trust in the red bar until developers start ignoring it, which loses much of the value of the automated tests.

Tests that run only in memory using local variables or fields are usually repeatable with no extra effort, whereas Unrepeatable Tests usually arise from a Shared Fixture (including any persistence implemented in the SUT), which then requires the tests to be self-cleaning.

When test cleanup is necessary, prefer a generic Automated Teardown mechanism over hand-written per-test teardown code, because per-test teardown causes Erratic Tests when it is not implemented correctly in every test.
Keep tests simple enough to read quickly, because testing the tests themselves is impractical, so you must rely on reading them to catch any problems that creep in.

Minimize Test Overlap so that only a few tests are affected by any one change; contrary to popular opinion, having more tests pass through the same code does not improve quality if most of them do exactly the same thing.
Verify One Condition per Test: write a separate Test Method for each unique combination of pre-test state and input, each driving the SUT through a single code path.
exception: for customer tests that express real multi-step usage scenarios, which may legitimately be long

statement: Close the expressiveness gap by building a library of Test Utility Methods (such as Creation Methods and Custom Assertions) that form a domain-specific testing language, so testers can express concepts without translating them into much more detailed code.

Apply the DRY principle to test code as to production code by avoiding duplication within tests, while keeping the core test logic visible in each Test Method and moving only supporting code into Test Utility Methods where it is changed in one place.

Separate concerns in tests: keep test code out of production code and have each test focus on a single concern; do not test business logic and the user interface in the same test, because a change to either concern would force all such tests to change.

Write robust tests by minimizing overlap between tests and isolating the SUT from its environment, so that ideally only one kind of change forces any given test to require maintenance; encapsulate fixture setup and teardown behind Test Utility Methods to reduce the tests directly affected by a change.

Write the tests first so the design of the system is inherently testable; retrofitting automated tests onto finished or legacy code is much harder and unlikely to succeed without modifying the production code, even when the system was designed for testability.

Writing the tests first and writing only enough code to make them pass tends to produce more minimalist production code: optional functionality and unnecessary error-handling are not written, and only the methods the tests need are provided.

Writing tests first makes it natural to substitute dependencies with Test Doubles because substitutable dependency is designed in from the start, and can avoid smells like Sensitive Equality by asserting on the correct object attributes rather than on string representations.
Test-driven development interleaves writing tests and code in fine-grained increments (test a bit, code a bit), rather than writing all tests before any code.
A reasonable compromise is to identify all of a task's unit tests up front (possibly as empty Test Method skeletons) but code only a single Test Method body at a time.
For customer tests, prepare all the tests for a single story before beginning development of that story, rather than feeding the tests to the developer one by one.

Design software outside-in by thinking first about black-box customer tests for the whole system and then about unit tests for each piece, which forces you to think like the client before thinking like a developer.

When coding outside-in, use Test Stubs to stand in for software not yet written and to inject impossible indirect inputs (specific return values, out-parameters, or exceptions) so you can verify the SUT handles those cases correctly.
Keeping Test Doubles in tests after the real subordinate classes have been built provides better Defect Localization at the cost of potentially higher test maintenance.

Behavior verification specifies the calls the SUT makes to its dependencies (its indirect outputs, using Mock Objects or Test Spies) and tests a unit better in isolation but can make refactoring more difficult, whereas state verification only checks the SUT's end state.
Prefer custom-designing a Minimal Fixture for each Test Method instead of designing one big fixture upfront, an approach most consistent with using a Fresh Fixture.
Apply the test automation principles to both unit tests and storytests, deviating only when fully aware of the consequences.
exception: Verify One Condition per Test may not be practical for customer tests that exercise more involved chunks of functionality

statement: Write the tests first, because the unit tests save debugging effort that often offsets the cost of automating them, and writing tests first forces the code to be designed for testability without treating testability as a separate design condition.
Design for testability, which is especially important for anyone who does not write tests first because automated tests cannot be added after the fact if testability was not designed in.
Use the front door first: using Back Door Manipulation to set up the fixture or verify the outcome of a test produces Overcoupled Software that needs more frequent test maintenance.
Do not overuse Behavior Verification and Mock Objects, because it results in Overspecified Software with more brittle tests that may discourage developers from doing desirable refactorings.

When choices are equally effective, prefer round-trip tests that exercise the SUT through its public interface and use State Verification, escalating to layer-crossing tests with Behavior Verification only when that is not sufficient to describe the expected behavior.
When a slow or unavailable depended-on component must be replaced with a Test Double, prefer a Fake Object because it encodes the fewest assumptions into the test.
condition: when a slow or unavailable depended-on component must be replaced

statement: Communicate intent in tests: because a test is read by the test maintainer, tests with a lot of code or Conditional Test Logic become Obscure Tests that cost more to own; call Test Utility Methods with intent-revealing names so it is readily apparent how the fixture influences each test's expected outcome.

Do not modify the SUT: putting in Test Hooks, overriding behavior in a Test-Specific Subclass, or replacing a depended-on component with a Test Double is dangerous because you may no longer be testing the code you plan to put into production.

Test the software in a configuration truly representative of how it will run in production; if you must replace something the SUT depends on to control its context, do so in a representative way and never replace the very part you are trying to test.

The SUT is relative to the tests being written: when X depends on Y which depends on Z, you may replace Y and Z with Test Doubles to test X, but you cannot replace Z with a Test Double when Z itself is what you are testing.

When using a Test-Specific Subclass, override only the methods the test specifically needs to null out or use to inject indirect inputs, and if you reuse a subclass created for another test ensure it does not override any behavior the current test is verifying.
A Test Method longer than about ten lines is getting to be too much.

Keep tests independent, because interdependent or order-dependent tests fail in groups (Interacting Tests) so you cannot tell which code is actually at fault, depriving you of the feedback that individual test failures provide.

An Independent Test can be run by itself and sets up its own Fresh Fixture; tests that build a Fresh Fixture are much more likely to be independent than tests that use a Shared Fixture, which can cause Lonely Tests, Interacting Tests, and Test Run Wars.

Isolate the SUT from software whose behavior you cannot control, because otherwise your tests may fail when that other software changes (Context Sensitivity) and you cannot verify behavior for all its possible return values; instead inject all possible reactions of the depended-on component under the complete control of your tests.

Design the software so that each depended-on component can be replaced with a Test Double using Dependency Injection or Dependency Lookup, or overridden with a Test-Specific Subclass, giving the tests control of the SUT's indirect inputs and making the tests more repeatable and robust.
Choosing which tests to write is an exercise in risk management, because proving that all of an application's functionality works correctly in all possible combinations is nearly impossible.

Structure tests so that as few tests as possible depend on any one piece of functionality, and cover each test condition by exactly one test, no more and no less, because tests that verify the same functionality fail together and need the same maintenance without improving quality.

Minimize the amount of untestable code (such as GUI components, multithreaded code, and Test Methods), because code without Fully Automated Tests is unprotected against bugs and is more dangerous to refactor or modify.

Refactor untestable code by moving the logic you want to test out of the class that causes the lack of testability: use a Humble Executable for active or multithreaded objects, a Humble Dialog for user-interface objects, and extract a Test Method's untestable logic into Test Utility Methods that can be tested.

Keep test logic out of production code: it should contain no conditional statements of the 'if testing then' kind and no test logic, because a system that behaves differently under test cannot be trusted to work in production and the test hooks could cause the software to fail in production.

Do not combine the verification of two test conditions in one Test Method by reusing one condition's end state as the next condition's starting state, because when one assertion fails the rest of the test does not execute, which makes Defect Localization harder.

Each scripted test should verify a single test condition; when several tests need the same fixture, either move them into a single Testcase Class per Fixture using Implicit Setup or call Test Utility Methods using Delegated Setup.

Structure each test as four distinct phases executed in sequence (fixture setup, exercise SUT, result verification, fixture teardown), with a single exercise phase and a single verification phase, avoiding alternating exercise/verify/exercise/verify sequences that would verify several distinct conditions.

Do not be dogmatic about literally one assertion per test: verifying one condition does not require a single assertion; extract a Custom Assertion or Verification Method to reduce multiple assertions to one call when it makes the test more readable, but not when it does not.

Test each concern separately, because testing several concerns in one Test Method breaks the test whenever any of those concerns is modified, hides which concern is at fault (forcing manual debugging), and makes it harder to refactor the eager class into separate single-concern classes.

Ensure commensurate effort and responsibility: writing or modifying a test should take no more effort, and require no more tool expertise, than implementing the corresponding functionality; for example, verify metadata-configured behavior with a Data-Driven Test rather than by writing code.

A test-automation decision is strategic if it is hard to change, affecting so many tests that many or all would need to be converted to a different approach at once; make such decisions consciously and just in time, avoiding both big design upfront and deciding too late.

The choice of test automation tool is a strategic decision, because once you have invested time in learning a tool and automating many tests with it, switching to a different tool becomes much harder.
Recorded Test tools typically record actions at the user-interface-element level of granularity, which results in Fragile Tests.

Performance, response-time, capacity, and stress tests generally must be automated because human testers cannot create enough load to verify behavior under stress, but the xUnit framework is not particularly well suited to automating performance tests.

Start running cross-functional tests such as performance tests early, as soon as the key architecture components are roughed in and the functional skeleton is executable, and run the same tests continuously throughout the project as new features are added.

Usability tests and exploratory testing cannot be meaningfully automated because they require subjective human assessment or hypothesis-forming; automated tests can at most set up the SUT in preparation for them.

The stop-on-first-failure behavior of xUnit assertions is a tool philosophy, not a property of unit tests; unit-test writers generally prefer it, whereas longer customer tests may need per-step pass/fail reporting such as Fit's color coding.
Treat the need to change xUnit's fundamental behavior for a use case as a trigger to consider whether some other tool would be a better fit.

The xUnit sweet spot is a large set of small tests, each requiring a small fixture that is easy to set up, testing single classes or small groups of classes in isolation through their APIs, with a Fresh Fixture (a new Minimal Fixture per test).

For customer tests, define a Higher-Level Language that raises the level of abstraction toward the business concepts customers understand, from which converting the tests to Data-Driven Tests is a small step.

The test fixture management strategy is strategic because it strongly affects test execution time and robustness, and the cost of a wrong choice is not felt until there are hundreds of tests (Slow Tests) or several months of development have passed (High Test Maintenance Cost), by which point changing it is expensive.

Set up the fixture through the front door by calling the appropriate methods on the SUT most of the time, using Back Door Setup (inserting records directly into a depended-on component) mainly with databases or when using a Mock Object or Test Double.

Test fixtures fall into three strategies: Transient Fresh Fixture (lives in memory and disappears after the test), Persistent Fresh Fixture (persists beyond the test and needs explicit per-test teardown), and Shared Fixture (persistent and reused across many tests, needing construction and teardown triggering and prone to Interacting Tests).

A Transient Fresh Fixture makes each test completely independent because the fixture's visibility is restricted to that one test, so the test cannot depend, accidentally or on purpose, on the output of any other test.

The main disadvantage of a Fresh Fixture is the additional CPU cycles needed to create all the objects for each test, so the tests may run more slowly than under a Shared Fixture, especially with a Persistent Fresh Fixture.

When a component is tightly coupled to a database, prefer making the database a substitutable dependency rather than adopting a Persistent Fresh Fixture, and use a Persistent Fresh Fixture only when substitution is impractical, as with legacy software.

Address Slow Tests caused by a Persistent Fresh Fixture by constructing a Minimal Fixture, replacing the provider of any slow-to-set-up data with a Test Double, and using an Immutable Shared Fixture for objects that are referenced but not modified.

Replacing the entire database with a Fake Database backed by hash tables, injected via Dependency Injection or Dependency Lookup, made the author's project teams' tests run on average about 50 times faster (about 2 percent as long).

Minimize the size and complexity of the test fixture, because a Minimal Fixture is easier to understand and highlights the cause-effect relationship between the fixture and the expected outcome, making it a major enabler of Tests as Documentation.
Use Entity Chain Snipping (a Test Stub) to eliminate the need to instantiate objects on which a test depends only indirectly, which makes the fixture smaller and speeds up its instantiation.

A Shared Fixture saves setup and teardown time but risks a Stale Fixture and Interacting Tests; most of its benefits can instead be obtained by applying other patterns to Fresh Fixtures, since a Standard Fixture avoids per-test fixture design without actually sharing the fixture.
The more tests that share a fixture and the less often it is reconstructed, the longer the effects of a corrupted fixture persist, so limit how widely a fixture is shared and reconstruct it often.

Avoid Unrepeatable Tests and Test Run Wars by setting up a Shared Fixture each time the test suite is run using Lazy Setup, Suite Fixture Setup, or Setup Decorator; Suite Fixture Setup and Setup Decorator also tear the fixture down when the run finishes, whereas Lazy Setup does not.
When using Chained Tests, have each test use Guard Assertions to verify that its pre-conditions have been met, so that the cascading failures that follow a failed predecessor are easier to diagnose.
Retrofitting unit tests onto an existing or legacy application is the hardest and least productive kind of test automation, so do not make it your first attempt at automated unit testing.

Big-design-upfront design for testability is hard because it is difficult to know in advance what control points and observation points the tests will need, so you risk building testability mechanisms that are insufficient or unnecessary.

With test-driven testability, writing the test first defines the control points and observation points the SUT must provide, so once the tests pass you know you have a testable design without designing for testability as a separate step.

Any control points provided strictly for tests (for example ones that bypass input validation or short-circuit the normal lifecycle of the SUT or an object it depends on) must not be used by the production code.

A round-trip test interacts with the SUT only through its public interface and does not violate encapsulation, whereas a layer-crossing test watches the back door using a Test Spy or Mock Object, which is powerful for verifying architectural requirements but produces Overspecified Software if overused.

To write layer-crossing tests, build in a substitutable dependency mechanism for the components the SUT depends on, using Dependency Injection, Dependency Lookup (such as an Object Factory or Service Locator), or an inversion-of-control framework, falling back to a Test-Specific Subclass.

Treat the Test Hook as the solution of last resort, acceptable only as a temporary measure to act as a safety net while refactoring to retrofit testability, because continued use of Test Hooks results in Test Logic in Production.

Avoid asynchronous tests that interact with the SUT through real messaging with wait-based synchronization in unit and component tests, because waiting for message responses that might never arrive can make them very slow; instead use a Humble Executable to move the message-handling logic into a class that can be tested synchronously.
You can turn almost any Hard-to-Test Code into easily tested code through refactoring, as long as you have enough tests in place first to ensure you do not introduce bugs during the refactoring.

Avoid the user interface for customer tests by writing Subcutaneous Tests that bypass the UI and exercise the business logic through a Service Facade exposing synchronous interaction points, which lets you verify the business logic even before the UI is hooked up.

A layered architecture lets you test the UI logic before the business logic is finished by replacing the Service Facade with a Test Double that provides deterministic behavior, and that Test Double should be independent of the real implementation so the UI tests need only know which data evokes which behavior.
The key test-automation-strategy decision is which test-to-SUT interaction styles to use and which to avoid, and then ensuring the software is designed to support that decision.
Automate Hand-Scripted Tests in the same programming language as the SUT, because the tests then have easy access to the SUT's API and require less effort to learn.

The most common test types are the Simple Success Test (verifies correct behavior with valid inputs), the Expected Exception Test (verifies the SUT raises an exception when used incorrectly), and the Constructor Test (verifies the constructor builds new objects correctly).

Organize tests into a hierarchy of Suites of Suites (a class's suite into its package's suite into the whole system's suite) so developers can run subsets of varying completeness and run all tests with a single command before committing changes to the repository.
A single test failure does not prevent the remaining tests from being run, in keeping with the principle Keep Tests Independent.

Do not catch all errors raised by the SUT in order to convert them into test failures; it is unnecessary, and a test error's stack trace usually pinpoints the problem code in the SUT better than a test failure's stack trace, which only shows where the failed assertion was made.

Use Guard Assertions (such as assertNotNull on a returned object reference before accessing its fields) to avoid executing Test Method code that would raise a test error from within the test itself, since this is a normal part of verifying the expected outcome and preserves useful diagnostic tracebacks.
Prefer automatic Test Method Discovery over manual Test Enumeration, because implementing the suite method by hand takes more effort and is more likely to lead to Lost Tests.

Testing procedural (non-object-oriented) code is possible but makes Self-Checking Tests more labor-intensive and reusable Test Runners harder to build; one option is to encode the tests as data for a single Data-Driven Test interpreter, which moves test writing to end users and suits customer tests.
