How you set up a Fresh Fixture affects how much effort it takes to write and maintain the tests and whether you achieve Tests as Documentation.
In a Fresh Fixture strategy each test builds a brand-new fixture before exercising the SUT and rebuilds it every time it is rerun, which completely avoids the problems of Interacting Tests.

Build a Fresh Fixture using In-line Setup (all fixture logic inside the Test Method), Delegated Setup (calling Test Utility Methods), Implicit Setup (a setUp method the framework calls), or a combination of these approaches.

In-line Setup tends to cause Test Code Duplication because every Test Method must construct the SUT, which leads to High Test Maintenance Cost via Fragile Tests, to Obscure Tests when setup is complex, and to Hard-Coded Test Data; move the fixture setup out of the Test Method to prevent these smells.

Refactor duplicated fixture setup out of Test Methods into Creation Methods; Creation Methods with intent-revealing names make the test's pre-conditions apparent, remove duplication, and let both reader and author focus on what is created rather than how it is created.
Use Creation Methods to eliminate every test's need to know how the objects it requires are created, which helps prevent Fragile Tests caused by changes to constructor method signatures or semantics.

When a test does not care about an object's identity, use an Anonymous Creation Method that generates unique keys with a Distinct Generated Value, which guarantees no other test uses the same object and prevents Unrepeatable Tests, Interacting Tests, and Test Run Wars even against a shared persistent repository.

When a test cares only about certain attributes of a created object, use a Parameterized Anonymous Creation Method that takes those outcome-relevant attributes and defaults the rest, because what is not important to be seen in the test method should not be seen in it.

For input-validation tests, use the One Bad Attribute technique: create a valid object with a Creation Method and then replace a single attribute with an invalid value the SUT should reject, instead of hand-building many nearly-invalid objects.

Reuse a test for fixture setup only if the reader can readily identify what the other test sets up; because few tests are named to convey this, wrap the called test in a Creation Method with an intent-revealing name.

Implicit Setup (putting all fixture creation in the setUp method) removes Test Code Duplication but makes tests harder to understand, because within the Test Method you cannot see how the pre-conditions correlate with the expected outcome and must look in setUp.
When using Implicit Setup, name the Testcase Class after the fixture created in the setUp method, but only when all of the Test Methods genuinely need the same fixture (Testcase Class per Fixture).

With Implicit Setup, hold fixture objects in instance variables rather than local variables or class variables so the fixture is newly constructed for each test, and give the instance variables intent-revealing names.
Do not feel obligated to use the setUp method just because it is provided; it is only one of several code-reuse mechanisms available and is as prone to overuse as inheritance once was.

The setUp method is most misused when it builds a General Fixture with multiple distinct parts each dedicated to a different Test Method, which causes Slow Tests with a persistent fixture and Obscure Tests by hiding the cause-effect relationship between the fixture and the expected outcome.

If you use the setUp method but do not group Test Methods by identical fixture, build only the lowest-common-denominator part of the fixture in setUp and keep it a Minimal Fixture rather than a General Fixture.

A General Fixture causes Slow Tests and Obscure Tests and often evolves into a Fragile Fixture as the relationships between its elements and the tests that use them are forgotten over time, so that changes made for a new test break existing tests.

Holding a fixture object in a class variable crosses into a Persistent Fresh Fixture, and using Lazy Setup to populate it crosses into a Shared Fixture, where later tests in the suite reuse objects created by earlier tests and become dependent on them.

Combine fixture-setup styles where useful (for example, call Creation Methods from within a Test Method or from setUp), because Creation Methods can be unit-tested much more easily than in-line fixture construction logic or the setUp method.

Tearing down a Transient Fresh Fixture takes almost no effort in garbage-collected languages: as long as the references to the fixture are held in variables that go out of scope, Garbage-Collected Teardown cleans it up.

In a Fresh Fixture strategy each run of each Test Method uses a newly created fixture that is not reused; 'fresh' means not reused, not necessarily transient, so a Fresh Fixture can be persistent as long as it is torn down after each test.

A fixture becomes persistent either because the SUT is stateful (holding state in a database or in class variables) or because the Testcase Class holds a reference to an otherwise transient fixture in a way that makes it survive across Test Method invocations.

Avoid Unrepeatable Tests caused by a rerun recreating an already-existing persistent fixture (such as a unique-key violation or a duplicate filename) either by tearing the fixture down at the end of each test or by using Distinct Generated Values for any identifiers that might conflict.

Fixture teardown code is pure housekeeping that does not help understand the SUT and can obscure the test's intent, so the best teardown code is none: prefer Garbage-Collected Teardown and avoid writing teardown code whenever you can.

Naive in-line teardown at the end of a Test Method will not run when the test fails or errors, because the assertion throws an exception before the teardown; wrap the exception-prone code in a try/finally so the teardown always executes.

Prefer Implicit Teardown, where the framework calls a tearDown method after every Test Method regardless of pass or fail; it keeps error-handling out of the Test Method but requires the fixture to be held in instance, class, or global variables and the tearDown to work correctly for every Test Method's fixture.

Because teardown code need not be visible to the test reader, choose the setup organization you want and pair it with the equivalent or a more hidden teardown: Implicit Teardown works even with In-line or Delegated Setup, whereas In-line Teardown is not recommended except with In-line Setup.

Build an Automated Teardown mechanism from a well-tested loop that deletes a list of objects and catches errors, a per-object-kind dispatch mechanism, and a registration mechanism; register objects from Creation Methods and clean up in a Testcase Superclass tearDown, and optionally extend it to delete SUT-created objects via an observable Object Factory.

For fixtures built entirely in a relational database, use Table Truncation Teardown only when each Test Runner has its own Database Sandbox, or Transaction Rollback Teardown when the SUT uses a Humble Transaction Controller so the test controls the commit, and implement both via Implicit Teardown to keep teardown logic out of the Test Methods.

Teardown is needed for three reasons — leftover objects slow tests, alter the SUT's behavior or assertion results, or block creating a Fresh Fixture — addressed respectively by periodic cleansing, by Delta Assertions (snapshot the fixture before and verify the expected differences after exercising the SUT), and by giving each run's fixture objects totally unique identifiers, including the user ID when the fixture is shared beyond a single Test Runner.

Avoid fixture persistence entirely where possible: when the SUT causes it, replace the persistence mechanism with a Test Double such as a Fake Database the test can wipe out at will; when the test causes it, use a less-persistent fixture reference.

Tests that access a database typically run 50 to 100 times slower than in-memory tests, largely because setting up and tearing down the fixture takes many more disk accesses than the SUT's own fixture access; switching to a Shared Fixture is at best about 10 times slower and sacrifices test independence, so prefer replacing the disk-based database with an In-Memory Database or Fake Database, a choice best made early in the project.

Do not use Hard-Coded Values in database lookups to access Shared Fixture objects, because it couples the tests to the fixture implementation and documents poorly (an Obscure Test); use Finder Methods with intent-revealing names that return references to the existing fixture objects.

When sharing a fixture across many Testcase Classes, avoid having one class own the fixture-holding variable that others reference, because it creates unnecessary coupling; instead move the declaration to a Test Fixture Registry that exposes parts of the fixture via variables or Finder Methods.

Lazy Setup builds a Shared Fixture the first time any test needs it, but because there is no signal that the last test in a suite has run you cannot tear it down after each run, which can cause Unrepeatable Tests as the fixture survives across test runs.

Suite Fixture Setup (a setUp that runs once per Testcase Class with a corresponding tearDown after the last Test Method) guarantees a fresh fixture is built for each test run and prevents Unrepeatable Tests, but it does not prevent Interacting Tests within the run.

A Setup Decorator brackets a test suite's run with fixture setup and teardown so the fixture can be shared beyond a single Testcase Class, but its biggest drawback is that tests depending on the decorator cannot be run by themselves, making them Lonely Tests.

A Prebuilt Fixture built before the tests run (for example via database scripts or by copying a golden database) offers the most construction options but requires a Manual Intervention before each run if any tests are Unrepeatable, so it is often combined with a Fresh Fixture to form an Immutable Shared Fixture.

Do not put assertions after the fixture setup phase to check that the fixture was set up correctly, because it almost always contributes to Obscure Tests; write unit tests for the Test Utility Methods instead, except that with a Shared Fixture a Guard Assertion that documents and checks the fixture is worthwhile.
exception: when using a Shared Fixture, a Guard Assertion documenting and checking the fixture is worthwhile

statement: There are two ways to verify the SUT's behavior: State Verification, which asserts on the post-exercise state of the affected objects, and Behavior Verification, which observes the method calls the SUT makes to its depended-on components; State Verification is the simpler and Behavior Verification builds on it.
State Verification inspects only the SUT's direct outputs through direct method calls and does not instrument the SUT in any way to detect how it interacts with other components of the system.

Prefer describing the expected state as an Expected Object compared with a single Equality Assertion over Procedural State Verification (a sequence of field-by-field assertions), because the Expected Object minimizes Test Code Duplication and increases test clarity.

Prioritize assertions first for coverage (the more you verify, the finer the safety net and the higher your confidence) and second for documentation value, so that each test reads as: when the system is in state S1 and I do X, the result is R and the system is in state S2.

Almost always include an Assertion Message on each assertion, to avoid Assertion Roulette (being unable to tell which assertion failed without running the test interactively) and to make integration-build failures easier to reproduce and to troubleshoot.

For Stated Outcome Assertions such as assertTrue, use an Argument-Describing Message that incorporates the argument values, because such assertions' default failure messages (for example 'Assertion failed') are unhelpful.

When a Shared Fixture causes Interacting Tests because each test keeps adding rows, use Delta Assertions: take a snapshot of the relevant tables at the start of the test and verify only the expected differences after exercising the SUT, refactoring the extra complexity into Custom Assertions or Verification Methods.

External result verification using files and an external comparison program suits regression-testing an application that has not changed much, but it usually produces a Mystery Guest because the expected results are not visible inside the test; mitigate by having the test write the expected file, which is practical only when the data is small (another argument for a Minimal Fixture).

For Procedural Behavior Verification, configure the SUT to use a Test Spy (or a Self Shunt) in place of the depended-on component, then after exercising the SUT retrieve the recording of its behavior and verify it with assertions.

For Expected Behavior Specification, configure a Mock Object with the method calls you expect the SUT to make and install it before exercising the SUT, an approach typically used with layer-crossing tests to verify indirect outputs.

Test Code Duplication is harmful when it leads to Fragile Test, Fragile Fixture, or High Test Maintenance Cost by coupling too many tests to the Standard Fixture or the SUT's API, or when it is a symptom of an Obscure Test; reduce repeated verification assertions using Expected Objects, Custom Assertions, or Verification Methods.

Replace many field-by-field Equality Assertions with a single Equality Assertion that compares whole objects (an Expected Object), which works as long as the equals method compares only the fields of interest and you are able to create the Expected Object.

When you need test-specific equality, cannot construct the Expected Object, or the SUT's equals compares identity rather than equality, implement either a Custom Assertion or a test-specific equals on the Expected Object's class, which may be a Data Transfer Object or a Test-Specific Subclass that overrides only equals.

Be pragmatic about relying on the SUT's equals method in assertions: use it when reasonable, otherwise define a Custom Assertion or a test-specific Expected Object, and consider how hard it would be to change strategy if the equals method later changes.

A Custom Assertion is a domain-specific assertion you write that hides the verification procedure behind a declarative name, making the result-verification logic intent-revealing, preventing Obscure Tests, and making the assertion logic itself unit-testable.

Create Custom Assertions either by refactoring existing complex test code (Extract Method on the repeated assertions, giving an intent-revealing name and an Assertion Message) or by coding calls to not-yet-existing Assertion Methods as you write tests and filling in the bodies later; either way defining a set of Custom Assertions is the first step toward a Higher-Level Language for specifying tests.

Use an outcome-describing Verification Method when a group of tests share identical exercise and verify sections that differ only in setup: Extract Method the common code into a meaningfully named method for less code, more understandable tests, and testable verification logic; unlike a Custom Assertion, a Verification Method also interacts with the SUT and may take arbitrary parameters.

When the fixture-setup logic is the same but uses different data, extract the common setup, exercise, and verify phases into a Parameterized Test method, then define simple Test Methods that call it and pass in the data that makes each test unique.

A Data-Driven Test is a generic Test Method the framework runs directly that reads its arguments from a test-data file; it is a Parameterized Test turned inside out, with the data file acting as a Higher-Level testing language and the test method as its interpreter.

Avoid Conditional Test Logic, because a test with branches may execute differently in different circumstances and its Test Method code is Untestable Test Code that can be verified only by manually breaking the SUT to trigger the error.

Reuse test logic by extracting utility methods, never by reusing a whole Test Method across different cases, because reusing the Test Method itself merges several tests into one and produces Conditional Test Logic (Flexible Tests).

Do not put verification loops in a Test Method, because the looping code is Untestable Test Code, obscures the test's real intent, and its complexity may discourage developers from writing the Self-Checking Test; delegate the logic to an intent-revealing Test Utility Method that can itself be tested and reused.

Write tests backward by writing the assertions first on suitably named local variables and then filling in the code needed to execute them, because declaring and initializing a variable only after it has been used forces better understanding of it and yields better names, avoiding meaningless names like invoice1 and invoice2.

Work outside-in by keeping the Test Method at a consistent level of abstraction focused on what must be in place to induce the SUT's behavior, delegating the mechanics of setup and verification to lower-layer Test Utility Methods, and stub a not-yet-written utility with a call to fail() as a placeholder reminder.

Use test-driven development to write Test Utility Methods, starting from the simplest case and working up only to the most complicated case the Test Methods actually require, because TDD finds the minimal implementation rather than an unnecessary generic solution; add Guard Assertions to fail tests for cases the method does not support.

Put reusable verification logic (Custom Assertions or Verification Methods) in the Testcase Class, and pull it up to a Testcase Superclass or move it into a Test Helper when it needs to be reused more broadly.

Testing a class together with all its dependencies makes it hard to cover all code paths, because the depended-on component may return values or throw exceptions that are difficult or impossible to induce, may deliver unpredictable indirect inputs such as the system clock or calendar, or may be unavailable or nonexistent in the test environment.

Test the SUT paths that handle a depended-on component's return values and exceptions rather than leaving them as Untested Code, because those paths are the hardest to exercise yet the most likely to cause catastrophic failures if first run in production; force the component to return each value and throw each exception.

Verify the SUT's indirect outputs — the side-effect calls it makes to a depended-on component that are not visible on its own interface, such as logging messages — using an observation point, to avoid Untested Requirements.
To control the SUT's indirect inputs, provide a control point that can make the depended-on component return every possible return value, updatable-argument value, or exception.

Where possible, use the real component as the control or observation point, for example Back Door Setup (inserting database values so the component returns the desired results) or Back Door Verification (querying the file system, database, or email component, or using triggers and notifications to learn how it was used).

Replace the real component with a Test Double when it cannot be manipulated to produce the desired indirect input or output, when doing so is not cost-effective or would have unacceptable side effects, or when the real component is not yet available.

To inject indirect inputs, configure a Test Stub with the set of values to return and install it in place of the depended-on component, so the stub becomes the control point that forces the SUT through all of its code paths.

There are two styles of indirect-output verification: Procedural Behavior Verification, where a Test Spy records the SUT's calls during execution and the test retrieves and asserts them afterward, and Expected Behavior, where a Mock Object loaded with the expected calls during fixture setup compares the actual calls as the SUT runs.

A Mock Object fails the test immediately when it receives an unexpected call, and the failure traceback pinpoints the exact location in the SUT because the assertion is made from the Mock Object, which is in turn called by the SUT.

The four kinds of Test Double are the Dummy Object (a placeholder passed to the SUT but never used), the Test Stub (controls indirect inputs, with a Test Spy being a more capable stub that also captures indirect outputs), the Mock Object (verifies indirect outputs), and the Fake Object (an alternative working implementation of the depended-on component).

A Dummy Object is passed around from method to method but never used (often null, or a type-compatible object in statically-typed languages), and is not the same as a Null Object, which is actually used by the SUT but designed to do nothing.

A Test Stub acts as a control point delivering indirect inputs to the SUT to exercise otherwise-unreachable code paths: a Responder injects valid or invalid inputs via normal method returns, and a Saboteur raises exceptions or errors to inject abnormal indirect inputs.
A Test Spy adds to a Test Stub the ability to quietly record all calls the SUT makes to it, which the test then checks afterward using Procedural Behavior Verification.

A Mock Object compares actual calls against previously-defined expectations and fails the test itself, unlike a Test Spy, so its indirect-output verification logic is reused across all tests that use the same Mock Object.

Mock Objects come in two flavors: a strict Mock Object fails the test when the correct calls are received in a different order than specified, and a lenient Mock Object tolerates out-of-order calls and sometimes ignores unexpected or missed calls.

A Fake Object replaces the real depended-on component with a simpler alternative implementation of the same functionality, used not to verify indirect inputs or outputs but because the real component is not yet built, is too slow, or is unavailable in the test environment.

Provide a Test Double either hand-built (coded by the test automater, tending to be hard-coded but able to be made configurable) or dynamically generated at runtime by a framework or toolkit, which is always configurable.
In statically-typed languages, define base classes called Pseudo-Objects so that each Test Stub, Test Spy, or Mock Object need implement only the methods it expects to be called.

A Hard-Coded Test Double receives its return and expected values at design time, whereas a Configurable Test Double is told them at runtime by the test; a Test Stub or Test Spy needs only the return values, while a Mock Object also needs the expected method names and arguments.

Prefer Configurable Test Doubles, because they are reusable across many tests and make tests more understandable by keeping the double's return or expected values visible within the test, avoiding a Mystery Guest.
Treat the installation of a Test Double as part of fixture setup, using In-line Setup, Implicit Setup, or Delegated Setup.

Install a Test Double via Dependency Injection (the client tells the SUT which depended-on component to use), Dependency Lookup (the SUT delegates constructing or finding the component to another object), or a Test Hook (modifying the component or the calls to it in the SUT); an inversion-of-control framework removes the need to build the injection or lookup mechanism yourself.

Dependency Injection decouples the SUT from the depended-on component so the SUT knows only a generic interface, which makes the design more easily tested and the SUT more reusable; its flavors are Setter Injection, Constructor Injection, and Parameter Injection.

Use Dependency Lookup when the software is not designed for testability or Dependency Injection is not appropriate: the SUT asks a well-known Object Factory or Service Locator to create or find the depended-on component, and the test configures that intermediary to return a Test Double.

When no injection or lookup mechanism is built in, retrofit testability with a Test-Specific Subclass of the SUT to add one or to override methods with test-specific behavior; this requires the SUT to make self-calls to nonprivate, small single-purpose methods, and carries the risk of accidentally overriding the behavior under test.

Subclassing the depended-on component rather than the SUT to insert test-specific behavior is safer because it avoids accidentally overriding the SUT parts under test, but you must still get the SUT to use the subclass via Dependency Injection, Dependency Lookup, or a Substitutable Singleton.

Avoid Singletons in code you need to test: a Singleton used as an Object Factory or Service Locator with hard-coded behavior must be made a Substitutable Singleton to override, and Singletons used for other purposes almost always cause test headaches, so prefer an inversion-of-control tool or a manually coded Dependency Injection mechanism, which also make the test's dependency on a Test Double more obvious.

Test Hooks are a legitimate transition strategy for getting legacy code under test when other techniques are too hard or dangerous, providing a safety net during large-scale refactoring, and should ideally be removed once the code has been made more testable.

When standard injection and lookup are unavailable, place legacy code under test using object seams (such as replacing a depended-on library with a test-specific one) or aspect-oriented programming (a test point-cut that redirects the SUT's call to a Test Double without deploying the AOP code to production).

Endoscopic testing passes a Mock Object into the method under test to verify internal behaviors of the SUT not visible from outside, and a failing internal mock assertion surfaces the full internal call stack in the failure report.

In need-driven development, define the SUT's dependencies as the tests are written and build and test the software outside-in layer by layer starting from the outermost layer, combining test-driven development with incremental design and removing speculation about how a depended-on class will be used.

Replace a complex network of hard-to-create objects with a single Test Double to speed up Fresh Fixture setup (Entity Chain Snipping), and replace a slow component such as a relational database with an in-memory Fake Object to cut test execution time by an order of magnitude, since the extra coding cost is more than offset by faster feedback and more frequent runs.

Because many tests replace a real depended-on component with a Test Double, write a substitutable-initialization test (a form of Constructor Test) to verify that the real component is installed properly, triggered by the first test that replaces the component with a Test Double.

Avoid overusing Test Doubles, especially Mock Objects and Test Stubs, because it produces Overspecified Software that encodes implementation-specific design details into the tests, making the design much harder to change since many tests break when the design changes.
The basic unit of test-code organization is the Test Method, and how tests are organized becomes a critical factor in keeping them easy to find and understand once you have hundreds of them.

A test that verifies too many test conditions is an Eager Test, a code smell; verify one condition per test so that a single test executes a single repeatable code path and a failure localizes the defect, accepting that full coverage needs as many test methods as there are code paths.

Use the 'While We're at It' compromise to leverage an already-set-up fixture for a few extra checks and assertions, clearly marking them with comments so they can be easily deleted if a change to the SUT obsoletes that part of the test.

Choose a Testcase Class organization by circumstance: Testcase Class per Class as a default that you split as it grows, Testcase Class per Feature to keep all of a feature's conditions together at the cost of duplicated fixture setup, or Testcase Class per Fixture to group tests needing the same fixture, which enables Implicit Setup but scatters a feature's conditions.

Use Testcase Class per Fixture when unit-testing stateful objects that must be tested in each state, and Testcase Class per Feature for customer tests against a Service Facade or when using a Prebuilt Fixture; when each test needs a slightly different fixture, use Testcase Class per Feature with Delegated Setup.

Name tests systematically so the combined package, Testcase Class, and Test Method names convey the SUT class, the method or feature exercised, the important input characteristics, the relevant SUT and dependency state, and (via a 'should' prefix) the expected outputs and post-exercise state, so that test coverage can be read from an IDE outline view.

Create an AllTests Test Suite Factory per package and Named Test Suites or Subset Suites for collections you want to run together (for example tests that do or do not need the database or the web server), composing AllTests as a Suite of Suites so tests added to a subset also run in AllTests without extra maintenance effort.

To run a single test, prefer selecting it in a Test Tree Explorer or applying an Ignore attribute over commenting out or renaming the other Test Methods, which risk creating Lost Tests; alternatively define a Single Test Suite.

Do not reuse a whole Test Method in different circumstances such as with different fixtures, because that produces a Flexible Test; achieve most test reuse through Implicit Setup or Test Utility Methods, and ensure the reuse does not compromise the value of Tests as Documentation.

When creating Testcase Superclasses for shared utility methods, keep the root superclass from depending directly on SUT types scattered across packages to avoid a cyclic dependency graph; alternatively use a Test Helper per domain package so a Testcase Class can simply use the appropriate helpers rather than inheriting a single superclass.

Store Testcase Classes in the source code repository alongside the production code; the key constraints are to keep test logic out of production code while still being able to find the corresponding test for each piece of code or functionality.

Built-in self-tests, which embed the tests in the production code, are a poor option for organizations that want to keep test logic out of production, especially in memory-constrained environments where test code should not take up space.

In Java, store tests in the same logical package but a parallel source tree to avoid the problem of tests not being able to see package-protected methods on the SUT, and use a build-time test stripper to exclude test packages from production builds.
Eliminate any Test Dependency in Production, where the production code needs the tests present to run, because even a test stripper cannot remove tests that the production code depends on.

When there is any way to test without a database, test without the database, because tests that require a database run on average about two orders of magnitude (roughly 100 times) slower than the same tests run without one.
Give each developer and tester their own Database Sandbox to isolate them from production and from each other, because sharing a single Database Sandbox among developers is false economy.

Databases are a prime source of test smells: their persistence causes Unrepeatable Tests and Interacting Tests, sharing the fixture causes Lonely Tests, Chained Tests, and Test Run Wars, and databases tend to evolve into a large General Fixture that appears as a Mystery Guest in every test.

Test business logic without the database using Layer Tests that replace the data access layer with a Test Double, or, if the architecture is not sufficiently layered, using a Fake Database or an In-Memory Database that both run at in-memory speed, with a Fake Database better ensuring test independence because it is created fresh as a Transient Fresh Fixture.

Replacing the database with a Test Double works well when the database is used only as a data repository; vendor-specific functionality such as sequence-number generation or stored procedures requires encapsulating all database interaction within the data access layer and providing test-specific implementations (a Test Stub) for the vendor-specific parts.

Provide vendor-specific in-memory database functionality via a Strategy object that defaults to a null object doing nothing in production and providing the functionality when run in memory, which also makes switching to a different database vendor easier later.

Still test the database itself but keep the number of slow database tests to the bare minimum and focused, unit-testing the logic of any stored procedures and testing the data access layer's functionality, writing stored-procedure tests either as Remote Stored Procedure Tests in your normal unit-test language or as In-Database Stored Procedure Tests in the stored-procedure language that run inside the database.

Data access layer tests can mostly be round-trip tests, but include a few layer-crossing tests (using a database testing extension such as DbUnit to insert data for read tests or verify post-test contents for create, update, and delete tests) to ensure information is put into the correct columns.

Keep the fixture from persisting during data-access-layer testing with Transaction Rollback Teardown: build the data access layer as a Humble Transaction Controller so its read and write code never commits a transaction, letting the test roll back all the changes the SUT made.

Even after layering the system so most tests run without the database, run at least a representative sample of customer tests against the real database (Subcutaneous Tests usually suffice) to confirm the SUT behaves the same with and without the database: as few database tests as possible, but no fewer.

Test difficulty increases roughly in the order simple entity objects, stateless service objects, stateful service objects, hard-to-test code (user-interface, database, multithreaded), object-oriented legacy code, and non-object-oriented legacy code; because retrofitting tests onto legacy code is the hardest, do not start learning test automation there.

Learn and build tests in a maturity order: exercise the happy path, verify its direct outputs, verify alternative paths, verify indirect-output behavior, and then optimize test execution and maintainability.

Exercise a SUT's alternative code paths by varying the arguments passed in, varying the SUT's prior state, or varying the results returned by the components it depends on using a Test Stub, using a Responder for success paths and a Saboteur for error paths.

Replacing a real depended-on component with a Test Stub also makes tests more robust and repeatable by substituting a possibly-nondeterministic component with one that is completely deterministic and under test control, an application of the Isolate the SUT principle.

To speed up slow tests, prefer replacing a depended-on component with a functionally-equivalent but faster Fake Object over reusing the fixture through a Shared Fixture, which typically brings its own problems.

Reduce the risk of false negatives (tests that pass when they should not) by encapsulating complex test logic in Test Utility Methods with intent-revealing names and verifying the behavior of nontrivial Test Utility Methods with Test Utility Tests.

Tests serve two often-contradictory purposes, acting as documentation of how the SUT should behave and as a self-verifying executable specification, and the level of detail needed for executability can make a test so verbose that it becomes hard to understand.

An Obscure Test raises maintenance cost, precludes Tests as Documentation, and can hide test-coding errors that become Buggy Tests, and it can be caused by either too much or too little information in the Test Method.

The root cause of an Obscure Test is a lack of attention to keeping test code clean; test code is just as important as production code and needs refactoring just as often, and a 'just do it in-line' mentality is a major contributor.

A Mystery Guest, where fixture setup or result verification depends on data not visible within the test, prevents Tests as Documentation and risks Resource Optimism (someone deleting the external resource); fix it with a Fresh Fixture built via In-line Setup so the data is visible (hiding construction behind evocatively-named Creation Methods), or with Finder Methods and clearly-named resource files if a Shared Fixture or external file is unavoidable.

A General Fixture, a fixture larger than a test needs that arises from a Standard Fixture, Implicit Setup, or a Shared Fixture serving diverse tests, obscures the cause-effect relationship and causes Fragile Fixture and Slow Tests; fix it by moving to a Minimal Fixture with a Fresh Fixture per test, or Make Resource Unique to create a virtual Database Sandbox per test if a Shared Fixture is required.
Irrelevant Information, where a test exposes many details about the fixture that do not affect the SUT's behavior, distracts the test reader from what really determines the outcome.

Remove Irrelevant Information from fixture setup by replacing direct constructor or Factory Method calls with Parameterized Creation Methods that take only the relevant parameters, defaulting the values that do not affect the outcome inside the Creation Methods or replacing them with Dummy Objects, so the reader knows the values they do not see do not affect the expected outcome.

Hide Irrelevant Information in result verification by asserting on entire Expected Objects rather than on individual fields and by creating Custom Assertions that hide complex procedural verification logic.

Hard-Coded Test Data obscures the cause-effect between inputs and expected outputs and, with a Shared Fixture, causes collisions; replace literals with named constants, default the values that do not matter inside Creation Methods, replace verification values that derive from inputs with Derived Values, and use Distinct Generated Values (Anonymous Creation Methods) for fields that serve as unique keys under a Shared Fixture.

Indirect Testing, where the test interacts with the SUT via another object (for example testing business logic through the presentation layer), cannot test everything that could break, is unclear, and causes Fragile Tests when the intermediate objects change; its root cause is software that was not designed for testability.

Fix Indirect Testing by improving the SUT's design for testability, for example an Extract Testable Component refactoring that moves the logic into an easily-tested object and leaves behind a Humble Object; when you cannot refactor, encapsulate the forced complexity behind named Test Utility Methods, Creation Methods, and Verification Methods (SUT API Encapsulation).

Writing tests outside-in, by first outlining the Four-Phase Test with calls to not-yet-existing Test Utility Methods and then implementing those methods, minimizes the likelihood of producing an Obscure Test that later needs refactoring and clarifies what the utility methods must do.

Test Methods must be simple enough that they do not themselves need tests, because the recursion of testing the tests has to stop somewhere; Conditional Test Logic is a factor that makes tests more complicated than they should be.

View any control structure (if, loop, or switch) within a Test Method with extreme suspicion, because multiple execution paths mean you cannot be sure what the test does, make it nondeterministic and hard to debug, and make it more likely to become a Buggy Test.

Conditional Test Logic is introduced for several reasons: if statements steering execution to a fail or skipping code when the SUT returns invalid data, loops verifying collections, conditional verification of complex or polymorphic objects, conditional building of the fixture or Expected Object to reuse one test across cases (Flexible Test), and if statements to avoid tearing down nonexistent fixture objects (Complex Teardown).

A Flexible Test, which verifies different functionality depending on when or where it runs (for example building the expected result from the current time), is caused by a lack of control over the environment; fix it by decoupling the SUT from the dependencies via a substitutable dependency and a Test Double, then write a separate test for each circumstance.

Replace if statements that steer execution to a fail with a Guard Assertion (except in an Expected Exception Test, which should use the standard idiom), replace conditional verification of complex objects with an Equality Assertion on an Expected Object or a Custom Assertion for test-specific equality, and move any verification loops into a Custom Assertion verified by Custom Assertion Tests.

Production Logic in Test, where the test replicates the SUT's expected-value calculation (often in nested loops over input combinations), results from trying to verify many conditions in one Test Method; instead enumerate sets of precalculated input and expected values rather than computing the expected values inside the test.

Complex Teardown, where many persistent resources are torn down in nested try/finally blocks within one Test Method, is likely to leave the environment corrupted and cause data leaks that make later tests fail; avoid it with Implicit Teardown or Automated Teardown, or eliminate teardown entirely by using a Fresh Fixture and Test Doubles instead of persistent objects.

Multiple Test Conditions, applying the same logic to many input sets in one Test Method, is the most innocuous Conditional Test Logic but stops at the first failure and loses Defect Localization; address readability by extracting a Parameterized Test from the loop, restore Defect Localization by calling it from a separate Test Method per condition, and use a Data-Driven Test for large sets of values.

Automated testing delivers its benefit of fast development on a large code base only if most of the code is protected by Fully Automated Tests, so make the tests easy to write; Hard-to-Test Code is a factor that makes it difficult to write complete, correct automated tests cost-efficiently.

Break the coupling to test Highly Coupled Code, which cannot run in isolation; this happens naturally with test-driven development, and the common decoupling technique is a Test Double such as a Test Stub or Mock Object.

Test asynchronous code by separating the logic from the asynchronous access mechanism, for example using a Humble Object (Humble Dialog or Humble Executable) to restructure the code so it can be tested synchronously, because asynchronous tests add complexity and run much more slowly.

Remove the need to test a Test Method's body by keeping the method extremely simple and relocating any Conditional Test Logic from it into Test Utility Methods, for which you can easily write Self-Checking Tests.

Cut-and-paste code reuse creates many copies of the same test code that must be maintained in parallel whenever the SUT's method semantics change, greatly raising the cost of new functionality; fix it with an Extract Method refactoring into a Test Utility Method that is then generalized (Creation or Finder Methods for setup, Custom Assertions or Verification Methods for verification), using Introduce Parameter to turn literals into parameters.

Avoid most Test Code Duplication by writing Test Methods outside-in and focused on intent: whenever something takes several lines, call a not-yet-existing Test Utility Method to do it, write all the tests this way, and then fill in the utility method implementations.

Reinventing the Wheel, accidentally writing the same sequence of statements in different tests, is caused by a lack of awareness of which Test Utility Methods already exist; the fix is a process one, looking around for existing utilities before writing new code.

Avoid Test Logic in Production, because a system that behaves one way in the test lab and a different way in production is a recipe for disaster and a Test Hook of the form 'if testing then' can accidentally run in production.

Instead of putting test logic in production code, move it into a substitutable dependency: put production-only code in a Strategy object installed by default and replaced by a Null Object in tests, and put test-only code in a Strategy that defaults to a Null Object and is replaced by a test-specific version, verifying the initialization with a Constructor Test.

For-Tests-Only code (methods or attributes used only by tests) makes the SUT more complex and can confuse clients with methods they should not use; expose the needed private information via a Test-Specific Subclass, or, if the extra methods cannot be moved there, label them clearly with a convention such as an FTO_ name prefix.

Eliminate any Test Dependency in Production, where production code cannot build or run without test code present, by managing inter-module dependencies so that no production code depends on test code even for type definitions, putting anything required by both into a production module accessible to both.

Do not implement test-specific equality in the SUT's equals method (Equality Pollution), because it can break the equals logic required by business rules; instead use a Custom Assertion for test-specific equality, a Comparator with dynamic Mock Object tools, or an equals method on a Test-Specific Subclass of the Expected Object.

Break up an Eager Test that verifies too much into a suite of Single-Condition Tests using Extract Method or by cloning the test per condition and removing irrelevant code, extracting fixture setup into Creation Methods; for long customer tests, use Back Door Setup to create the fixture for a later part independently so one test can be split into two, improving Defect Localization.

Include at least a minimal Assertion Message whenever a test has more than one call to the same kind of Assertion Method, to avoid Assertion Roulette where you cannot tell which assertion failed, which is especially important when using a Command-Line Test Runner not integrated with the editor.

Test boundary conditions, such as what happens when a number exceeds the maximum value that can be stored, so that an overflow or similar exception does not occur for the very first time in production (as illustrated by the Ariane 5 overflow failure).

Do not remove a failing Erratic Test to keep the bar green, because that is an intentional Lost Test and a known failure obscures other failures, since a red bar looks the same whether one or two tests are failing.

Interacting Tests arise from a Shared Fixture where anything that outlives a test causes interaction, so avoid static variables, Singletons, and Registries in both the SUT and the Test Automation Framework, and if you must use them, reinitialize their static variables at the start of each test.

Do not depend on the order of test execution, because most xUnit variants make no ordering guarantee; use a Fresh Fixture, which almost always solves Interacting Tests, or if you must share use an Immutable Shared Fixture that recreates from scratch the parts it intends to modify.
Regularly run the whole test suite in a different order, such as reverse order, to detect tests that accidentally depend on one another.

For an unsatisfied cross-test fixture dependency, use Lazy Setup in both tests so the first to run creates the shared objects (placing the setup in a Creation Method, or a Test Helper if the tests are on different Testcase Classes), and use Automated Teardown for collisions caused by objects that were not cleaned up.

A test that passes in its own suite but fails inside a Suite of Suites has Interacting Test Suites, usually because two suites create the same resource; note the clash may be between the Suite Fixture Setup or Setup Decorators of several classes rather than between the Test Methods, and more than one pair may be interacting.

A Lonely Test runs as part of a suite but cannot run by itself because it depends on a Shared Fixture created by another test or by suite-level setup; fix it by converting it to a Fresh Fixture or adding Lazy Setup so it can run alone.

Resource Leakage, where the tests or the SUT allocate finite resources without freeing them, makes tests progressively slower and then start to fail; fix a leaking SUT as a real bug and a leaking test with Guaranteed In-line Teardown or Automated Teardown, and set all resource pool sizes to 1 so leaks surface much sooner.

Fix Resource Optimism, where a test that depends on an external resource passes in one environment and fails in another, by creating the resource in the test's own fixture setup as a Fresh Fixture (using relative file addressing), or store the required external resources in the source code repository so all Test Runners run in the same environment.

An Unrepeatable Test behaves differently on its first run versus later runs because a fixture outlasts the test run (a Shared Fixture, a Lazy-Setup class variable, or a Prebuilt Fixture); fix it with a Fresh Fixture where no shared resource outlasts a single test, a Fake Database, Distinct Generated Values for all database keys, or Automated Teardown.

A Test Run War, where test failures occur at random when several people run tests simultaneously against a globally Shared Fixture (most likely near a deadline), is best fixed with a Fresh Fixture or by giving each Test Runner its own Database Sandbox, or an Immutable Shared Fixture; Automated Teardown may reduce but not eliminate it.

Nondeterministic Tests, which fail at random even with a single Test Runner, are caused by using different values each run for inputs the SUT treats differently (such as random integers near boundaries or random strings of varying length) or by Conditional Test Logic; random values decrease your understanding of coverage and violate the Repeatable Test principle.

Fix Nondeterministic Tests by making them execute completely linearly (removing Conditional Test Logic) and replacing random values with deterministic ones, and if coverage suffers add tests for the boundary values of the equivalence classes, extracting a Parameterized Test or a Data-Driven Test if that produces Test Code Duplication.

A Fragile Test fails to compile or run when the SUT is changed in ways that do not affect the part the test exercises, which raises maintenance cost and is especially damaging under highly incremental agile delivery; diagnose it by asking what the broken tests have in common to reveal how they are coupled to the SUT and then minimize that coupling.

Diagnose the four sensitivities in order: a failure to compile (or a runtime type error) indicates Interface Sensitivity; running with incorrect results that disappear when recent code is backed out indicates Behavior Sensitivity; still failing with the code backed out plus a Shared Fixture or changed setup indicates Data Sensitivity, otherwise Context Sensitivity.

For Interface Sensitivity of an internal-only API, use SUT API Encapsulation — a Higher-Level test language of Creation Methods and Verification Methods that hide the SUT's API so only the encapsulation layer changes when the API changes; for external, anonymous clients put the interface under strict change control with backward-compatible changes and deprecation before removal.

For Behavior Sensitivity, encapsulate assumptions about the SUT's behavior used during fixture setup behind Creation Methods and assumptions about its post-test state behind Custom Assertions or Verification Methods to reduce the test code that must change; and if the changed code is not part of the SUT under test, you are testing too large a SUT (Context Sensitivity) and should separate the SUT from the components it depends on.

Data Sensitivity, where a test fails because the test database's data has been modified, means the verification logic looks for data that no longer exists or accidentally includes newly added records, or the SUT is exercised with inputs referencing missing or modified data; fix it by checking the exercised logic's preconditions and removing unreasonable data assumptions from the verification logic.

The best fix for Data Sensitivity is a Fresh Fixture that makes tests independent of the database's existing contents; failing that, use a Database Partitioning Scheme so one test's data does not overlap another's, or Delta Assertions that compare before-and-after snapshots and ignore unchanged data.

Context Sensitivity, where a test consistently fails after the SUT's context (the time or date, or a depended-on system) changes, often stems from confusion about which SUT you are verifying, because failing to isolate the specific unit tests too much software at once; fix it by controlling all the SUT's inputs with a Test Stub for other systems and a Virtual Clock that lets the test set the time or date and simulate its passage.

Overspecified Software, a test that says too much about how the software is structured or behaves through extensive use of Mock Objects in layer-crossing tests, passes only when the software is implemented in a particular way; avoid it by applying Use the Front Door First wherever possible to keep implementation knowledge out of the tests.

Do not verify objects by converting them to strings and comparing against an expected string (Sensitive Equality), because it makes the test sensitive to behavior it is not in the business of verifying.

Frequent Debugging, where most test failures require a debugger, is caused by a lack of Defect Localization: missing detailed unit tests that would pinpoint a logic error inside a class, or missing component tests that would catch an integration error between classes, which is common when Mock Objects do not match the real behavior of the depended-on objects.

Avoid Frequent Debugging with storytest-driven test-driven development — writing unit tests for individual classes and component tests for clusters of related classes to get good Defect Localization — and by running the tests after every small change so you remember what you just changed.
When manual testing reveals a bug that no automated test caught, write a test that exposes it and use that failing test to do test-driven bug fixing.

Manual Intervention, where a test needs a person to act each run, makes tests run rarely — leading to Frequent Debugging and High Test Maintenance Cost — and makes a fully automated integration build and regression process impractical.

Fix Manual Fixture Setup by writing Fully Automated Tests, opening test-specific APIs to set up the fixture and, where the software cannot run in the development environment, refactoring to decouple the SUT from the otherwise-manual steps.

Fix Manual Result Verification by making tests self-checking with Assertion Method calls inside the Test Method, because tests that are not self-checking give a false sense of security by failing only when an error or exception is thrown.

Fix Manual Event Injection, where an event is hard to generate under program control (such as unplugging a cable, dropping a database connection, or clicking a button), by testing without the manual action: pass a simulated event object for asynchronous events, or replace part of the SUT with a Test Stub that simulates the circumstance for synchronous ones.

Do not reach for a Shared Fixture as the first reaction to Slow Tests, because it almost always causes Erratic Tests; instead replace slow components with a Fake Object, and only if you must share make the fixture immutable.

Diagnose Slow Tests by running subsets to see which run slowly, or build a mini-profiler by logging each test's start and end time in the Testcase Superclass setUp and tearDown, importing the log into a spreadsheet and sorting by duration to focus effort on the longest-running tests.

A General Fixture built fresh for each test is slow because it contains many more objects than a Minimal Fixture and that cost is multiplied by the number of tests; do not fix it by sharing (which causes Erratic Tests unless the fixture is immutable) but by reducing the amount of fixture each test builds.

Asynchronous Tests with explicit sleep delays slow the suite badly (a dozen two-second delays take about half a minute versus hundreds of normal tests per second); avoid asynchronicity by testing the logic synchronously via an Extract Testable Component refactoring to a Humble Executable.

When there are Too Many Tests to run every time, you need not run them all always: run a Subset Suite with a representative cross-section before every commit and schedule the rest to run less often (a build pipeline), and for a large system break it into independent subsystems each with its own tests plus a few essential end-to-end tests kept out of the pre-commit suite.

Buggy Tests give dangerous false negatives (false security) or false positives (which discredit the tests like crying wolf); their root causes are Fragile Test, Obscure Test, or Hard-to-Test Code smells, fixed by removing sensitivities with Test Doubles and refactoring, refactoring tests toward Tests as Documentation, and improving testability, plus addressing project-level causes such as giving developers time to learn, to refactor legacy code, and to write tests first.

Developers Not Writing Tests puts the system into test debt where the development pace becomes unsustainable, adding functionality takes ever longer, and refactoring becomes perilous; when the cause is lack of time, temporarily adjust the schedule while developers climb the learning curve, after which they can write tests and code in the time it once took to write and debug the code alone.

High Test Maintenance Cost's root cause is neglecting the principles of test automation, with the immediate cause being too much Test Code Duplication and tests too closely coupled to the SUT's API; reduce it by protecting against the four sensitivities with Test Doubles, refactoring the system into smaller individually-testable components, and using SUT API Encapsulation such as Creation Methods that encapsulate constructors.

Infrequently Run Tests, where developers do not run the tests often or commit without running them, is usually caused by Slow Tests or Unrepeatable Tests that force a restart or manual intervention; fix it by switching to a Fresh Fixture for unrepeatable tests or by speeding up the slow ones.

A Lost Test, a Test Method or Testcase Class that is disabled or never added to the AllTests suite, usually happens when someone disables a failing test; avoid it by running a single test via a Single Test Suite or Test Tree Explorer instead of disabling it, using the framework's Ignore mechanism that reports the ignored count, failing the CI build when the ignored count exceeds a threshold, comparing test counts before and after check-in, and using Test Discovery or a name pattern to pick up all tests.

Missing Unit Tests, where all unit tests pass but a customer test fails, happen when a team writes customer tests but skips unit-level test-driven development so a later refactoring breaks a class undetected; avoid them with true test-driven development rather than writing tests merely to raise the count.

Untested Code is most often SUT paths that react to how a depended-on component behaves and cannot otherwise be exercised; fix it by using a Test Stub to feed the various kinds of indirect inputs into the SUT, or by configuring the real component to return them, to cover all the code paths.

Untested Requirements are behavior not visible through the SUT's public interface (indirect outputs or side effects), so a test that does not verify them passes even when the behavior is broken or absent; verify indirect outputs with Behavior Verification using Mock Objects, and for a whole application write enough customer tests that all components integrate, possibly separating the presentation layer from the business logic.

A Neverfail Test passes even when the functionality is absent, making it useless for Defect Localization; its causes include miscoded assertions (such as assertTrue(variable, true) instead of assertEquals) and asynchronous tests where failures thrown in another thread are not seen by the Test Runner; fix it with cross-thread failure detection or by refactoring to a Humble Executable.

How you prepare automated test scripts determines which purposes they can serve (regression, documentation, or specification), how robust they are to changes in the SUT, and how much skill and effort they take to prepare.

Recorded Tests let you rapidly create regression tests after the SUT is built and before it changes and are quicker to produce than Scripted Tests; use them when an application is running and not expected to change much, or to obtain a regression net before refactoring a legacy application that lacks Scripted Tests.

Most Recorded Test tools interact through the user interface, making them prone to Interface Sensitivity (a small change like renaming a button breaks playback) and recording at a low, detailed level that yields Obscure Tests hard to repair by hand, so plan to rerecord them regularly if the SUT keeps evolving.

Because commercial Recorded Test tools generally do not let you define a Higher-Level Language, prefer Scripted Tests when you want Tests as Documentation or to drive new development, or build the recording capability into the application, or use a Refactored Recorded Test.

Use a Refactored Recorded Test (record, refactor, playback): extract reusable action components or verbs from the recordings, turn literal values into parameters, and rewire the test cases to call them, so that when a screen changes you rerecord only the component; this is equivalent to using Test Utility Methods and enables a Higher-Level Language for Scripted Tests.

To use recorded tests to drive development, pick a tool whose recording file format is hand-editable and easily understood (making it effectively a Scripted Test), or build the recording into the SUT so the scripting language is high-level enough to hand-script tests before the system is built.
Manually-inserted clarifying comments in a recorded test are lost when the test is rerecorded after a change to the application.

Almost always use Scripted Tests for unit tests, because you can access the individual units directly from software written in the same language and can exercise all code paths including the pathological cases.

Use a Scripted Test whenever you use automated storytests to drive development, because Recorded Tests need an existing application to record from; alternatively define a Higher-Level Language implemented as a Data-Driven Test interpreter (such as Fit, FitNesse, or Canoo WebTest) so non-programmers can participate.

Prefer writing Scripted Tests with a Test Automation Framework such as xUnit in the same language as the SUT, capturing each test as a Test Method that is both Self-Checking and Repeatable to minimize Manual Intervention.

A Data-Driven Test puts the common logic in an interpreter and the varying data in a file, giving excellent coverage while minimizing the test code to write and maintain, so that a test that would otherwise need a series of complex steps can be reduced to a single line of data.

Data-Driven Tests are an ideal way to involve business people in writing automated tests: keep the data-file format simple so a business person can populate it and run the tests without a technical person writing code for each test.

Use a Data-Driven Test when you have many different data values exercised by the same sequence of steps, a similarity usually discovered over time by refactoring first to a Parameterized Test and then to a Data-Driven Test.

Make tests data-driven when the SUT's behavior is driven by configuration data, so that changes to the configuration data are driven by changes to the tests rather than forcing a source-code commit whenever the configuration data changes.

Keep both the Data-Driven Test interpreter and the data files under version control, storing the data files in a Repository and, for business users, making that transparent through an authoring tool such as FitNesse or a version-controlled document management system.

Run Data-Driven and customer tests as part of continuous integration so tests that once passed do not silently start failing; because not all customer tests need to pass before a commit, keep two input files and migrate tests from a 'still red' file into an 'all green' file used for regression as they begin to pass.

Fit suits customer tests (less code than a custom interpreter, business-readable output, does not stop at the first failure, many fixture types) but xUnit suits unit tests, because Fit requires well-understood scenarios translated into tables, needs the same SUT interaction logic in each test, and its tests are not normally part of developers' xUnit regression runs.

A naive xUnit Data-Driven interpreter (one Test Method looping over the data file) makes the whole set count as a single test and stops at the first failure, losing Defect Localization; fix it by wrapping each iteration in try/catch and reporting which subtest failed, or better generate a Testcase Object per data-file entry so each counts separately and the run continues past failures.
Add a verb or action word to each data-file entry so that one Data-Driven Test interpreter can dispatch to a different Parameterized Test for different kinds of tests in the same file.

Use a Test Automation Framework to minimize the effort of writing Fully Automated Tests by providing the common mechanisms (finding tests, assembling suites, running, verifying, reporting failures and errors, and cleanup), which isolates the test-running logic from the test logic, reduces Test Code Duplication and Obscure Tests, and lets different authors' tests run in one report.

Use the smallest and simplest fixture possible for each test, because a Minimal Fixture is easier to understand (enabling Tests as Documentation) and avoids Slow Tests, and it is easier to define for a Fresh Fixture serving one test than for a Shared Fixture serving several: if an object is not important to understanding the test, it is important not to include it.
Minimize a fixture in two ways, eliminating objects entirely and hiding unnecessary attributes, and test whether an object is necessary by removing it and seeing whether the test then fails.

Eliminate objects the SUT does not actually use by passing Dummy Objects or using Entity Chain Snipping; if an object is necessary but does not help understanding, hide it inside a Creation Method that defaults the 'don't care' attributes, while keeping boundary-value objects and attributes visible.

A Standard Fixture reuses the fixture design across many tests (a big-design-upfront of the fixture) and is independent of the Fresh-versus-Shared choice: a Shared Fixture is always a Standard Fixture, but a Standard Fixture need not be shared.

In the xUnit community, using a Standard Fixture merely to avoid designing a Minimal Fixture for each test is undesirable (the General Fixture smell); an accepted use is Implicit Setup with Testcase Class per Fixture where a few tests genuinely need the same fixture design.

Making a Standard Fixture reusable across tests with disparate needs makes it grow larger and more complex, leading to a Fragile Fixture, a Mystery Guest, and Slow Tests, so you are often better off with a Minimal Fixture that avoids constructing objects only other tests need.

A test is not a unit test if it talks to the database, communicates across the network, touches the file system, cannot run correctly at the same time as your other unit tests, or requires special environment setup such as editing config files; such tests are often worth writing but should be kept separate from the fast unit tests.

Use a Fresh Fixture, where each test builds its own private fixture and tears it down afterward, to avoid the interdependencies that cause Erratic Tests such as Lonely Tests and Interacting Tests; if it is too slow, prefer an Immutable Shared Fixture before resorting to a full Shared Fixture.
A Database Partitioning Scheme that gives a test a private Database Sandbox is not a Fresh Fixture, because subsequent test runs could reuse the same fixture.

A fixture persists either because it lives in persistent objects such as a database (risking Unrepeatable Tests, Interacting Tests, and Test Run Wars, so keep it private and tear it down after each test) or because of the variable holding it: local variables are garbage-collected, instance variables need explicit teardown only if the framework reuses Testcase Objects, and class variables usually persist and should be avoided with a Fresh Fixture.

In practice a unit-test fixture is not persistent unless the application logic is tightly coupled to the database; a fixture is more likely to be persistent when writing customer tests or component tests.

Choose the Fresh Fixture setup location by test organization: In-line Setup for simple fixtures, Delegated Setup when Test Methods are organized as Testcase Class per Class or per Feature, and Implicit Setup when using Testcase Class per Fixture.

For a Persistent Fresh Fixture, tear it down (In-line, Implicit, Delegated, or Automated Teardown) or avoid teardown by using Distinct Generated Values for each unique fixture object as a Database Partitioning Scheme that isolates tests and runners and prevents Resource Leakage if teardown fails, and combine both approaches to be doubly sure.

Reusing a persistent fixture across many tests to save setup violates the Keep Tests Independent principle, and the resulting Shared Fixture invariably leads to Interacting and Unrepeatable Tests eventually, so do not go down that road without fully understanding the consequences.

A Shared Fixture reuses a single fixture instance across many tests (a Standard Fixture that outlasts a single Testcase Object) to make tests faster, but its baggage is interactions and Erratic Tests, a more complex Fragile Fixture, and Obscure Tests because the fixture is not built inside the test; mitigate the last with Finder Methods that have intent-revealing names.

Use a Shared Fixture only for good reasons such as when you cannot afford to build a Fresh Fixture for each test (Slow Tests, typically with real databases), but a better solution is usually to make the tests not interact with the database at all.

Replacing a real database with a Fake Database backed by hash tables plus an object-query interpreter ran the author's tests about 50 times faster (10 minutes down to 10 seconds) and let the team defer building a real database until the object model stabilized several months into the project.

A large team cut its check-in test suite from about 8 hours against the database to under 8 minutes through an in-memory database, a database-less test framework (a tenfold cut), a remote test server, and a clustering framework, keeping run time under 5 minutes (treating 8 minutes as the trigger to try a new technique) and choosing to speed up all tests rather than run only a subset.

Use a Shared Fixture for Incremental Tests (a long sequence of dependent actions) by putting each action in a separate Test Method that builds on the shared fixture (Chained Tests), and start each Test Method with Guard Assertions documenting its assumptions about the fixture so that a failure points to an earlier test or to the run order.

Do not hard-code fixture-object identifiers such as database keys in the tests, because that produces a Fragile Fixture; instead keep a reference to the fixture when it is created and make that reference accessible to all tests.

Set up a Per-Run Fixture once at the start of a run: if it is shared within one Testcase Class, use a class variable with Lazy Setup or Suite Fixture Setup; if it is shared across Testcase Classes, use a Setup Decorator with a Test Fixture Registry.

An Immutable Shared Fixture avoids Erratic Tests by partitioning the fixture into an immutable part every test needs but never modifies and per-test mutable objects built as Fresh Fixtures on top; the hard part is deciding what counts as a change, and if any test would perceive another test's action as a change to a shared object, that change must not be allowed in any test sharing the fixture.

Use Back Door Manipulation, which sets up the fixture or verifies the outcome directly through the SUT's state store while bypassing its API, when a round-trip test is not possible or desirable, provided a back door to the state exists.

Back Door Manipulation's main drawback is that it couples the tests to how the SUT's state is represented (risking Fragile Tests) and can produce Obscure Tests by hiding the fixture-to-outcome relationship; reduce both by encapsulating all back-door access in Test Utility Methods and using Finder Methods, or by keeping the test data inside the Testcase Class.

Test CRUD operations with layer-crossing tests that use Back Door Manipulation (Back Door Setup for a Read test, Back Door Verification for a Write test), because round-trip tests cannot detect systemic problems such as writing information into the wrong database column.

Back Door Setup can make tests faster and can create impossible or invalid fixtures the SUT's API would not allow (useful for testing configurations another application sharing the database might create), but because it bypasses object-creation business rules the fixtures may become unrealistic or even invalid over time.

Build fixture-loading data such as an XML dataset within the Testcase Class rather than in an external file, to avoid the Mystery Guest smell, and hide the loading and teardown mechanics behind intent-revealing Test Utility Methods.

Maintaining a Database Population Script and its input files raises test maintenance cost because both must change whenever the data store's structure or semantics change; a Data Loader written in a programming language (for example reusing ORM domain objects, as DbUnit does) is more flexible and works even for non-relational state.

The most common form of Back Door Manipulation replaces the depended-on component with a Test Double — a preloaded Fake Object that avoids using the SUT to set up its own state, or a Configurable Test Double such as a Mock or Stub — and making the double's state visible within the Test Method avoids Obscure Tests.

Sometimes a database or query schema is really a front door, a formal interface that reporting tools or load scripts depend on; when a customer relies on a stable query, reporting, or data-loading interface, treat it as a requirement, write customer tests against it, and use query views so the underlying database can still be refactored.

Test a layered architecture by testing each layer in isolation as its own SUT, where the tests take the place of the layer above and optionally replace the layer below with a Test Double, which gives better coverage than top-to-bottom testing that forces Indirect Testing on some parts of the application.
Layer Tests make it simpler to inject 'should never happen' error scenarios as indirect inputs across a layer boundary so you can verify defensive error-handling code that would otherwise rarely run.

Layer boundaries make natural team boundaries because each layer tends to need different knowledge and technology, and Layer Tests are a good way to nail down and document the semantics of the layer interfaces.

Even with a Layer Test strategy, include a few top-to-bottom tests covering one or two basic scenarios to verify the layers integrate correctly, without retesting every business condition since those are already covered by the per-layer tests.

Test the presentation layer separately from the business logic, and design it so its logic can be tested independently of the presentation framework using a Humble Dialog that separates a testable presentation-behavior layer from the presentation-graphic layer, so you can verify button and menu state without instantiating the real graphical objects.

Test the Service Layer directly, where most unit and component tests concentrate, rather than through the presentation layer, because testing it via the presentation involves Indirect Testing and Sensitive Equality that lead to Fragile Tests, and replace the persistence layer with a Fake Database to avoid Slow Tests.

Round-trip persistence-layer tests suffice when your application is the only user of the data store, but they will not catch putting information into the wrong columns when the column types are compatible and read and write make the same error; when other applications share the store, add layer-crossing tests using Back Door Manipulation that verify data goes into the correct columns.

A Subcutaneous Test bypasses the presentation layer to interact directly with the Service Layer (usually without isolating the layers below); it needs less separation of concerns than a Service Layer Test, is easier when retrofitting tests onto an application not designed for testability, and makes customer tests more robust because a whole category of presentation changes will not break it.

Write Layer Tests as round-trip tests where possible, since they are easier and sufficient for Simple Success Tests (leaving the real components in place or using Fake Objects for the layer below), and use layer-crossing tests when verifying the error-handling logic in the layer of interest.

Control a layer's indirect inputs with a Test Stub that returns canned results (useful for Expected Exception Tests or behavior depending on upstream data), and verify its indirect outputs with a Mock Object or Test Spy replacing the layer below, or use Back Door Manipulation for either.

Encode each test as a single Test Method following one of the three standard templates — Simple Success Test, Expected Exception Test, or Constructor Test — so readers can recognize the test type, and keep only Expected Exception Tests using error-handling constructs like try/catch so basic-behavior tests are easy to find as documentation.

In a Simple Success Test, do not catch exceptions; let the Test Automation Framework catch and report them, because catching them creates Obscure Tests, misleads the reader into thinking exceptions were expected, and the framework's report pinpoints the actual error deep in the SUT, which is easier to troubleshoot than an assertion failure.

Write an Expected Exception Test for each kind of exception the SUT is expected to raise (from an invalid client request, or by translating or passing through another component's error), verifying the type and message with an Equality Assertion when it matters such as when shown to a user, and calling fail if the error is not raised.

Do not write an Expected Exception Test for exceptions the SUT might raise but that you cannot force on cue, because those should surface as failures in the Simple Success Tests; to verify their handling, force them using a Test Stub that controls the SUT's indirect input.

Prefer the framework's ExpectedException attribute or annotation, or a block-based assertion in languages that support blocks, over a hand-coded try/catch; but because the attribute can only check the exception's type and message, use try/catch when you must assert on other contents of the exception to avoid Sensitive Equality.
