Test constructors separately with a Constructor Test whenever a constructor does anything more than a simple field assignment, for better Defect Localization and to avoid Test Code Duplication, verifying each attribute (an Equality Assertion for initialized attributes and a Stated Outcome Assertion like assertNull for uninitialized ones) and using an Expected Exception Test for invalid constructor arguments.

Write a Dependency Initialization Test, a Constructor Test asserting that a substitutable-dependency attribute is initialized to the real depended-on component when the software runs in production, often in a separate Test Method to improve its visibility.

Use comments to mark the four phases of a test as a source of self-discipline, because it makes it obvious when a test is not a Single-Condition Test, such as when it has multiple exercise phases separated by verification or interspersed fixture-setup and exercise phases.

Implement the Four-Phase Test either free-standing with all four phases in the Test Method (In-line Setup plus Garbage-Collected or In-line Teardown, suiting Testcase Class per Class or per Feature) or with Implicit Setup and Teardown in setUp and tearDown methods (leaving only exercise and verify in the Test Method, suiting Testcase Class per Fixture).

When teardown is in-line and might not run after an assertion throws, wrap it in a try/finally; with Implicit Teardown the tearDown method runs automatically even after a failure, but then the fixture must be held in instance variables rather than local variables.

Make tests self-checking by encoding the expected outcome as calls to Assertion Methods (framework-provided or Custom Assertions) rather than as Conditional Test Logic, which is verbose, hard to read, and more likely to produce Test Code Duplication and Buggy Tests.

Choose the most appropriate Assertion Method so it both fails on the wrong outcome and documents how the SUT should behave; the built-in categories are Single-Outcome (fail), Stated Outcome (assertTrue, assertNotNull), Expected Exception, Equality, and Fuzzy Equality assertions.

In an Equality Assertion, put the expected value first and the actual value second because the framework's diagnostic message only makes sense in that order; since equality is determined by the expected object's equals method, assert on individual fields or implement test-specific equality on a Test-Specific Subclass when that equals is not what you want.

Use a Fuzzy Equality Assertion with a tolerance or comparison mask when you cannot guarantee an exact match, such as comparing floating-point numbers for arithmetic precision or comparing XML documents while ignoring fields with unpredictable content.

Use the fail Single-Outcome Assertion as an Unfinished Test Assertion to remind you a test is not yet written, or after the exception-throwing call in an Expected Exception Test's try block, but do not use Single-Outcome Assertions inside Conditional Test Logic, since there is almost never a good reason for conditional logic in a Test Method and a Guard Assertion is preferable.

Include an Assertion Message especially when a Test Method has several calls to the same kind of Assertion Method or is run via a Command-Line Test Runner that rarely provides failure-location information; testers who write only one assertion per test can instead rely on the assertion's own argument output.
Use an Assertion-Identifying Message, such as the name of the variable or attribute being asserted on (or a number), to distinguish which of several assertions of the same type failed.
Include an Expectation-Describing Message stating what should have happened, which is done automatically for an Equality Assertion but which you must supply yourself for a Stated Outcome Assertion.

For a Stated Outcome Assertion like assertTrue, whose default failure message is unhelpful, use an Argument-Describing Message that includes the evaluated expression and the actual values, made even clearer by giving the variables intent-revealing names.

Group related Test Methods on a Testcase Class rather than as global functions so each can become a Testcase Object at runtime, and factor common code into Test Utility Methods (kept on the class or moved to a Testcase Superclass, Test Helper, or Test Helper Mixin) to avoid Test Code Duplication.

At runtime the framework creates one instance of the Testcase Class per Test Method, each of which is a distinct test case; do not put each Test Method on its own class, which adds overhead, clutters the namespace, and makes reuse between tests harder.

Use a standard Test Runner so that tests written by different people can run together in a single report; it obtains a Composite test object (a single test, a suite, or a Suite of Suites) via Test Enumeration, Discovery, or Selection and reports the counts of tests run, failures, and errors.

Have a Command-Line Test Runner set its exit code to the number of failed or errored tests so a non-zero exit code is interpreted as a build failure by an automated build tool, and use a File System Test Runner's directory search (Testcase Class Discovery) to avoid building a Suite of Suites in code and to help avoid Lost Tests.

Most xUnit members create a separate Testcase Object per Test Method to fully isolate the tests (Independent Test), but NUnit 2.x and TestNG reuse a single Testcase Class instance across all methods, which creates an implicit Shared Fixture and lets one test's member variable leak into another as an execution-order dependency (an anti-pattern); with NUnit, make the member variables static as truth-in-advertising so no one assumes a fresh instance per test.

Treating each test as a first-class Command object (a Testcase Object) lets the framework hold tests in collections, iterate over, count, run, and display them, and lets a Test Tree Explorer run a single test without needing a Single Test Suite class.
A Test Suite Object is a Composite that implements the same interface as a single Testcase Object, so the Test Runner treats a single test, a Testcase Class Suite, and a Suite of Suites identically.

A Test Suite Procedure, needed in languages without objects, forces Test Enumeration that increases the effort to write tests and the likelihood of Lost Tests and loses the ability to manipulate tests at runtime, making a graphical tree Test Runner harder to build.

Use Test Discovery whenever the Test Automation Framework supports it, because it reduces the effort of automating tests and greatly reduces the possibility of Lost Tests; use Test Enumeration only when the framework lacks Discovery or when defining a Named Test Suite subset chosen from other suites and the framework also lacks Test Selection.

Identify Test Methods for discovery via a naming convention such as starting with 'test' or via a method attribute or annotation like [Test] or @Test, and identify Testcase Classes via a superclass or marker interface, a class attribute like [TestFixture], a common directory, or a filename naming pattern.

It is common to combine Test Suite Enumeration at the Testcase Class level with Test Method Discovery, because many xUnit members support method-level Discovery but still require Enumeration at the class level.

Test Suite Enumeration risks Lost Tests if you forget to add a new suite to AllTests; reduce the risk with an IDE-regenerated AllTests (such as Eclipse marker comments), a Discovery-capable Test Runner, or comparing the test count before and after check-in.

Use Test Selection (running a subset chosen by test attributes) when you want a subset from other suites without maintaining a separate Test Enumeration structure, such as a Smoke Test suite; implement it most flexibly with class or method attributes or annotations (a Category) in the framework rather than by directory placement or naming conventions, which serve only one classification scheme and reduce Tests-as-Documentation value.
Use In-line Setup only when the fixture setup is very simple and straightforward; as soon as it grows complex, move part or all of it to Delegated Setup or Implicit Setup.

In-line Setup is a good starting point for a first draft of tests (applying Red-Green-Refactor to the tests themselves) before you know which setup repeats, and for refactoring obtuse setup by In-lining all Creation Methods and setUp and then using Extract Method to define new intent-revealing Creation Methods.

When tests become hard to understand because of behind-the-scenes setup (a Mystery Guest) or you find yourself modifying the same setup fixture in many tests, refactor the test class into multiple classes based on the fixture each builds (In-line Method, then Extract Class, then Extract Method).

Use Delegated Setup, where each test calls Creation Methods, to avoid Test Code Duplication while keeping the fixture's nature visible in the Test Method; encapsulate the essential-but-irrelevant setup steps and leave only the values essential to understanding the test, which avoids the Mystery Guest and Obscure Test smells.

Delegated Setup, unlike Implicit Setup, does not force tests that need the same fixture into the same Testcase Class, and it reduces Fragile Tests by moving nonessential interaction with the SUT out of the many Test Methods into a few Creation Method bodies where it is easier to maintain.

Write tests in terms of intent-revealing Creation Methods that you pretend already exist, passing only the values that are verified or that affect the outcome, then implement them to encapsulate object-creation complexity by calling constructors with default values and first creating any depended-on objects.

Use a Creation Method whenever constructing a Fresh Fixture has significant complexity and you value Tests as Documentation, or when building the system incrementally with a frequently-changing API, because encapsulating fixture-object creation (SUT API Encapsulation) avoids Fragile and Obscure Tests; its main cost is that it creates another API for team members to learn.
In a Parameterized Creation Method pass only the attributes expected to affect the outcome (or that you want to demonstrate do not affect it), otherwise you slide down the slope toward Obscure Tests.

Use an Anonymous Creation Method that automatically generates a Distinct Generated Value as the object's unique identifier even when its arguments are not unique, to avoid Unrepeatable Tests by ensuring every created object is unique across test runs.

For a state-rich SUT, test each method from each possible starting state as separate Single-Condition Tests rather than chaining them into an Eager Test, reaching the starting state via a Named State Reaching Method with Delegated Setup or by grouping same-starting-state tests into a Testcase Class per Fixture with Implicit Setup.

If you set up a fixture by calling another Test Method, wrap that call in a Creation Method rather than calling the Test Method directly, because Test Methods are named for what they verify not for the fixture they leave behind; the Creation Method gives an intent-revealing name and solves the Lonely Test problem by running the other test explicitly, though it does not fix Interacting Tests and runs more slowly.

Avoid calling object constructors directly in tests when building the application incrementally, because every change to a constructor's parameters forces revisiting many tests or keeping the constructor backward-compatible; encapsulate construction in a Creation Method so only that one method updates when the constructor changes.

Use Implicit Setup, placing fixture setup in the setUp method, when several Test Methods on the same Testcase Class need an identical Fresh Fixture (Testcase Class per Fixture); it is called implicit because the calls to the setup logic are not visible within the Test Method.

With Testcase Class per Feature or per Class where tests need different fixtures, set up in the setUp method only the essential-but-irrelevant parts (don't-care values and hidden plumbing such as database connections) and leave setup that affects the SUT's state to each Test Method, unless every Test Method needs the same starting state.

Implicit Setup removes a lot of Test Code Duplication and helps prevent Fragile Tests, but it can cause Obscure Tests by making the fixture a Mystery Guest and a Fragile Fixture if not all tests in the class really need the identical fixture.

With Implicit Setup, communicate the fixture from the setUp method to the Test Methods via instance variables rather than class variables (which would risk a Shared Fixture), and tear down in the tearDown method anything the setUp method created that is not automatically cleaned up.

Use a Prebuilt Fixture (built before the run and reused across runs) when constructing a Shared Fixture is extremely costly or hard to automate; because rebuilding needs Manual Intervention and it is reused, treat it as an Immutable Shared Fixture and build a Fresh Fixture for anything you plan to modify, to avoid Erratic Tests from fixture pollution.

A Global Fixture (a Prebuilt Fixture shared between multiple test automaters, common when using a single shared Database Sandbox without a partitioning scheme) risks Test Run Wars from multiprocessing; avoid this with a Database Partitioning Scheme or Distinct Generated Values for any fields with unique-key constraints.

For a Prebuilt Fixture, implement Finder Methods by storing the identifiers generated during fixture construction in a persistent Test Fixture Registry such as a file, or by hard-coding them, and avoid searching for matching objects at runtime, which can cause Nondeterministic Tests because each run could pick a different object.

A Fixture Setup Testcase (a Testcase Class with only a setUp method that persists the fixture and saves its keys, no Test Methods, and an empty tearDown) is a convenient xUnit way to regenerate a Prebuilt Fixture on demand while avoiding hard-coding fixture knowledge into the tests.

Use Lazy Setup (build the Shared Fixture in the first test that needs it and store a reference in a class variable) when you need a Shared Fixture but still want each test to be runnable by itself, or when teardown is not crucial, such as when Garbage-Collected Teardown applies or when Distinct Generated Values and Delta Assertions let you tolerate leftover records.

Lazy Setup's major drawback is that although it is easy to detect the first test and construct the fixture, it is hard to detect the last test and tear it down; most xUnit members provide no way to do so except a Setup Decorator for the whole suite (some support Suite Fixture Setup), and Runners that reload classes each run make this a non-issue via garbage collection.

Merely moving fixture setup into the setUp and tearDown methods does not speed up tests, because the framework calls setUp and tearDown for each Testcase Object; convert to Lazy Setup by putting Lazy Initialization in setUp and removing the teardown that would undo it, so the fixture is set up only once per run.

Lazy Setup carries all the baggage of Shared Fixtures; to share a lazily-set-up fixture across several Testcase Classes, move the Lazy Initialization logic and its class variable to a Testcase Superclass (only if the language inherits class variables) or to a Test Helper.

Use Suite Fixture Setup, which the framework calls before the first and after the last Test Method, when all the Test Methods needing the fixture are on one Testcase Class and your xUnit variant supports it (such as VbUnit, NUnit, or JUnit 4.0 and newer); it is especially useful when you must tear the fixture down after the last test.

Suite Fixture Setup requires holding the fixture in a class variable, Registry, or Singleton between Test Method calls (except in NUnit); do not dump all fixture setup into it but call Creation Methods so complex construction lives in a Testcase Superclass or Test Helper where it is testable and reusable.

To share a fixture more widely than a single Testcase Class use a Prebuilt Fixture, a Setup Decorator, or Lazy Setup, and to share only the setup code rather than the fixture instance use Implicit Setup or Delegated Setup.

Use a Setup Decorator, which brackets the whole test suite's run with matching setUp and tearDown bookends, when a Shared Fixture must be set up before every run and torn down after: for example when tests use hard-coded values that would fail on rerun without cleanup (Unrepeatable Tests), to avoid a limited resource filling up, or to change a global parameter such as swapping in a Fake Database and then change it back.

A Setup Decorator's key drawback is that its decorated tests cannot be run by themselves; work around it with a Decorated Lazy Setup that augments the decorator's setUp with Lazy Setup so an undecorated Testcase Object builds its own fixture, or a Pushdown Decorator that pushes the decorator down to each test (which, however, negates the Shared Fixture's speed advantage).

Make a Setup Decorator reusable across several test suites with a Parameterized Setup Decorator whose constructor takes the Test Suite Object to run, coding the setup and teardown logic in the decorator and avoiding a separate Test Helper class.

Chained Tests reuse the fixture left over by earlier tests in the suite — Self-Checking Tests that perform no setup and assume a predecessor ran and left something usable — similar to how a human tester builds up a complex fixture through a verified sequence of actions; unlike Reuse Test for Fixture Setup, they do not call the other Test Method but merely assume it has run.

Use Chained Tests only as a pragmatic fixture strategy for existing long, sequential tests whose steps build on one another; treat it as a transitional refactoring toward independent tests rather than as the normal target design.
condition: when existing tests are overly long and contain dependent steps

statement: Chained Tests can reduce sensitivity to SUT API changes because later tests reuse fixture state created through earlier tests instead of repeating setup interactions with the SUT.
Chained Tests create fixture fragility because a change, failure, or error in an earlier test can leave the shared fixture different from what later tests assume.
condition: when later tests depend on leftovers from preceding tests

statement: Do not rely on Chained Tests when test execution order is not controlled, because many xUnit frameworks do not guarantee suite order and order changes can make tests fail after framework upgrades or method renames.
condition: when the xUnit framework does not provide a reliable ordering mechanism
exception: when the framework or suite construction explicitly guarantees the required order

statement: Expect Chained Tests to be lonely tests: dependent tests usually cannot be run by themselves during failure diagnosis because their assumed fixture has not been built.
condition: when a test depends on previous tests for setup
exception: the first test in the chain may be runnable alone

statement: Chained Tests make fixture context harder to understand because the setup is outside the current test; named Finder Methods can partially reduce that mystery by making shared fixture access explicit.
condition: when a chained test must read objects left by earlier tests

statement: Use a Fixture Setup Testcase only when a shared fixture must be built before a suite and Lazy Setup, Suite Fixture Setup, Setup Decorator, or similar mechanisms are unavailable.
condition: when other shared-fixture setup patterns cannot be used

statement: Implementing Chained Tests requires solving two separate problems: making the suite run tests in the intended order and giving later tests access to fixture objects left by earlier tests.

If the predecessor and dependent tests are methods on the same Testcase Class, store shared fixture references in class-level fields rather than instance fields because typical xUnit frameworks create separate Testcase Objects per test method.
condition: when chained methods are on the same Testcase Class under the usual per-test-object xUnit lifecycle
exception: frameworks whose lifecycle shares instance variables across test methods

statement: When a chained test depends on tests in other Testcase Classes, use an external fixture registry or similar shared store because class fields on one Testcase Class will not make the fixture visible across a suite of suites.
condition: when fixture leftovers must be accessed across Testcase Classes

statement: Chained Tests are incompatible with Fresh Fixture cleanup because the predecessor must leave reusable fixture state behind instead of tearing it down after each test.
condition: when a later test relies on a previous test's leftovers

statement: Refactor an incremental tabular test into one test method per subcase when later subcases should still be reported even if an earlier subcase fails.
condition: when a single multi-step test stops at the first assertion and hides later outcomes

statement: When converting a sequential test into Chained Tests, preserve the required order with the framework's ordering mechanism or, for name-sorted frameworks, stable sequence numbers in method names.
condition: when the split tests must execute in a specific order

statement: Use State Verification when the expected outcome is the SUT's final state and the path taken to reach that state is not part of what the test should specify.
condition: when only final state matters
exception: when indirect outputs or interactions are the behavior under test

statement: State Verification helps preserve encapsulation by limiting the test to observable end state instead of specifying internal collaboration details.
condition: when final state is sufficient to define correctness

statement: When retrofitting tests and the relevant state is not directly observable, expose the state through test-specific access techniques such as a Test-Specific Subclass rather than adding test logic to production code.
condition: when existing APIs do not expose the state needed for verification

statement: State Verification may inspect state stored outside the SUT, such as a database, while Behavior Verification instead checks the SUT's interactions with that external component.
condition: when the SUT's effects are persisted or delegated to another component

statement: Use Behavior Verification rather than State Verification when the outcome that matters is an indirect output or side effect that is not visible in the SUT's final state.
condition: when important behavior occurs as interactions with collaborators

statement: Avoid overspecifying interactions in Behavior Verification because excessive behavioral detail can make tests fragile.
condition: when using behavior verification for indirect outputs

statement: Procedural State Verification is easy to write but can obscure the test and duplicate verification code when many attributes or repeated assertion sequences are required.
condition: when several assertions are needed to describe expected state

statement: Prefer Expected State Specification when many attributes or many tests must compare expected state, because constructing expected objects or tables lets the test use a concise equality-style assertion.
condition: when expected state has multiple attributes or repeated comparisons
exception: when a suitable comparable expected object or table cannot be constructed

statement: Build expected-state objects with parameterized creation methods when many necessary attributes do not matter to the behavior being verified, so the test highlights only the relevant inputs and expectations.
condition: when expected objects require incidental attributes

statement: If production equality is unsuitable for test expectations, use a Custom Assertion, test-specific equality object, Test-Specific Subclass, DTO, or Fake Object instead of changing production equality only to support tests.
condition: when the production class's equality semantics do not match the test's comparison needs

statement: Build expected-state objects during fixture setup when their attributes are also used as SUT inputs or as the basis for derived values, because it makes the relationship between setup and expected outcome clearer.
condition: when expected-state attributes feed the exercise phase or derived fixture values

statement: To refactor State Verification into Behavior Verification, first replace the relevant dependency with a Test Double so the test can observe the SUT's indirect outputs through a Test Spy or Mock Object.
condition: when the behavior to verify is expressed as interactions with collaborators rather than final SUT state

statement: To move from an expected-behavior mock style to procedural behavior verification, install a Test Spy and assert on the values it records after exercising the SUT.
condition: when replacing a Mock Object with a Test Spy while preserving the expected interaction checks

statement: To move from procedural behavior verification to an expected-behavior style, configure a Mock Object with the expected values formerly asserted from the Test Spy and install that mock in place of the spy.
condition: when replacing captured-output assertions with mock expectations

statement: Procedural Behavior Verification captures indirect outputs with a Test Spy and verifies those captured values through inline assertions.
Expected Behavior Specification configures a Mock Object with the expected interaction before exercise and relies on the mock framework to verify that interaction.
Create Custom Assertions to hide repeated or complex verification mechanics behind assertion methods whose names reveal the test intent.
condition: when verification logic is repeated, complex, or distracting in test methods

statement: A pure Custom Assertion should receive every value it needs as parameters and should have no side effects other than failing the current test.
exception: if it must query or mutate the SUT, it is a Verification Method rather than a pure Custom Assertion

statement: Custom Assertions are often found by refactoring repeated assertion patterns, but in test-driven work it can be reasonable to call the desired assertion first and implement it afterward.
Consider a Custom Assertion when result verification duplicates assertion logic across tests.
condition: when the same assertion sequence appears in multiple tests

statement: Consider a Custom Assertion when result verification contains conditionals or loops, because moving the logic behind a named assertion avoids Conditional Test Logic in the Test Method.
condition: when verification code branches or iterates in the test method

statement: Consider a Custom Assertion when procedural verification makes tests obscure, because declarative assertion names can communicate the expected outcome more clearly.
condition: when inline assertions hide the test's intent

statement: Consider a Diagnostic Assertion when failures force frequent debugging because built-in assertions do not explain the relevant difference between expected and actual values.
condition: when assertion failures lack enough type-specific diagnostic information

statement: Moving verification logic into a Custom Assertion can make that logic testable separately, reducing the amount of important behavior hidden in untested test code.
Use a Verification Method instead of a pure Custom Assertion when verification must interact with the SUT to discover the actual outcome.
condition: when checking the result requires calls into the SUT

statement: Use a Parameterized Test rather than only a Custom Assertion when the setup and exercise phases are also identical across cases apart from data values.
condition: when repeated tests differ mainly by actual and expected values across the whole flow

statement: Custom Assertions are highly reusable when they are independent of context and communicate only through their parameter list.
A Custom Equality Assertion should take an expected object, an actual object, and an assertion message so failures can identify which comparison failed.
condition: when implementing test-specific equality checks

statement: An Object Attribute Equality Assertion compares selected attributes of objects supplied as parameters; unlike a Verification Method, it does not interact with the SUT.
Use Domain Assertions to state expected outcomes in domain terms and raise the test's verification language closer to business or domain vocabulary.
condition: when domain-level wording communicates intent better than low-level attribute comparisons

statement: Verification Methods can simplify tests by combining SUT interaction and outcome checking, but their names should signal that they verify behavior rather than acting as pure assertions.
condition: when the reusable helper includes the exercise phase or changes SUT state

statement: Implement Custom Assertions with built-in assertions where possible, and include null-handling behavior consistent with the framework's equality assertion style when the assertion will be used that way.
condition: when implementing a reusable assertion helper

statement: Write Custom Assertion Tests when an assertion helper has nontrivial comparison logic; treat the assertion helper as the SUT and test both cases that should pass and cases that should fail.
condition: when the Custom Assertion is complex enough that defects in it would undermine test trust

statement: For equality-style Custom Assertion Tests, include cases for equivalent objects, self-comparison, each attribute whose inequality should fail, and attributes that should be ignored by equality.
condition: when testing a custom equality assertion

statement: When a Custom Assertion Test expects the assertion to fail, structure it as an expected-exception test and, where useful, assert the failure message.
condition: when validating negative behavior of an assertion helper

statement: If an xUnit implementation logs failures before caught assertion errors can be inspected, use an encapsulated test runner to execute and inspect the Custom Assertion Test in isolation.
condition: when caught assertion failures still pollute the runner's failure log

statement: Refactor repeated inline attribute assertions by extracting the common assertion method and, when necessary, introducing an Expected Object that carries the values formerly passed one by one.
condition: when several tests compare the same group of attributes

statement: Pass a contextual message into Custom Assertions and propagate it into individual built-in assertions so failures avoid Assertion Roulette.
condition: when a Custom Assertion contains multiple internal checks or may be called several times in one test

statement: To convert a state check into a Delta Assertion, snapshot the relevant data before exercising the SUT and then assert on the difference between the before and after collections.
condition: when shared fixture state may contain pre-existing objects

statement: Delta Assertions should verify both the newly expected changes and the preservation of pre-existing data, such as checking inclusion of the new object, inclusion of prior objects, and the expected size delta.
condition: when verifying additive effects against an existing collection

statement: Use Custom Assertions for Delta Assertions when otherwise the test method would need conditional logic or repeated collection-difference mechanics.
condition: when delta comparison logic is complex or repeated

statement: Delta Assertions are safer when the pre-exercise snapshot cannot be mutated by the SUT during exercise, such as when the snapshot contains transfer objects rather than live mutable domain objects.
condition: when relying on saved pre-test values for after-the-fact comparison

statement: A Delta Assertion can be implemented either by comparing the after-state against both prior and new expected objects or by subtracting the prior objects and verifying only the newly expected remainder.
condition: when verifying changes relative to pre-existing data

statement: Replace conditional branches in result verification with Guard Assertions that fail explicitly when required preconditions are not met.
condition: when a test uses conditionals to avoid errors from unexpected SUT-returned values

statement: Use Guard Assertions to turn unexpected setup or result-shape problems into clear test failures instead of less-informative test errors.
condition: when executing subsequent test statements would error unless a condition holds

statement: A Guard Assertion documents that a required condition is expected to be true and eliminates the need to infer that expectation from if/else verification code.
Place a Guard Assertion between the exercise and verification phases when values returned by the SUT must satisfy a condition before detailed assertions can safely run.
condition: when post-exercise values must be checked before later verification statements

statement: Place Shared Fixture State Assertions at the beginning of tests that depend on shared fixture contents so the test documents and checks the fixture assumptions it needs.
condition: when a test reads a Shared Fixture that previous tests or prior runs may have changed

statement: Use ordinary stated-outcome or equality assertions as Guard Assertions when they naturally express the condition that must hold before the test continues.
condition: when framework assertions can express the required guard condition

statement: Refactor nested conditional verification into a linear sequence of Guard Assertions so the test has a single obvious execution path.
condition: when a Test Method contains nested or even simple conditional verification logic

statement: Guard Assertions improve defect localization by identifying violated test preconditions, especially when a shared fixture assumption is the real failure source.
condition: when failures could otherwise be mistaken for SUT defects

statement: Make unfinished tests fail intentionally by adding an assertion that always fails with a message identifying the test as unfinished.
condition: when roughing in test methods before their bodies are complete

statement: Do not deliberately write placeholder tests that can pass accidentally, because a green test run can hide unimplemented tests.
condition: when adding incomplete or outline test methods

statement: Keep an Unfinished Test Assertion until the test is properly implemented, then remove it only when the test logic is complete enough to be meaningful.
condition: when iteratively filling in a test body

statement: If incomplete tests must be checked in before implementation is done, mark or exclude them with the framework's supported mechanism rather than deleting them or removing their unfinished assertions merely to get a passing run.
condition: when source control must receive unfinished tests

statement: If the xUnit framework lacks a fail method, implement a clear custom failing assertion and test it instead of scattering opaque always-false assertions through the code.
condition: when no built-in fail assertion exists

statement: Wrapping the unfinished-test failure in a named helper makes unfinished placeholders easy to find and remove later.
condition: when an IDE or codebase can search method references

statement: Use Garbage-Collected Teardown whenever the fixture resources are ordinary garbage-collected objects referenced only by locals or per-test instance variables.
condition: when the runtime supports garbage collection and the test-created resources require no explicit external cleanup

statement: Repeatable tests with Fresh Fixtures depend on each test's fixture being discarded after the test so the next run starts from a new fixture.
condition: when using a Fresh Fixture strategy

statement: Objects referenced only by discarded Testcase Objects become eligible for garbage collection after a fresh test suite is built for a new run.
condition: when the framework creates per-test objects and discards the old suite between runs

statement: Explicit teardown is still required for resources that are not cleaned by garbage collection, such as files, sockets, database records, or objects in runtimes without garbage collection.
condition: when resources outlive object reachability or the language lacks garbage collection

statement: Garbage-Collected Teardown usually does not fit Shared Fixtures because shared references must remain reachable across tests unless deliberately scoped to expire after the suite.
condition: when fixture references are kept globally or at class scope for sharing

statement: Use In-line, Implicit, or Automated Teardown when resources must be released explicitly rather than left to garbage collection.
condition: when fixture resources need deterministic release

statement: Do not rely on IDE class-reloading behavior as the only teardown mechanism for class-variable fixtures, because command-line and CI test runs may not provide the same lifecycle.
condition: when teardown depends on reloading test classes or clearing class variables between suite runs

statement: To convert unnecessary explicit cleanup to Garbage-Collected Teardown, remove cleanup for nonpersistent objects and change class-variable fixture references to local or instance references when moving from Shared Fixture to Fresh Fixture.
condition: when cleanup code deletes only in-memory objects that GC can reclaim

statement: Write explicit teardown whenever a test creates resources that will not be freed automatically, because leftover objects, records, files, or connections can slow later tests, make them fail, or destabilize the system.
condition: when test-created resources are not automatically reclaimed

statement: For In-line Teardown, track the resources created by the test and add cleanup logic after exercise and verification, using language constructs that run the cleanup regardless of the test outcome.
condition: when each test has different explicit cleanup needs

statement: Use In-line Teardown only when tests have different objects to clean up; prefer Automated Teardown or Implicit Teardown when cleanup can be generalized or shared.
condition: when choosing an explicit teardown style

statement: Accumulated test-run detritus that causes unrepeatable or slow tests is evidence that explicit teardown is missing or inadequate.
condition: when persistent resources accumulate across test runs

statement: Teardown logic rarely improves tests as documentation and can raise maintenance cost, so avoid manually written teardown when garbage collection or automated teardown can handle the resources.

statement: Use Finder Methods with intent-revealing names to retrieve Shared Fixture objects while hiding lookup mechanics and clarifying which fixture object the test depends on.

condition: when designing finder helpers

statement: Wrap non-target SUT API calls or complicated SUT signatures in SUT Encapsulation Methods to reduce coupling and keep tests focused on the method or behavior under test.

condition: when several tests share the entire test algorithm and differ only by data

statement: Keep Test Utility Methods small and self-contained by passing required inputs explicitly and returning needed outputs explicitly.

statement: Write tests for Test Utility Methods when they contain nontrivial reusable logic that would otherwise be untested test code.
condition: when helper defects could undermine many tests

condition: when evolving helper code from concrete tests

condition: when several tests share the same full test flow

condition: when classifying reusable test helpers

condition: when many tests share the same algorithm

condition: when using one Test Method to execute many table rows

condition: when looping over a known table of inputs and outputs

condition: when expected values are derived procedurally inside the test

condition: when evaluating big-picture readability of per-class organization

condition: when one test class covers many states or features

condition: when per-fixture organization obscures feature boundaries

statement: Refactor to Testcase Class per Fixture by splitting methods into classes by fixture requirement, naming each class for its fixture, and moving needed instance variables with the tests.

condition: when completing a Testcase Class per Fixture refactor

statement: Use method names in Testcase Class per Fixture to show action and expected outcome, because the starting fixture is supplied by the class name.
condition: when naming tests after fixture-based splitting

statement: Testcase Class per Fixture can reveal missing tests by making the lineup of operations for each starting fixture easy to compare in an outline view.
condition: when verifying coverage across states or fixtures

condition: when shared test logic has broad reuse and inheritance is available

statement: Put reusable Testcase Superclass methods at a visibility level subclasses can access, such as protected in languages that enforce visibility.

condition: when documenting or reviewing an Object Mother

statement: Implement stateless Test Helper functionality as class methods, but avoid class variables unless deliberately building a shared fixture registry.
condition: when designing a helper class API

statement: Use Test Helper Objects with instance methods when the helper must hold fixture or SUT references while avoiding accidental shared fixture state.
condition: when helper state should be per test rather than global

condition: when coordination of several mocks is part of the helper's role

statement: Before moving a Test Utility Method to a Test Helper, convert any use of test instance variables for inputs or outputs into explicit arguments and return values.

statement: Use a Database Sandbox to give each developer or tester a separate test database so tests do not accidentally interact through shared persistent records.

statement: Make database selection externally configurable for tests so each user or test runner can point the application at its own database without code changes.
condition: when using Database Sandbox-style isolation

condition: when database licensing and infrastructure make separate instances practical

statement: Use DB Schema per Test Runner when separate database instances are impractical but the database supports multiple schemas.
condition: when each user needs apparent database isolation inside one database instance

statement: DB Schema per Test Runner can combine a shared immutable fixture schema with private mutable schemas for each user or runner.
condition: when tests need common read-only reference data and isolated mutable data

statement: Do not choose DB Schema per Test Runner when developers must freely evolve schema independently, because all users still share one database structure.
condition: when evolutionary database development requires private schema changes

condition: when users or tests can share one schema but must not touch each other's records

statement: Database Partitioning is inappropriate for evolutionary database development because it does not let developers change the schema independently.
condition: when database structure changes are part of the work

statement: Use unique per-test or per-runner keys in a Database Partitioning Scheme to prevent Interacting Tests within the same database.

statement: Replace literal database values with generated values seeded by runner-specific data when partitioning a shared database to avoid Test Run Wars.
condition: when tests create records with unique constraints in a shared database

statement: Write Fully Automated Tests for nontrivial stored procedures so database-resident logic is verified independently of the client application.
condition: when stored procedures or triggers contain meaningful behavior

condition: when indirect client tests are insufficient to validate database logic

condition: when designing setup and verification for database-resident logic

statement: Use In-Database Stored Procedure Tests when the stored-procedure team works primarily in the database language or keeps procedure code and tests in a database-focused repository.
condition: when database-language feedback and repository locality matter more than one unified application test run

statement: Be cautious with In-Database Stored Procedure Tests that access implementation details, because deeper access can produce overspecified tests.
condition: when testing stored procedures inside the database environment

statement: Even with in-database procedure tests, keep application-language tests for the data access layer so client-side connection and error-handling behavior is covered.
condition: when client code uses a data access layer to call stored procedures

statement: Use Remoted Stored Procedure Tests when keeping tests in the application language and running them with the application build is more valuable than in-database execution.
condition: when application developers need stored procedure tests in their normal xUnit environment

statement: Treat Remoted Stored Procedure Tests as black-box component tests through a Remote Proxy such as a facade or command wrapper.
condition: when calling stored procedures from outside the database

statement: Use Remoted Stored Procedure Tests as acceptance tests for procedures supplied by another team when confidence in their own procedure tests is low.
condition: when a consuming team must validate externally delivered stored procedures

statement: Place slow Remoted Stored Procedure Tests in a separate subset suite when they require a live populated database and would slow in-memory test runs.
condition: when database-dependent procedure tests make the full suite slow

statement: Use Remoted Stored Procedure Tests to preserve existing application-language tests when logic is moved into the database, reducing translation risk while checking equivalent results.
condition: when recoding previously tested logic as stored procedures

statement: Hide stored-procedure call mechanics behind a proxy or facade so tests read like ordinary function tests and can also cover connection and error cases.
condition: when writing remoted tests for stored procedures

statement: Use Table Truncation Teardown to remove all data from database tables modified by tests instead of writing complex per-object cleanup logic.
condition: when tests use database tables whose entire mutable contents may be cleared

statement: Prefer Transaction Rollback Teardown for database fresh fixtures when it is practical; choose Table Truncation Teardown when rollback is unsuitable, especially for shared fixtures.
condition: when selecting database teardown strategy

statement: Use Table Truncation Teardown only when all data in affected tables may be removed and each Test Runner has its own Database Sandbox.
condition: when considering truncation or delete-all cleanup

statement: Do not use Table Truncation Teardown with Database Partitioning Scheme isolation because clearing whole tables would remove other users' or tests' data.
condition: when tests share one schema through partitioned data

statement: Table Truncation Teardown fits DB Schema per Test Runner with immutable shared data in a separate schema, because the runner can clear its private mutable schema without touching shared fixtures.
condition: when immutable reference data and private mutable data are separated by schema

statement: If truncation cannot be used, use Automated Teardown to delete only records created by the test or use Delta Assertions to avoid needing teardown for verification.
condition: when table-wide cleanup is unavailable or too broad

statement: Implement Table Truncation Teardown by deciding the delete command, the handling of foreign keys and triggers, and any ORM cache clearing required after deletion.
condition: when building database table cleanup helpers

statement: Use native TRUNCATE where supported; otherwise issue delete-all commands through In-line, Implicit, or Lazy Teardown as appropriate.
condition: when selecting database cleanup commands

statement: Handle foreign-key constraints during table cleanup with cascade support or by truncating tables in dependency order; encapsulate the order behind a Test Utility Method.
condition: when table dependencies affect cleanup

statement: Disable constraints or triggers during table cleanup only if other tests exercise the SUT with those database behaviors enabled.
condition: when considering bypassing database-side behavior for teardown

statement: Clear ORM caches after database cleanup when cached objects might otherwise make subsequent lookups see deleted data.
condition: when tests use an ORM with identity or query caches

statement: Use Lazy Teardown by clearing tables at the beginning of fixture setup when cleanup can be performed without remembering what the previous test created.
condition: when table cleanup is identical regardless of prior test activity

statement: Lazy Table Truncation Teardown simplifies tests by ensuring a known database state before setup and by eliminating try/finally cleanup from the Test Method.
condition: when stale data from prior tests is the main cleanup risk

statement: When database cleanup is delegated to a helper, protect that helper so a failure inside cleanup does not prevent the rest of teardown from completing.
condition: when cleanup spans multiple tables or resources

statement: With ORM-based table cleanup, delete root domain classes when cascade rules will remove children, reducing coupling to the physical table layout.
condition: when using ORM APIs instead of raw SQL for teardown

statement: Use Transaction Rollback Teardown by keeping test database changes uncommitted and rolling back the transaction during teardown.
condition: when database transactions can isolate all changes made by the test

statement: For Transaction Rollback Teardown, start a transaction before fixture setup, perform setup, exercise, and verification inside it, then roll the transaction back at teardown.
condition: when a test's database work can remain inside one transaction

statement: Use Transaction Rollback Teardown with Fresh Fixtures when the database supports rollback and the test can keep all changes uncommitted.
condition: when database-backed tests need repeatable cleanup

statement: Transaction Rollback Teardown requires SUT methods that run inside an existing transaction and do not start or commit their own transaction.
condition: when tests rely on the outer test transaction for cleanup

statement: Refactor transaction-controlling service methods toward a Humble Transaction Controller before applying Transaction Rollback Teardown to existing code.
condition: when the SUT currently starts or commits transactions internally

statement: Transaction Rollback Teardown leaves database contents as they were before the test without requiring the test to know which records need cleanup.
condition: when many database changes may occur during a test

statement: Database schema or content changes normally do not force changes to rollback teardown logic, unlike table-specific truncation or object-by-object cleanup.
condition: when database cleanup logic is costly to maintain

statement: Expect real-database rollback tests to be much slower than in-memory tests; use an In-Memory Database for most tests when possible, but ensure any fake used for rollback semantics supports ACID-like behavior.
condition: when balancing speed against transactional behavior coverage

statement: Do not use Transaction Rollback Teardown when the test or exercised code performs commits, including implicit commits from operations such as DDL.

statement: Transaction Rollback Teardown can reduce post-failure inspectability because the database changes a failing test made may already have been rolled back.
condition: when diagnosing database test failures requires inspecting changed records

statement: Do not mix tests that must commit with tests that assume rollback-preserved base state in the same rollback-dependent suite.

statement: When framework support is absent, Transaction Rollback Teardown is straightforward to code, but the harder issue is exposing nontransactional SUT methods for tests to call.
condition: when implementing rollback teardown manually

statement: For subcutaneous tests through transaction-controlling facades, expose nontransactional variants via a Humble Transaction Controller, transactional decorator, or self-delegating wrapper method.
condition: when facade methods currently own transaction control

statement: If nontransactional SUT methods exist but are not visible to tests, expose them through public API, a Test-Specific Subclass, or an Extract Testable Component refactoring.
condition: when tests need access to transaction-free behavior

statement: Read updated database state from within the same transaction used by the test, or verification may not see uncommitted fixture and exercise changes.
condition: when verifying database state under rollback teardown

statement: Flush ORM-managed changes before direct database reads inside the same transaction when the ORM might otherwise keep changes only in memory.

statement: To refactor from In-line Teardown to Transaction Rollback Teardown, begin the transaction before fixture setup, replace object-specific cleanup with rollback, and make creation helpers avoid commits.

statement: A generic rollback call can live in tearDown instead of each test's finally block when every test follows the same transaction pattern.

statement: For transaction-script style code, create the database connection and transaction in setup, attach commands to that transaction, then roll back and close in teardown.

statement: If the xUnit framework reuses Testcase Objects, clear transaction and connection fields in teardown to avoid stale references between tests.
condition: when the framework does not instantiate a fresh test object per method

statement: Prefer Dependency Injection for unit tests when practical because it makes collaborator replacement explicit at the point where the SUT is exercised.

statement: Use Test Hooks only as a last-choice substitution mechanism compared with Dependency Injection or Dependency Lookup.
