statement: Use a Humble Container Adapter to keep logic components container-independent and adapt them to application-server interfaces only at the edge.
condition: when container interfaces make otherwise testable logic slow or difficult to exercise

statement: All Humble Object variants should expose the meaningful logic through synchronous tests, regardless of whether the exposure uses extracted methods, extracted classes, or subclassing.
condition: when designing a testability refactor for hard-to-test components

statement: When feasible, verify that the Humble Object delegates to extracted logic by replacing that logic with a Test Double.
condition: when testing the thin adapter itself is worthwhile

statement: Use a Poor Man's Humble Object by extracting testable logic into visible methods when the framework object can still be instantiated and the method does not depend on unavailable context.
condition: when a full extracted class is unnecessary and direct instantiation is possible

statement: Use a Test-Specific Subclass to make a Poor Man's Humble Object instantiable or to expose private extracted methods when constructors or visibility block tests.
condition: when poor-man extraction still leaves testability barriers

statement: A subclassed spy can test a Poor Man's or Subclassed Humble Object by recording calls to extracted methods for later assertions.
condition: when verifying delegation inside a subclass-based humble object

statement: Use a True Humble Object by extracting logic into a separate class and delegating from the framework object to an instance of that class.
condition: when code control allows a clean separation between adapter and logic

statement: If a framework forces some data to remain on the Humble Object, prefer giving the testable component a reference to the Humble Object over leaving substantial untested update logic in the adapter.
condition: when framework-owned state must be manipulated by extracted logic

statement: Refactor to a True Humble Object by extracting methods that separate the public framework-facing interface from implementation logic, then extracting the implementation methods into a new testable class.
condition: when converting a framework-bound class into adapter plus logic component

statement: Initialize the extracted testable component through a field, constructor, or lazy initialization in the Humble Object's interface methods.
condition: when wiring a true humble adapter to its logic class

statement: For Humble Objects invoked on another thread, prefer a Lazy Mock Object or Test Spy over an Active Mock Object because assertion failures on the wrong thread may not reach the Testcase Object.
condition: when verifying delegation from asynchronous framework code

statement: Use an observable or replaceable factory to verify that a Humble Object instantiates the extracted component correctly.
condition: when construction of the extracted component is itself part of wrapper behavior

statement: Subclassed Humble Object variants can expose testable logic through inheritance or abstract-method delegation when a full separate testable class is impractical.
condition: when language or framework constraints favor subclass-based separation

statement: Avoid testing active objects primarily through sleeps and asynchronous execution, because startup delays make suites slow and exceptions on the active thread may not fail the test reliably.
condition: when code runs in its own thread or process

statement: For a Poor Man's Humble Executable, expose the extracted logic methods so tests can call them synchronously without starting the thread or process.
condition: when the executable component can still be instantiated cheaply

statement: When exposing executable logic for synchronous tests, remove context dependencies from the extracted methods by introducing parameters or fields.
condition: when extracted logic would otherwise reach into the active object's runtime context

statement: For a True Humble Executable, extract the request-processing and initialization logic into a separate testable component and leave the executable shell to delegate to it.
condition: when active-object logic should be tested without asynchronous execution

statement: Use synchronous tests against the extracted Humble Executable component to cover individual transactions without per-test startup delays.
condition: when many active-object scenarios need focused tests

statement: Verify the Humble Executable's delegation separately with a Test Spy or recording stub, accepting that this wrapper test may still need a short asynchronous wait.
condition: when confirming that the executable shell calls the extracted component

statement: Move slow asynchronous wrapper tests to a less frequent suite when the extracted synchronous component tests already cover the main logic before check-in.
condition: when wrapper tests are few but still slower than normal unit tests

statement: Use a Test Spy rather than a Mock Object for cross-thread Humble Object delegation checks unless assertion failures can be relayed back to the test thread.
condition: when the collaborator is called from a different thread than the Test Method

statement: Add a constructor or wiring test when a Humble Object must initialize its delegate to a specific default implementation.
condition: when delegate instantiation is part of the wrapper contract

statement: For Humble Dialog, extract view/controller logic into a nonvisual component that can be tested synchronously outside the presentation framework.
condition: when GUI framework coupling makes direct view tests difficult or slow

statement: Pass the Humble Dialog or a test double for it into the nonvisual component when extracted logic must update view state.
condition: when nonvisual UI logic still needs to read or modify view data

statement: Let the nonvisual component register directly for framework events when doing so avoids delegation without introducing unmanageable framework-context dependencies.
condition: when GUI event registration can be moved safely out of the view object

statement: Extract a Humble Dialog by moving both methods and fields needed by the logic into a testable component, leaving the view object as a thin shell.
condition: when refactoring presentation logic out of a framework-bound view

statement: Use a Test Hook only as a method of last resort when neither Dependency Injection nor Dependency Lookup can introduce the needed test-specific behavior.
condition: when a hard-coded dependency blocks testing and better substitution mechanisms are unavailable

statement: A Test Hook changes SUT or DOC behavior for tests through a flag checked inside the production code path.
condition: when identifying a test hook

statement: Use Test Hooks as a temporary safety-net strategy for legacy code, then refactor toward more testable designs and discard hook-dependent tests when modern coverage exists.
condition: when bringing legacy hard-coded-dependency code under test

statement: A Test Hook can divert control to a Test Double, embed test-double behavior inside the real object, or act as a test-specific decorator around the real object.
condition: when implementing a hook-based test seam

statement: Prefer compile-time or preprocessor-controlled Test Hooks over runtime flags when possible, because they can be removed or optimized out of production builds.
condition: when a Test Hook cannot be avoided

statement: If a Test Hook must be introduced, placing it in the depended-on component is usually less intrusive than modifying the SUT under test.
condition: when choosing where to put hook-based behavior

statement: Use Literal Values when a test requirement specifies exact fixture or expected values and seeing those values inline improves clarity.
condition: when exact data values are part of the specification

statement: Avoid overusing inline Literal Values when relationships between setup and expected outcome matter, because duplicated hard-coded values can obscure cause and effect.
condition: when expected values derive from fixture values

statement: Consider Data-Driven Tests instead of manually copying large sets of exact Literal Values into many Test Methods.
condition: when requirements provide substantial tabular example data

statement: Do not use the same Literal Value for unrelated attributes, because a defect that reads the wrong attribute may still pass the test.
condition: when several attributes share the same type or shape

statement: Avoid unexplained literal filenames or database keys when the referenced file or record content drives behavior, because the value alone does not document the test.
condition: when a literal key hides the meaningful fixture data

statement: Use Derived Values when expected outcomes are calculated from fixture setup values, and use Generated Values when specific values are irrelevant to the behavior under test.
condition: when deciding between literal, derived, and generated values

statement: Replace duplicated Literal Values with Symbolic Constants whose names explain the role of the value and reduce maintenance cost.
condition: when the same value appears in setup and verification or across tests

statement: Use Self-Describing Values for unconstrained strings or irrelevant mandatory attributes so failures and fixture setup communicate the value's role.
condition: when a value's exact content does not affect the behavior under test

statement: Use Distinct Values for same-kind attributes when the test must prove that the SUT uses the correct attribute rather than another similar one.
condition: when multiple attributes could be confused by the implementation

statement: Use Derived Inputs to make relationships between similar fixture values explicit, such as deriving one value from a base value plus a named allowable difference.
condition: when the SUT compares or reasons about relationships between input values

statement: For input-validation tests on complex objects, create a valid object with a Creation Method and then change exactly one attribute to an invalid value in each test.
condition: when validating each attribute independently

statement: Keep each One Bad Attribute case in a separate Single-Condition Test because the first rejected value may stop the SUT before later invalid values are examined.
condition: when testing validation failures for multiple attributes

statement: Use Derived Expectations when the expected output is deterministically related to fixture values or SUT arguments, so the test shows the relationship instead of hiding it in a precalculated literal.
condition: when expected results are calculated from setup or input values

statement: Use Derived Values for deterministic relationships, but add a few literal pathological cases when the test and SUT could share the same calculation or rounding mistake.
condition: when derived test math could mirror production math incorrectly

statement: Use Generated Values when the exact attribute value is irrelevant or must be decided at runtime, especially inside Creation Methods that hide incidental fixture data.
condition: when specific values distract from the behavior under test

statement: Generate values at runtime to satisfy properties such as uniqueness that may only be knowable as the test run unfolds.
condition: when uniqueness or noncollision is a runtime concern

statement: Generated Values can prevent Unrepeatable Tests and Test Run Wars when unique attributes would otherwise collide across reruns or parallel runs.
condition: when persistent stores or unique constraints are involved

statement: Avoid Generated Values unless uniqueness or runtime selection is needed, because changing values can expose different bugs and make tests nondeterministic.
condition: when a fixed Literal or Derived Value would be adequate

statement: Use sequence-based Distinct Generated Values for repeatable uniqueness; prefer database sequences for shared database scope and in-memory counters for per-run scope.
condition: when implementing generated unique values

statement: In-memory sequence generators that restart each test suite can improve debugging because generated values repeat across runs.
condition: when uniqueness is needed only inside one run

statement: Use Random Generated Values only when the additional coverage is worth nondeterminism, and log or expose the chosen value so failures can be reproduced.
condition: when randomized test data is necessary

statement: Use Related Generated Values by deriving all fields of one object from the same generated root when recognizing the object during debugging matters.
condition: when generated fields should be visually associated with the same fixture object

statement: Add role-describing text to generated strings so the generated value remains intent-revealing.
condition: when producing generated string attributes

statement: Do not generate values that affect the behavior being verified, because verification then has to accommodate irrelevant variation.
condition: when the tested logic depends on that value, such as price calculation depending on price

statement: Use a Dummy Object for required arguments or attributes that the SUT path under test should not use.
condition: when constructing real irrelevant collaborators would clutter fixture setup

statement: A Dummy Object should have no meaningful implementation and should fail loudly if the SUT unexpectedly invokes it.
condition: when implementing a dummy object

statement: Use Dummy Objects to reduce Obscure Tests by removing irrelevant construction and making unused dependencies explicit.
condition: when fixture setup includes objects unrelated to the behavior under test

statement: Use a Test Stub or Mock Object instead of a Dummy Object when the test needs to control indirect inputs or verify indirect outputs.
condition: when the collaborator's behavior matters to the test

statement: Use a Fake Object instead of a Dummy Object when the SUT will use the object and the real object cannot be supplied.
condition: when a collaborator must provide behavior but not the full production implementation

statement: Use Literal, Generated, or Derived Values rather than Dummy Objects when the SUT genuinely uses the value in the behavior under test.
condition: when the argument or attribute affects execution

statement: Passing null is the simplest dummy only when the called code accepts null and will not dereference it; otherwise use a more descriptive or type-compatible dummy.
condition: when considering null as a dummy argument

statement: In dynamically typed languages, use a simple self-describing object or value as a dummy when the argument will never be used.
condition: when runtime type is irrelevant because no methods will be called

statement: In statically typed languages, make Dummy Objects type-compatible through an interface implementation, Pseudo-Object, trivial real instance, or Test-Specific Subclass.
condition: when the parameter type constrains dummy construction

statement: Do not confuse Dummy Objects with Null Objects: a dummy should not be used, while a Null Object is used deliberately and supplies do-nothing behavior.
condition: when choosing a placeholder object pattern

statement: Inline a simple Dummy Object constructor call when the dummy is needed only for that one call and no later test code should refer to it.
condition: when a dummy has no role beyond satisfying a constructor or method signature

statement: Extract a Testable Component when logic is tied to an untestable context; move the logic into a synchronous component and leave the original context-bound object as a Humble Object.
condition: when context coupling blocks direct tests of important logic

statement: When extracting a testable component, have the context-bound object retrieve context data and pass it to the component through method or constructor arguments.
condition: when extracted logic still needs data from its original environment

statement: Keep delegation tests for an Extracted Testable Component minimal and run them in the build if they are too slow for every local check-in.
condition: when the remaining context-bound adapter is small and stable

statement: Inline external resource contents into test fixture setup when a hidden file, database record, or external object creates a Mystery Guest.
condition: when test preconditions are hidden in an unseen resource

statement: If inlining an external resource would require large data, first consider whether the test is eager and whether Extract Method or Minimize Data would make it smaller.
condition: when a resource is too large to inline cleanly

statement: Creating and deleting an external resource inside the test can turn a prebuilt fixture into a persistent fresh fixture, improving visibility at the cost of slower execution.
condition: when replacing unseen prebuilt files or records

statement: Replace an external resource with a Test Stub initialized inside the test when the SUT can be redirected to the stub and the resource contents should be visible.
condition: when resource access can be substituted

statement: Alternatively, extract the logic that consumes a resource into a testable component that receives the resource contents directly, and test the resource-reading Humble Object separately with a stub or mock.
condition: when resource access and resource-consuming logic can be separated

statement: Make every test-created resource name unique across tests and simultaneous runs to prevent accidental sharing of resources.
condition: when tests allocate files, database records, directories, queues, or other named resources

statement: Include the owning test name in unique resource identifiers when possible so leaked resources can be traced back to the test that allocated them.
condition: when generated resource names are visible in logs, databases, or file systems

statement: Combine time- or sequence-based unique resource names with Automated Teardown so resources do not collide and are removed after the test.
condition: when tests create named resources that persist outside process memory

statement: Minimize test fixture data to the bare essentials so tests document the relevant behavior and become less sensitive to unrelated fixture changes.
condition: when fixture setup is large or hard to understand

statement: When reducing a General Fixture in Testcase Class per Fixture, remove suspected unused setup incrementally so a failing test identifies the last removed dependency.
condition: when trimming shared setup for one fixture-focused class

statement: When minimizing data in per-feature or per-class test organization, move only the needed fixture setup into the tests that require it via Creation Methods, then convert fixture instance variables to locals where possible.
condition: when shared setup is larger than any one test needs

statement: For Replace Dependency with Test Double, choose the substitution mechanism first: Dependency Injection usually fits unit tests, while Dependency Lookup often fits broader customer tests.
condition: when a dependency blocks testing

statement: After choosing the substitution mechanism, choose the Test Double role according to test purpose: Fake Object for runnable replacement, Test Stub for indirect inputs, Test Spy for captured indirect outputs, or Mock Object for expected interactions.
condition: when replacing a depended-on component

statement: For stubs and mocks, decide between hard-coded and configurable implementations before shaping the test, because mocks especially front-load setup with expectations.
condition: when designing a test double implementation

statement: Modify tests using a replacement dependency to construct the double, configure it if needed, install it into the SUT, and call final verification when the mock framework requires it.
condition: when implementing Replace Dependency with Test Double

statement: In statically typed languages, extract an interface when needed so the real dependency and fake implementation can share a substitutable type.
condition: when the compiler blocks installing a Test Double

statement: Use Setup External Resource when the SUT must use an external file, directory, or database resource and the access cannot be replaced with a stub or fake.
condition: when an external resource is unavoidable

statement: Setup External Resource avoids Mystery Guest and Resource Optimism by creating the resource in the test setup and releasing it afterward, but it does not by itself prevent Test Run Wars.
condition: when deciding what external-resource refactoring solves

statement: Pull external resource contents into the Test Method, setUp method, or a Test Utility Method so readers can see the resource data and the test can create it every run.
condition: when implementing Setup External Resource

statement: Use precise Test Double role names: Dummy Objects are not called, Test Stubs supply indirect inputs, Test Spies capture indirect outputs for later assertions, Mock Objects verify indirect outputs against expectations, and Fake Objects provide a runnable alternative implementation.
condition: when documenting or reviewing tests that use doubles

statement: Because testing terminology varies across authors and tools, clarify the intended Test Double role instead of relying on ambiguous words such as stub or mock.
condition: when communicating test-design advice across teams or frameworks

statement: Account for xUnit framework differences in lifecycle hooks, suite setup/teardown, expected-exception support, and test discovery names when applying xUnit patterns across languages.
condition: when porting or generalizing xUnit testing practices

statement: Do not use HTTP-level web testing tools that bypass the browser when the application behavior depends heavily on browser-side scripting such as AJAX.
condition: when selecting a web application test tool

statement: Use higher-level web test utility methods or DSL-like helpers when they make web tests more expressive than raw protocol-level calls.
condition: when building web application tests on top of lower-level HTTP tooling

statement: Prefer mock frameworks with readable fluent configuration interfaces when expected interactions would otherwise be hard to understand.
condition: when choosing or evaluating dynamic mock tooling

statement: Recorded-test tools are most useful when recorded scripts can be refactored into reusable test components rather than left as brittle raw recordings.
condition: when using record/playback testing tools

statement: Use customer-facing table or wiki-style test tools when the desired separation is for customers to define examples while programmers implement fixtures that exercise the SUT.
condition: when choosing a customer-test automation style

statement: Design depended-on components as substitutable dependencies so tests can replace them with Test Doubles through Dependency Injection, Dependency Lookup, or Test-Specific Subclassing.
condition: when unit-testing a component independently of its collaborators

statement: Prefer synchronous tests where practical because method-call interactions do not require explicit coordination with a separately executing SUT.
condition: when choosing between direct logic tests and asynchronous end-to-end tests

statement: Describe a test condition in terms of starting state, exercise action, expected response, and resulting state.
condition: when specifying or naming a test scenario

statement: Never use the production database as the test database.
condition: when configuring database-backed automated tests

statement: Treat missing necessary tests as test debt because unprotected code can break without any test failing.
condition: when assessing test coverage risk

statement: For bug fixes, first write and automate a test that reproduces the bug, then debug and fix the code against that test.
condition: when repairing a reported defect

statement: Do not change production equality semantics merely to satisfy one test's comparison needs; use Custom Assertions for test-specific equality.
condition: when expected equality differs by test or differs from production equality

statement: Use a test suite to name and run a meaningful collection of tests together.
condition: when recurring subsets or grouped execution matter

statement: Use the observed test smell to drive remediation: erratic tests point toward interaction, resource, loneliness, or nondeterminism causes; obscure tests point toward overlarge fixtures, hidden guests, hard-coded data, or irrelevant detail; fragile tests point toward overspecification or sensitivity to data, context, behavior, interface, fixture, or equality.
condition: when diagnosing failing or hard-to-maintain test suites

statement: Choose result-verification patterns by the outcome to check: State Verification for final state, Behavior Verification through Test Spies or Mock Objects for indirect outputs, Custom Assertions for reusable comparison logic, and Delta Assertions for relative database or collection changes.
condition: when deciding how a self-checking test should verify behavior

statement: Choose fixture patterns by lifecycle need: Minimal or Standard Fixture for small setup, Fresh Fixture for independent tests, Shared Fixture only when setup cost justifies the risk, and explicit teardown patterns when resources outlive the test.
condition: when selecting setup and teardown strategy

statement: Choose testability patterns by the blocking force: use Test Doubles for troublesome collaborators, Humble Object or Test-Specific Subclass for hard-to-test code, Dependency Injection or Dependency Lookup for runtime replacement, and Test Hook only as the last resort.
condition: when code structure prevents focused automated tests

statement: Tests should be engineered to find bugs by exercising boundaries, corner cases, and unusual inputs, not treated merely as tool syntax or framework usage.
Developers share responsibility for the quality of the software they produce, so testing cannot be delegated away entirely to a separate role.
Tests provide both development feedback and bug-finding value; using them only as a design feedback tool leaves part of their purpose unused.
Manual testing by trying a few remembered inputs is too slow and narrow to explore enough cases in nontrivial code.
Ad hoc test selection based only on intuition can miss corner cases even when the developer is experienced.
A systematic approach to deriving tests reduces the chance that important input classes are forgotten.
Automating tests lets developers rerun many cases cheaply instead of spending excessive time on manual execution.
For methods that accept a list, reviewers should consider null, empty, single-element, and multiple-element inputs as distinct test classes.
condition: when a method receives a list-like input

statement: Invalid-input handling should be based on the surrounding product semantics rather than assumed from the implementation alone.
condition: when deciding expected behavior for edge inputs

statement: Once validation logic is added for invalid inputs, automated tests should lock in that behavior as regression protection.
condition: when invalid inputs are intentionally rejected or handled

statement: Each important invalid input class deserves a test that verifies the observable failure behavior, including the expected exception type when applicable.
condition: when the API contract specifies rejection behavior

statement: Boundary values between rejected and accepted inputs deserve dedicated tests because defects commonly occur around those transitions.
condition: when an input domain has a validity boundary

statement: Valid-path tests should include the smallest valid case as well as larger representative cases.
condition: when an input domain has a minimum valid size or value

statement: For algorithms over collections, input ordering should be treated as a potential source of defects and tested explicitly when order should not affect the outcome.
condition: when the algorithm processes collection elements
exception: unless the specification intentionally makes order observable

statement: Property-based testing is useful when a behavior can be stated as an invariant over many generated inputs rather than as one manually chosen example.
condition: when the expected behavior can be expressed as a property over an input space

statement: A property-based test can expose bugs missed by several example-based tests because it repeatedly exercises varied input combinations.
When a property-based test fails, the reported failing input should be used to understand and fix the underlying defect.
condition: when the property-testing framework reports a counterexample

statement: If a broader property-based test covers the same behavior as a narrow example test, keeping or deleting the example should be decided by whether it still helps explain the behavior.
condition: when a property-based test subsumes an example-based test

statement: Duplicate elements or equal values in collection inputs are common corner cases and should be considered during test design.
condition: when a method consumes collections or ranked values

statement: Tie-breaking behavior should be made explicit with stakeholders and then captured in tests.
condition: when multiple inputs are equally eligible for a result

statement: Testing can reveal missing product decisions, because thinking through edge cases may uncover requirements the team has not specified.
When all collection elements are equal or otherwise collapse a distinction the algorithm expects, that degenerate case should be considered separately.
condition: when the algorithm selects extrema or compares elements

statement: Code coverage can help identify implementation paths that tests have not exercised.
condition: when evaluating whether a test suite exercises the code

statement: High line or branch coverage is not sufficient proof that testing is complete, so coverage results should be supplemented by human review of remaining behavioral cases.
condition: when using coverage to assess a test suite

statement: A test suite should be judged against requirements-derived cases and implementation-derived gaps, not only against whether the initially observed bug is fixed.

Effective developer testing combines requirements-derived cases, structural analysis, boundary analysis, property-based exploration, contract thinking, and automation rather than relying on one technique.
Tests used to guide development and tests used to find bugs are distinct activities with different mindsets, even though both can happen in the same workflow.
Short TDD cycles can provide rapid feedback during implementation and support refactoring.
After implementing a unit or feature slice, developers should deliberately switch to bug-finding techniques such as domain, boundary, and structural testing.
condition: when the developer has a working unit or feature slice

statement: Larger tests can use the same domain, boundary, and structural reasoning at integration or system scope.
condition: when behavior spans multiple components or external boundaries

statement: Automated analysis techniques such as mutation testing, static analysis, and test generation can complement human-designed tests by finding cases humans often miss.
condition: after human-designed test cases have been engineered

statement: Effective testing is iterative: discoveries during testing can send the developer back to design, requirement clarification, bug fixing, or partial-feature testing.
Developers may adapt the order of testing and design techniques to what is productive for their context.
Separating the development mindset from the testing mindset can help developers focus first on design and implementation, then on systematic bug discovery.
condition: when the developer can defer remembered corner cases without losing them

statement: Potential test ideas that arise during coding should be recorded so they can be exercised later during focused testing.
condition: when a corner case appears while the developer is still implementing

statement: Generic testing checklists should be applied before relying on creativity and domain knowledge for additional cases.
condition: when a known input structure or code structure has standard test classes

statement: Simple and clean design lowers defect risk but does not eliminate the need for testing.
TDD should not be assumed to replace systematic testing because TDD tests often primarily guide design and development.
condition: when TDD is used during implementation

statement: Rigorous testing costs more than skipping testing, but production defects and repeated bug-fix loops can cost more than prevention.
Developers can reduce the cost of systematic test design through practice.
Effective testing means choosing tests that maximize bug-finding value while minimizing the effort spent to find bugs.
A testing technique should make clear where to start and what stopping criterion to use.
condition: when teaching or applying a test design technique

statement: Systematic testing aims for different developers to derive similar test suites for the same code, reducing dependence on individual intuition.
Much of test design can be systematized so human creativity can focus on context-specific and genuinely novel cases.
Testing frameworks mainly automate execution and reporting; they do not solve the harder problem of designing bug-revealing test cases.
Test case design and test case automation should be treated as separate concerns even if they are interleaved in practice.
Exhaustive testing is impossible for realistic systems, so developers must choose and prioritize which cases to test.
Testing should be guided by adequacy criteria that help decide when enough testing has been done for the current goal.
condition: when deciding whether to stop adding tests

statement: No single testing technique can reveal all defects, so teams should combine different testing strategies.
A suite concentrated at one test level can miss defects that only appear at another level, such as integration bugs missed by unit tests.
condition: when all testing effort is concentrated in one level or strategy

statement: Testing effort should be prioritized because defects are not uniformly distributed across components.
Historical project data and non-code signals can help identify components that deserve more rigorous testing.
condition: when such data is available and relevant

statement: Passing tests show that tested cases behave as expected; they do not prove the software has no bugs.
Teams should pair testing with production monitoring because some bugs will still escape test suites.
Testing strategy must account for context, because applications in different domains and platforms require different case design concerns.
Verification should not be confused with validation: code can satisfy specified behavior while still failing user needs.
Systematic testing can surface validation questions by exposing edge cases that product experts had not considered.
Unit testing focuses on a small unit of work in isolation from uncontrolled external systems.
Unit tests are valuable because they are fast, easy to control, and relatively easy to write.
Unit tests are limited because they do not fully represent real system execution and cannot reveal all integration-level defects.
A unit may be a method, class, or small collaborating set of classes if it represents one logical purpose that can be verified without external dependencies.
Dependencies on external systems may be simulated in unit tests when the focus is the local class and the external system would make automated tests harder to control.
condition: when the dependency is outside the unit focus and difficult to control in automated tests

statement: Integration testing should be used when the purpose is to verify communication between code and an external component, not the whole system end to end.
condition: when behavior crosses a component or external-system boundary

statement: Integration tests are usually harder than unit tests because they require setup, state management, schema or environment alignment, and cleanup.
System tests exercise the entire deployed system and treat internal implementation details as irrelevant to the expected input-output behavior.
System tests provide higher realism because they exercise the system in ways closer to how final users interact with it.
System tests are typically slower than unit tests because they start and coordinate the whole system and its dependencies.
System tests are harder to write when components such as databases require connection setup, authentication, fixture data, or other automation-only scaffolding.
condition: when the system test involves externally stateful components

statement: System tests are more prone to flakiness because they contain more uncontrolled timing, infrastructure, and dependency variation.
A test-level choice affects quality and cost because the wrong level can consume too many resources while still missing important defects.
The appropriate balance among unit, integration, and system tests depends on the system context rather than on a universal rule.
The testing pyramid favors many unit tests, fewer integration tests, fewer system tests, and minimal manual tests because higher levels are usually more realistic but more complex.
Unit tests are a good default for algorithmic or business-rule code because they provide high controllability and observability at low execution cost.
condition: when the code can be exercised without uncontrolled external dependencies

statement: Developers should think about unit contracts when relying heavily on unit tests, because those contracts increase confidence that separately tested units will collaborate correctly.
condition: when testing units that will later collaborate with other units

statement: Integration and system tests should focus on parts where unit tests are insufficient, such as risky integrations or high-impact user journeys.
condition: when unit-level tests cannot represent an important risk

statement: Retesting every behavior at every test level is usually too expensive to be worthwhile.
Business logic that cannot be unit tested may indicate design or architectural decisions that reduced testability.
condition: when the logic has no inherent need for external systems but can only be exercised through the whole application

statement: Infrastructure-facing code such as database access objects should be integration tested when the important question is whether the real query, transaction, or external communication works.
condition: when the class responsibility is communication with an external component

statement: Separating business rules from infrastructure code lets teams test business behavior mostly with unit tests and infrastructure behavior with integration tests.
condition: when designing code for testability

statement: System-level tests should be prioritized by risk, focusing on functions where a defect would have high customer or business impact.
condition: when system tests are costly to create and maintain

statement: Critical behavior should still be tested at lower levels even when it also receives system tests.
condition: when a feature is important enough to merit end-to-end coverage

statement: Exploratory manual testing can provide value for validation and insight even in a generally automated testing strategy.
condition: when the goal is to explore the built product or understand user-facing behavior

statement: A microservices-heavy system may justify more integration testing because important complexity often lies in inter-service communication.
condition: when the architecture is highly distributed and communication behavior carries substantial risk

statement: Even in integration-heavy systems, unit tests remain useful for verifying each service or component in isolation.
condition: when component-local behavior can be verified cheaply

statement: Distributed-system integration tests should cover normal communication variations such as delayed messages or duplicate deliveries.
condition: when testing distributed services or asynchronous communication

statement: Database-centric information systems may benefit more from integration and system tests than algorithm-heavy systems because core risk is the information flow through UI, persistence, and queries.
condition: when the application mainly stores, retrieves, and displays data with little complex business logic

statement: The choice between pyramid-like and trophy-like test mixes is partly contextual and experience-based rather than settled by strong scientific evidence.
Teams should choose the test mix that maximizes feedback and defect detection while minimizing writing cost, execution time, and flakiness for each part of the system.
Test-size classifications based on execution constraints can be more useful than boundary labels when the concern is speed and determinism.
condition: when comparing tests by execution cost and reliability

statement: Small tests are advantageous because they avoid major sources of slowness and nondeterminism.
condition: when a test can run in one process without external calls, threads, or parallelism

statement: Large tests should be reserved for full end-to-end scenarios because they involve multiple machines or unrestricted external calls.
condition: when tests require calls beyond localhost or multiple machines

statement: Methods and class-level testing techniques can often be generalized to coarse-grained components such as services, although larger components usually require more cases.
condition: when adapting unit-oriented examples to larger component boundaries

statement: The book’s techniques can find many important bug classes but should not be expected to find every possible defect.

statement: Requirements should be the first testing artifact because they define what the software must and must not do.

statement: Auxiliary methods in tests can improve maintainability and legibility by removing repetitive construction code.

statement: Whether a case is labeled as a partition or a boundary is less important than ensuring the case is tested.
condition: when a scenario could be modeled in either category

statement: Boundary discovery deserves extra effort because boundaries are often implicit and difficult for developers to notice.

condition: when a clear boundary and nearest off point exist

statement: Additional in/out points can be included when they improve understanding or represent realistic inputs at low maintenance cost.
condition: when extra points do not substantially bloat the suite

statement: Using small variations of a common input seed can make related partition tests easier to compare and debug.

statement: Specification-based testing may prefer controlled input similarity, while random or property-based testing can later explore broader input variation.

statement: When partition combinations explode, testers should reduce combinations using exception isolation and domain knowledge.

statement: Avoid complex input values unless they exercise a specific risk that simpler values do not.

statement: Inputs irrelevant to the behavior under test should use realistic values that do not distract from or interfere with the focused case.
condition: when a parameter is not part of the partition being exercised

condition: when considering exceptional-value tests

statement: Code close to the user interface deserves more weird input tests because it is more exposed to unsanitized values.
condition: when the component receives data near the external boundary of the system

statement: Parameterized tests should be considered when duplication across normal tests becomes large enough to harm readability or maintenance.

statement: State setup in tests is the main extra work when adapting input-output partitioning to object-oriented classes with state.

statement: A systematic recipe reduces but cannot eliminate the effect of tester experience and creativity on the final test suite.

statement: Source code can reveal missed requirement partitions and implementation-specific behavior that requirements do not explicitly mention.

statement: Code coverage should be used to identify unexercised code, not as a target number pursued for its own sake.

statement: If uncovered behavior is unclear from requirements, the tester should seek requirement clarification before deciding whether the code or the tests are wrong.

statement: Some uncovered code may not deserve a test, but the omission should be a conscious decision rather than an accidental gap.

statement: Coverage analysis should be iterated: add a needed test, rerun coverage, and inspect the remaining uncovered or partially covered code.

statement: For complex conditional expressions, each individual condition should be considered for both true and false evaluations.
condition: when a decision combines multiple boolean conditions

statement: Coverage reports can help a tester discover a missing partition, such as a requirement option not exercised by the current tests.

condition: when a statement can evaluate to true or false or otherwise choose among paths

statement: Condition plus branch coverage requires both each individual condition and the entire decision to evaluate true and false at least once.
condition: when decisions contain multiple conditions

statement: Basic condition coverage without branch coverage can miss behavior because individual conditions may vary while the whole decision never changes outcome.
condition: when a boolean expression combines conditions with operators such as OR or AND

statement: Path coverage is strongest in principle because it exercises all execution paths, but it is often infeasible as conditions and loops multiply combinations.

statement: For a decision with N binary conditions, full MC/DC can be achieved with about N+1 tests under the cited assumptions, which is cheaper than all 2^N combinations.
condition: when conditions have binary outcomes and an MC/DC-minimal set can be formed

statement: MC/DC test selection should use independence pairs where one condition changes, other conditions remain fixed, and the whole decision outcome changes.

condition: when multiple independence-pair selections satisfy the criterion

statement: Loop testing cannot exhaust every possible iteration count for long-running or unbounded loops.

condition: when a loop can be controlled into those iteration counts

statement: The multiple-iteration loop case may require domain understanding to decide whether two, five, ten, or several separate multi-iteration tests are needed.

condition: when one multi-iteration example is not representative enough

statement: Coverage criteria differ by rigor and cost, so criterion selection is an explicit trade-off.

Branch coverage subsumes line coverage, but full line coverage does not imply full branch coverage.
Condition plus branch coverage subsumes both branch coverage and basic condition coverage.
MC/DC is stronger than branch plus condition coverage because it requires each condition to independently influence the decision.
Weaker coverage criteria are cheaper and faster but leave more code behavior unexamined, while stronger criteria provide more rigor at higher cost.
Developers should choose a coverage criterion based on the desired rigor and acceptable testing cost for the code under review.
Basic condition coverage should not be used alone because it can miss unexecuted branches and therefore not even imply full line coverage.
condition: when a decision combines conditions such that the whole branch outcome can remain unchanged

statement: When testing unfamiliar code written by others, first build an understanding of the requirement and behavior before applying the same specification and structural techniques.
condition: when the tester did not implement the code

statement: After branch gaps are closed, testers should still inspect the implementation for behavior-relevant decisions that coverage alone does not demand.
condition: when structural coverage criteria have been satisfied

statement: Implementation decisions made for performance or object identity may deserve explicit tests if they are part of the intended behavior.
condition: when source code and comments indicate an observable implementation guarantee

statement: Boundary testing applies to source-code conditions as well as to specification partitions.
condition: when source code contains comparisons or boundary-like branches

statement: For comparison expressions in code, testers can identify on and off points directly from the condition and input domain.

statement: Equality comparisons in code have an on point at equality and off points on both neighboring sides when the domain is ordered and discrete.
condition: when analyzing equality-based code branches

statement: On/off analysis of source-code branches may be unnecessary when existing tests already cover the relevant branches, but it can reveal extra cases in other code.
condition: when branch coverage already exercises the meaningful code paths

statement: Loop conditions with unconventional or complex expressions may benefit from on/off boundary analysis in addition to loop boundary adequacy.
condition: when the loop guard itself contains meaningful boundary logic

statement: Structural testing alone is not enough because full branch coverage can still miss important requirement scenarios.

statement: Coverage-guided structural testing works best when combined with knowledge of the specification.

condition: when interpreting coverage from tests that may lack meaningful assertions

statement: Coverage metrics can be gamed when teams pursue a percentage target without asking whether the added tests are useful.

statement: Empirical evidence does not establish a universal coverage percentage that every project should target.

condition: when interpreting 100% line, branch, or condition coverage

statement: Coverage formulas and counted elements vary by tool, so developers should understand their specific tool’s definition before interpreting numbers.

statement: Coverage can be computed at method, class, package, or system scope depending on the testing question.

statement: Risk assessment should influence how rigorous a coverage criterion is chosen for a given code fragment.
condition: when deciding between line, branch, condition, MC/DC, or stronger criteria

statement: MC/DC is most valuable when expressions are too complex to simplify and path coverage would be impossible.

statement: Very complex boolean expressions should be avoided or broken into smaller testable parts when possible.
condition: when a decision contains many conditions or is difficult to reason about directly

statement: MC/DC is most useful when a complex expression cannot reasonably be simplified into smaller decisions.
condition: when path coverage is infeasible and decomposition is not practical

statement: Achieving the last portion of very high structural coverage can require disproportionately high effort.

statement: Unique-cause MC/DC requires an independence pair where only one condition changes and the whole decision outcome changes.

statement: If MC/DC cannot be achieved because a condition cannot independently affect the outcome, the expression should be revisited because it may be degenerate or poorly designed.

statement: The N+1 MC/DC test count is a theoretical lower bound and common in practice, but some expressions may require more tests.

statement: Data-flow coverage examines whether tests exercise the important ways variables are defined, modified, and used.

condition: when justifying an uncovered code path

statement: Coverage criteria measure code exercise, but they do not measure whether assertions are strong enough to detect introduced bugs.

statement: Mutation-testing ideas can apply beyond Java code, including web DOM behavior and SQL queries.

condition: when a class or method only makes sense for a restricted input domain

statement: Defining explicit contracts is preferable to ad hoc defensive coding when classes need clear responsibilities for valid inputs and guaranteed outputs.

statement: A class contract should state its preconditions, postconditions, and invariants.
condition: when designing behavior for a class or method

statement: Contract decisions often occur while implementing functionality because they guide design as well as testing.

Precondition checks let a method assume its inputs are inside the expected domain after the checks pass.
condition: when precondition checks are enforced at method entry

statement: Postcondition checks protect callers by preventing invalid outputs from silently propagating through the system.

statement: Failing fast with an exception can be safer than continuing computation with an invalid value in high-impact domains.

statement: Contracts should be documented as well as reflected in source code.

statement: The choice between language assertions and explicit exception-throwing checks should be made deliberately with the team.

statement: Explicit exceptions are preferable when callers need a specific exception type they can handle.

statement: Contract strength is a design decision: stronger preconditions reject more inputs, while weaker preconditions require the method to handle more inputs.

condition: when the method can compute an invalid output due to implementation error

statement: Returning an error value instead of throwing on invalid input is not the same as weakening a precondition; clients must still understand and handle the error convention.

statement: A contract design should explicitly decide what a method can handle, cannot handle, and should do when a contract violation occurs.

condition: when implementing operations that mutate object state

statement: Preconditions for mutating methods should prevent nonsensical state changes such as adding a null product or nonpositive quantity.

statement: Some postconditions require capturing old state before mutation so the new state can be compared against it.

statement: Contract changes should be evaluated by examining all clients that depend on the changed class or method.

statement: Strengthening a precondition is a breaking change for clients that were valid under the old broader input contract.

statement: Weakening a postcondition is a breaking change because clients may not be prepared for the broader set of returned values.
condition: when a method guarantees less about outputs than before

statement: Strengthening a postcondition is generally safe for existing clients because returned values remain within the old promised range.
condition: when a method guarantees a subset of its previous outputs

statement: A subtype must not strengthen the base type’s preconditions.

statement: A subtype must not weaken the base type’s postconditions.

statement: Design-by-contract is primarily a design technique even though it supports testing and debugging.

statement: The weak-versus-strong precondition choice should consider the whole API context and the expected clients.

statement: Validation protects the system from bad external data and should produce user-facing error feedback.

statement: Contracts protect communication between classes and normally indicate unexpected programmer or integration faults rather than polite user-correctable mistakes.

statement: Both validation and contracts can be needed because they address different failure boundaries.
