statement: Write the tests for code before writing the code itself.
TDD reframes testing away from merely keeping defects from users toward helping the team understand the features users need and deliver them reliably and predictably.
Applied thoroughly, TDD improves system quality, particularly reliability and flexibility in response to new requirements.
condition: based on the authors' professional experience rather than controlled study

statement: TDD is a core practice of Extreme Programming and is widely used across agile approaches such as Scrum and Crystal Clear.
Almost all non-routine software projects attempt something not done before, so elements of surprise are inherent.
Because everyone on a project must learn continuously, teams need a development process that helps them cope with uncertainty and anticipate unanticipated changes.
TDD works best when adopted as a whole; teams that perform only the raw practices of writing and running tests without the deeper design processes behind them struggle with the results.
condition: applies when a team adopts TDD
exception: unless the team also adopts the deeper processes behind the practices

statement: Grow software incrementally, keeping the code working at all times, always as well-structured as possible, and thoroughly tested.
Writing a test first forces you to clarify your intentions and to obtain an unambiguous description of a piece of work before starting it.
Writing a test first exposes when a design is too rigid or unfocused.
Existing tests give a regression safety net that makes it safer to follow through and fix a design flaw.
TDD requires skill, understanding, and sustained effort; it is a serious design activity, not an automatic technique.
Let the tests guide development: use the contents of the tests to stay focused on progress and the feedback from the tests to raise the quality of the system.
Writing tests first does not by itself guarantee good code; without letting the tests guide the design, the code can still be a mess and the tests merely raise maintenance cost.
exception: unless the team lets the tests guide development

statement: Mock objects are substitute implementations used to test how an object interacts with its neighbouring objects.
TDD can be crippled by organizational circumstances such as an early design freeze or stakeholders who do not communicate.
condition: in organizations with early design freeze or poor stakeholder communication

statement: Use empirical feedback to learn about the system and its use, then feed that learning back into the system through repeated cycles of adding features and measuring the work done.
Deploy completed work to a real-like environment on every cycle; without deployment the feedback is incomplete because assumptions are never checked against reality.

Organize a project as a system of nested feedback loops (pair programming, unit tests, acceptance tests, daily meetings, iterations, releases) so that a discrepancy missed by an inner loop can be caught by an outer one.
Get feedback about any aspect of the project as early as possible; more frequent releases give an order-of-magnitude increase in opportunities to respond to real-user feedback.
Develop incrementally: build the system feature by feature, each implemented as an end-to-end slice, keeping the system always integrated and ready for deployment.
Develop iteratively: progressively refine the implementation of features in response to feedback until they are good enough.
Automate testing as much as possible, because frequent manual testing is impractical for systems of any interesting size.
Keep code as simple as possible and optimize for reading, since developers spend far more time reading code than writing it.
Constantly refactor code as you work with it to improve and simplify its design, remove duplication, and make it clearly express what it does.
TDD turns testing into a design activity: write tests before the code to clarify your ideas about what the code should do.
Making code accessible for testing tends to drive it toward being cleaner and more modular.
The fundamental TDD cycle is: write a failing test, write just enough code to make it pass, then refactor to the simplest implementation of the tested features; then repeat.
Golden Rule of TDD: never write new functionality without a failing test.

Refactoring changes the internal structure of existing code without changing its behavior; apply a series of small, safe transformations and confirm the system still works (by running the tests) after each step.
Refactoring is distinct from redesign, but once a redesign decision is taken a team can use refactoring techniques to reach the new design incrementally and safely.
A project with only unit tests misses critical benefits of TDD; well-unit-tested code can still turn out to be uncalled or impossible to integrate.
Start implementing a feature by writing an acceptance test that exercises the wanted functionality: while failing it shows the feature is missing, and when it passes the feature is done.
Use a feature's acceptance test to decide whether the code you are about to write is actually needed, so you write only directly relevant code.
Wherever possible an acceptance test should exercise the system end-to-end, interacting only from the outside rather than calling internal code.
condition: wherever possible
exception: unless you need the speed-up and already have a stable set of end-to-end tests providing cover

statement: Prefer end-to-end tests that exercise both the system and the process by which it is built and deployed (check out, compile, unit-test, integrate, package, production-like deploy, then exercise through external access points).
Automate the end-to-end build-and-deploy cycle, because its steps are fiddly and error-prone and must be repeated throughout the software's lifetime.
Building a deployable system is only the start of a release in large or regulated organizations, so understand the whole technical and organizational release environment.
condition: in large or heavily regulated organizations

statement: Maintain a hierarchy of tests: acceptance tests ask whether the whole system works, integration tests ask whether your code works against code you cannot change, and unit tests ask whether your objects do the right thing and are convenient to work with.
Use integration tests to confirm that the abstractions you build over third-party code behave as you expect and to get faster feedback than end-to-end tests.
condition: in most professional development; in a small system acceptance tests may be enough

statement: Distinguish external quality (how well the system meets customers' and users' needs) from internal quality (how easy the system is for developers to understand and change).
Maintaining internal quality is what lets a team modify a system's behavior safely and predictably and minimizes the risk that a change forces major rework.
A class is easy to unit-test only when it has explicit, easily substitutable dependencies and clear, easily invoked responsibilities; that is, when it is loosely coupled and highly cohesive.
When a test is hard to write, treat the difficulty as design feedback: investigate why and refactor the code to improve its structure, rather than skipping the test ('listening to the tests').
Two elements are coupled if a change in one forces a change in the other; loosely coupled features are easier to maintain.
An element's cohesion measures whether its responsibilities form a meaningful unit; highly cohesive features are easier to maintain.
Object-oriented design focuses more on the communication between objects than on the objects themselves.
An object-oriented system is a web of collaborating objects, and the behavior of the system is an emergent property of the composition of those objects.

Distinguish values (immutable, without identity, equal when their state is equal) from objects (with identity and mutable state that model computational processes), and split the system into a value world and an object world.
Design objects to be easily pluggable by having them follow common communication patterns and by making their dependencies explicit.
Identify object roles with abstract interfaces rather than concrete classes.
Think about objects in terms of roles, responsibilities, and collaborators.
Never commit failing unit tests to the source repository; unit tests should pass soon after they are written.

Follow 'Tell, Don't Ask': make interactions between objects explicit and named by telling objects what to do, rather than chaining getters, so the code expresses what it is for, not how it happens to be implemented.
Query objects (as opposed to values) sparingly, because queries let information leak out of an object and make the system more rigid.
exception: except when getting information from values or collections, using a factory, or searching and filtering

statement: When you must query, ask the object the question you actually want answered (adding a query method that moves the behavior to the most appropriate object) and phrase the query to describe the calling object's intention rather than implementation.

To unit-test an object that only sends commands and exposes no state, replace its neighbours with mock objects and specify expectations for how the target object should communicate with them in response to a triggering event.

The collaborators of an object need not exist when you write its unit test; use the test to tease out the supporting roles the object needs, defined as interfaces, and fill in real implementations later ('interface discovery').

The essential structure of a mock-object test is: create required mock objects, create the real objects including the target, specify how you expect the mocks to be called, call the triggering method(s), then assert that resulting values are valid and all expected calls were made.
Make the intention of every test clear, distinguishing the tested functionality, the supporting infrastructure, and the object structure.
A test fixture is the fixed starting state of a test; it makes the test repeatable, since starting in the same state each run should produce the same result.
Creating a fresh instance of the test object for each test method keeps tests isolated from one another, because the object's fields are reset before each test.
Use self-describing matchers with an assertThat-style API so that failure messages clearly state what went wrong, instead of hand-writing condition checks and error messages.
A mock-object test often needs no explicit result assertions, because verifying that the expected interactions occurred can itself be the definition of success.

An expectation can precisely specify the minimum and maximum invocation counts, whether an invocation is required or merely allowed, parameter constraints, ordering relative to other expectations, and the response behavior (return value, exception, or other).

Keep the expectation block visually separate from the action-and-assertion code, so the description of how neighbours should be invoked is obviously distinct from the code that invokes objects and checks results.
The approach rests on two core principles: continuous incremental development and expressive code.

Deploy and test from the very start of a project to force the team to understand how the system fits into the world and to flush out unknown technical and organizational risks while there is still time to address them.

Build the whole automated build, deploy, and test cycle before the first feature, because the risk of deferring it is too high; projects have been cancelled for being unable to reliably deploy their system.

Resolve the first-feature paradox by first working out how to build, deploy, and test a 'walking skeleton', then using that infrastructure to write the acceptance test for the first meaningful feature.

A walking skeleton is the thinnest possible slice of real functionality that can be automatically built, deployed, and tested end-to-end; keep its application functionality trivially simple so the team can concentrate on the infrastructure.

'End-to-end' refers to the build-and-deploy process as well as the system: a test should start from scratch, build a deployable system, deploy it into a production-like environment, and then run through the deployed system.

Include the deployment step inside the testing process, because deployment is error-prone and its scripts must be exercised before the real release, and because this is where the team learns how the wider organization operates.
Nothing forces a team to understand a process better than trying to automate it.

If real end-to-end testing is initially too hard, start with stop-gap infrastructure that reflects the team's current understanding, but treat it as temporary and remember that unknown risks remain until the tests truly run end-to-end.
condition: when full end-to-end testing is impractical at the start
exception: treated only as a temporary stop-gap, not a permanent substitute

statement: When shaping the walking skeleton, decide only the broad-brush high-level structure (major components and how they communicate); a rule of thumb is that you should be able to draw it on a whiteboard in a few minutes.
If the need for end-to-end testing does not influence a system's design, the system becomes very difficult to test later, forcing risky architectural changes made without end-to-end coverage.

Incremental development front-loads project stress: a well-run incremental project starts unsettled and then settles into a routine, whereas a late-integration project starts calmly but turns difficult at the end when many moving parts must be assembled at once.
A walking skeleton flushes out issues early in a project, while there is still time, budget, and goodwill to address them.
Maintain a sense of direction with a concrete implementation to test assumptions, but limit early structural choices to whiteboard-level decisions and reserve the right to change them.

On an existing (brownfield) system you cannot start with a walking skeleton; the safest way to begin TDD is to automate the build and deploy process, then add end-to-end tests covering the areas you need to change before refactoring and introducing unit tests.
condition: when working with a pre-existing system rather than a new one

statement: It is risky to start reworking a system when there are no tests to detect regressions.
Begin an end-to-end test infrastructure with the simplest path through the system you can find, so you build up supporting infrastructure before tackling harder functionality.
Start each new feature by writing failing acceptance tests that demonstrate the system does not yet have the feature and that track progress toward completing it.

Write acceptance tests using only the application's domain terminology, not the underlying technologies, so the tests clarify what the system should do and are shielded from changes to the technical infrastructure.
Expressing requirements precisely enough to be automatically checked uncovers implicit assumptions and forces you to look at the system from the users' point of view rather than the implementers'.

Separate the tests that measure progress (new acceptance tests, expected to fail until a feature is done) from those that catch regressions (acceptance tests for completed features, which must always pass).
Unit and integration tests support the development team, should run quickly, and should always pass.

When requirements change, move the affected acceptance tests out of the regression suite back into the in-progress suite, edit them to reflect the new requirements, and change the system to make them pass again.

Start testing a new class or feature with the simplest success case rather than degenerate or failure cases, because success cases give more feedback about the validity of your ideas; 'simple' should not be read as 'simplistic'.
exception: a feature is not complete until it is robust, so failure handling must still be done, just possibly later

statement: Keep a notepad or index cards by the keyboard to jot down failure cases, refactorings, and technical tasks so you stay focused; the feature is finished only when every noted item has been done or explicitly decided against.
Write the test you would want to read: first express the desired behavior as clearly as possible (acting as if the supporting code exists), then build the infrastructure to support it.
Always watch a test fail before writing the code to make it pass, and check the diagnostic message; a failure in an unexpected way signals a misunderstanding or incomplete code.

Ensure a failing test produces a clear, relevant diagnostic message, adjusting the test and support code until the error messages guide you to the problem; taking the trouble to write a useful diagnostic also clarifies what the test and code are meant to do.

Develop a feature from the inputs to the outputs: start from the external events that trigger the behavior, work through the boundary objects and intermediate layers to the domain model, and then on to the boundary objects that produce an externally visible response.

Do not start by unit-testing new domain-model objects in isolation and hooking them into the application later; it feels like rapid progress but invites integration problems and wasted work because the right feedback was missing.

Unit-test behavior, not methods: focus on the features the object should provide and how to use it to achieve a goal, not on exercising every path through its code; high test coverage alone does not guarantee a maintainable codebase.
Choose test names that describe how the object behaves in the scenario being tested.
When code is difficult to test, ask why it is hard, not just how to test it: the difficulty usually means the design needs improving, and the same structure will make the code hard to change later.
Treat writing tests as an early warning of maintenance problems and refactor to fix the design while it is still fresh, rather than letting the code decay into 'software rot'.

Balance the grain of testing: testing at too large a grain causes a combinatorial explosion of paths, while testing at too fine a grain (class level only) misses problems that arise from objects not working together.

There is no single correct ratio of unit testing to integration testing; regularly reflect on how well TDD is working, identify weaknesses, and adapt the testing strategy, ensuring the confidence to change code without breaking it is justified.

Value code that is easy to maintain over code that is easy to write, because implementing a feature in the most direct way can damage maintainability by obscuring the code or introducing hidden dependencies.
Structure functionality into objects, objects into packages, and packages into programs, guided by two principal heuristics: separation of concerns and working at higher levels of abstraction.
Apply separation of concerns by gathering together code that will change for the same reason, so that a change to the system's behavior touches as little code as possible.
Manage complexity by working at higher levels of abstraction, building from components of useful functionality rather than manipulating variables and control flow directly.

Applied consistently, separation of concerns and higher abstraction push a system toward a ports-and-adapters architecture that isolates the business domain from technical infrastructure via interfaces (ports) and bridges (adapters).

Distinguish encapsulation (an object's behavior can be affected only through its API, controlling how changes ripple) from information hiding (concealing how the object implements its functionality behind its API); the two qualities are largely orthogonal.

Accidental aliasing (sharing references to mutable objects) can couple unrelated parts of a system and make it behave mysteriously; maintain encapsulation by defining immutable value types, avoiding global variables and singletons, and copying collections and mutable values when passing them between objects.

Deliberately decide what is inside versus outside each object; exposing too much of an object's internals through its API makes clients do its work, spreads behavior across coupled objects, and raises maintenance cost.

Give every object a single, clearly defined responsibility; a useful heuristic is that you should be able to describe what an object does without conjunctions like 'and' or 'or', and if you cannot, split it into collaborating objects.

Use a message-passing style between objects but a more functional, side-effect-free style within an object, because a little immutability inside a class leads to safer code assembled from smaller components with less risky shared state.

Classify an object's peers by relationship: dependencies are required services without which the object cannot function and so should be supplied at construction; notifications are fire-and-forget peers the object keeps updated without knowing or caring who is listening, which keeps objects decoupled.

Adjustments are peers that adjust an object's behavior to the wider needs of the system, such as policy objects that make decisions on its behalf (the Strategy pattern) or the component parts of a composite.

The peer stereotypes (dependencies, notifications, adjustments) are heuristics to aid design thinking, not hard rules; the same collaborator can be a dependency in one context and a notification in another depending on how it is used.

Notifications are one-way: a notification listener may not return a value, call back the caller, or throw an exception, because there may be other listeners in the chain; a dependency or adjustment may do these because it has a direct relationship.

Always create a valid object by passing its dependencies through the constructor; because dependencies are required, there is no point creating the object before they are available, and the constructor enforces this constraint in the object's definition.

Avoid partially creating an object and then finishing it by setting properties, because it is brittle: the programmer must remember to set every dependency, and adding a new dependency still compiles with existing client code that no longer builds a valid instance.

Notifications and adjustments may be passed to the constructor or initialized to safe defaults (a null object or empty collection) and overwritten later, but there is no safe default for a dependency.

Make a composite object simpler than the sum of its parts: its API must hide the existence of and interactions between its component parts, and the composite's API should not be more complicated than that of any of its components.

Prefer context-independent objects that have no built-in knowledge of the system they execute in; whatever an object needs to know about its larger environment should be passed in, either permanently at construction or transiently to the method that needs it.
A class that uses terms from multiple domains may be violating context independence.
exception: unless it is part of a bridging (adapter) layer

statement: Context independence makes object relationships explicit and defined separately from the objects, which simplifies the objects and concentrates relationship management in mapping-layer factory objects, yielding systems you change by reconfiguring how objects are composed.

Encapsulation is almost always good, but information can be hidden in the wrong place; discuss designs in explicit information-hiding terms to check that each detail is hidden at the level of the nested domain that actually owns it.

Writing a test first improves design because starting with a test forces you to describe what you want before how, helping maintain the right level of abstraction; if the intent of a unit test is unclear you are probably mixing up concepts and not ready to code.
Keep unit tests limited in scope; a unit test that is dozens of lines long, burying its point in setup, indicates the component under test is too large and should be broken into smaller components.

Because constructing an object for a unit test forces you to pass and therefore know its dependencies, unit testing encourages context independence and exposes objects with implicit or too many dependencies as painful to test, prompting cleanup.
Focus design effort on the communication patterns between objects—how they collaborate—because these matter more than achieving a well-designed static class structure.
An interface describes whether two components will fit together, while a protocol describes whether they will work together.
Use TDD with mock objects to make communication protocols visible, both as a tool for discovering them during development and as documentation when revisiting the code.

Mock an object's peers (its dependencies, notifications, and adjustments) but not its internals; a clumsy or unclear test can be a hint that too much implementation is exposed and responsibilities should be rebalanced between the object and its neighbours.

Define explicit types to represent value concepts in the domain, even if they do little, because they create a self-explanatory domain model, let you find all relevant code for a change, reduce the risk of confusing distinct quantities, and provide a natural place to hang behavior.

Introduce new value and object types by three techniques: breaking out (splitting a complex object into coherent helper types), budding off (adding a placeholder type to mark a new domain concept), and bundling up (grouping values that are always used together into a new type).

Prefer on-demand ('pull') design: when an object needs a service, define an interface for that service from the client's point of view, mock it in the client's unit tests, then implement it and follow the chain of collaborators, rather than 'pushing' out features you guess a class should provide.
When writing a test, ask 'If this worked, who would know?'; if the answer is not the target object, it is probably time to introduce a new collaborator.
Break up an object if it becomes too large to test easily or if its test failures become difficult to interpret, then unit-test the new parts separately.
When a test becomes too complicated to set up because there are too many moving parts to reach the relevant state, consider bundling up some of the collaborating objects.

Do not defer cleanup of unstructured exploratory code too long, because the cost of cleanup tends to arrive when the team can least afford it; sometimes it is better to treat such code as a spike and, once you know what to do, roll it back and reimplement cleanly.
Prefer narrow interfaces even though you then need more of them, because fewer methods make an interface's role obvious to the caller and make adapters and decorators easier to write.

Driving an interface into existence from its client keeps it as narrow as possible and avoids leaking excess information about its implementers, minimizing implicit coupling and keeping the code malleable.

Avoid meaningless 'Impl' class names, which merely duplicate 'implements X'; name an implementation after something specific about it, and if no good name exists the interface may be poorly named, unfocused, or actually a value type.

Refactor interfaces as well as classes: merge similar interfaces that represent a single concept to make components more plug-compatible, or deliberately distinguish similar-looking interfaces that represent different concepts so the compiler can enforce correct combination.

Compose system behavior from objects: use lower-level, well-understood objects as building blocks of more capable objects, which yields a flexible structure from relatively little code that is easy to extend by adding new plug-compatible components.

Organize code into an implementation layer (the graph of objects describing how the system behaves) and a declarative layer (small 'sugar' methods and syntax describing what it does, effectively an embedded domain-specific language), using a different coding style for each.

Emphasize interfaces over classes because an object's type is defined by the roles it plays, which is what other objects see; treat a class as an implementation detail, a way of implementing types rather than the type itself.

Discover object class hierarchies by factoring out common behavior, but prefer to refactor to delegation rather than inheritance where possible, because delegation makes the code more flexible and easier to understand.
condition: in languages without strong multiple-inheritance support; value types, having no peers, are less likely to use delegation

statement: You cannot use the pull/discovery design process to shape third-party code because you do not control it; instead focus design effort on the integration between your design and the external code.

Only mock types that you own; do not mock types you cannot change, because you cannot act on any design feedback the tests give and mocking external libraries tends to produce complex, brittle tests whose mess is really telling you the design is wrong.

Mocking an external type risks the stubbed behavior not matching what the library actually does, and that risk recurs whenever the library is upgraded; validity depends on how well the library is specified and implemented.

Instead of mocking an external API, write a thin layer of adapter objects that use the third-party API to implement interfaces defined in your application's domain terms, and verify those adapters with focused integration tests that confirm your understanding of how the API behaves.

Keep the adapter layer over third-party code as thin as possible to minimize brittle, hard-to-test code; there should be relatively few integration tests compared with unit tests, so they do not slow the build unduly.

Consistently adapting third-party code produces a set of interfaces that define the application's relationship with the outside world in the application's own terms and discourages low-level technical concepts from leaking into the domain model.

Mocking a third-party library is occasionally justified, such as to simulate behavior hard to trigger with the real library (for example throwing exceptions) or to test a sequence of calls like rolling back a transaction on failure.
exception: such tests should be few in the suite; the default is not to mock types you do not own

statement: When an adapter must call back into the application (as with event-based libraries), do use mock objects in the integration test, but only to mock the application-defined callback interfaces, to verify that the adapter correctly translates events between the external and application domains.
Follow the same isolation principle for third-party value types as for services, translating between external value types and application-domain value types.
exception: unless a third-party value type is so fundamental that using it directly is warranted

statement: A resilient development process assumes that people will misunderstand requirements and technologies and includes techniques to discover and recover from those errors as early as possible, because leaving problems in the code causes more expensive damage later.

Very incremental development lets a team make substantial changes in small, safe steps; keeping the system always clean and always working lets developers focus on just the immediate change and makes merging changes back never a crisis.
Large restructurings tend to lose their way and take unpredictably longer than a series of small incremental changes.
When stakeholders want more than can be delivered in a useful time, deliver a basic working application first and then make it more powerful, rather than attempting to deliver everything at once.
Agree on a shared domain vocabulary with stakeholders early, defining the basic terms, to avoid confusion when clarifying what to build.

End-to-end testing of asynchronous, event-based systems must cope with asynchrony, because the test runs in parallel with the application and cannot know precisely when it is ready, unlike a unit test that drives an object directly in the same thread.

Because an end-to-end test cannot peek inside the target application, have it poll for a visible effect such as a user-interface change or a log entry and fail if the effect does not appear within a time limit.

For asynchronous tests, control the application and step through the scenario: at each stage wait for an assertion to pass and then send an event to advance, rather than asserting on a value that only briefly flashes on screen.

End-to-end tests are slower and more brittle than unit tests, so their failures may need interpretation (some teams report a timing-related failure only after it recurs several times in a row), whereas unit tests must pass every time.
Judging where to set the boundaries of what to test, and how to eventually cover everything, is an important test-driven development skill.

When you must initially test against a fake instead of a real external service, record the substitution as a known project risk and schedule testing against the real service as soon as there is enough functionality to complete a meaningful transaction, because the sooner a discrepancy is found the less code is built on the misunderstanding.
Keep a fake or stub implementation minimal: since its only purpose is to support the test, it should implement just what the test requires and no more.

Give each developer their own test environment so developers do not interfere with each other's test runs, and also maintain at least one test rig that represents the production environment, including the network distribution of processing and a build cycle that exercises it.
Maintain a single command that reliably compiles, builds, deploys, and tests the application, run it repeatedly, and only start coding once that automated build-and-test is working.

Add functionality a tiny slice at a time, handling one test failure at a time; focusing on a single aspect ensures you understand it, makes progress more predictable, and means that once something works it tends to stay working, without taking longer overall.
Make test-failure diagnostics verbose and easy to understand—describing what was looked for and what was actually found—so that failures are easy to interpret.
Each acceptance test you write should introduce just enough new requirements to force a manageable increase in functionality.
When developing incrementally you defer many decisions, but sometimes consistency and symmetry justify retrofitting more detail into existing code while it is already 'cracked open'.
condition: when consistency and symmetry matter more than deferring the decision

statement: Using the same construct on both sides of a boundary (for example one constant to both create and check a message) removes duplication and expresses the link between the two sides, but it makes you vulnerable to getting both wrong with no test to catch the invalid content, so weigh the trade-off deliberately.

The critical question when writing a test is 'what do we think we're testing?'; decide deliberately what the test targets, because reasonable developers may legitimately reach different answers for different projects.

Practice outside-in development: start from the outside event that triggers the wanted behavior and work inward one object at a time until you reach a visible effect (such as a sent message or log entry) that shows the goal is achieved, using the end-to-end test to define the end points.
A failing end-to-end test defines the target for the next coding episode, telling you at a high level what you are aiming for, so you fill in implementation until it passes.

Because you cannot catch every configuration option in a whole system, push to exercise as much of the system as possible as early as possible and repeatedly, keep component quality high, and constantly push to simplify.
Configuration differences between the test and production environments can hide or introduce bugs, so match the test environment's configuration to production where it matters.
Make implicit behavior explicit before adding features: promote an anonymous or implicit class into a named top-level class whose responsibility is obvious.
Name a class from a description of its responsibility (for example, a class that translates messages becomes a Translator).

Avoid creating a dependency from non-UI logic on a user-interface component, because it is hard to unit-test (you would have to query a component running on the UI event thread) and it violates the single-responsibility principle and separation of concerns.

When an object needs to hand off work, delegate to a collaborator represented by an interface passed in at construction, even before you know the interface's contents or implementation, so you can focus on the immediate concern first.
Test method names can be long and fully descriptive because a reflection-based runner never requires them to appear in calling code; use the name to describe the behavior being verified.

Insulate a domain object from other concerns by introducing a listener interface so it reports status changes in its own terms rather than knowing another concern's implementation details (such as which thread a user interface uses).

Decide whether a collaborator is a dependency or a notification by asking whether the object can function without it: a dependency is required and should be supplied at construction, whereas a notification (listener) is not required.
Prefer method and type names that closely match what they do, because a closer match between a name and its behavior makes the code clearer.

Clarifying and restructuring code early is not wasteful gold-plating; in the authors' experience most teams spend too little time clarifying code and pay for it in maintenance overhead, and the single-responsibility principle is an effective heuristic for breaking up complexity, so developers should not be shy about creating new types.
When you are unsure how best to break a class up further, push on and see where the code takes you, recording the concern as a to-do rather than forcing a premature decision.

Use the strictness of a mock expectation to express intent about a relationship: require an exact count for a call that must happen precisely once, and use a looser 'at least once' expectation for a status-update call whose exact count does not matter.
The order in which expectations are declared need not match the order in which the methods are called; add an explicit sequence constraint only when the calling order actually matters.

Choosing how to express an expected value in a test is a trade-off: writing out the calculation can make the test more readable but risks reimplementing the target code in the test, and some calculations are too complicated to reproduce.

Use a 'null implementation'—a temporary empty implementation introduced to defer effort and let the programmer make progress, intended to be replaced—distinct from a permanent null object introduced to reduce complexity in calling code.
Break a dependency loop when wiring collaborators by exploiting that a notification can be attached after construction: create the object with a null listener, then add the real listener later.
Shipping well-structured source code with a library's distribution makes the library much easier to work with.
Express intent in an API by providing intention-revealing operations (such as an auction 'join' method) rather than exposing low-level detail like sending a raw string message.

Accepting a known-bad shortcut such as merely printing an exception can be acceptable to get tests passing and structure in place, provided you record a to-do item to replace it, but recognize it as normally bad practice.
condition: only as a temporary step with a recorded to-do to fix it

statement: Package related behavior together on the object it belongs to (for example, sending commands to an auction belongs on the Auction object) rather than scattering it across multiple levels of the code.
Setting no expectations on a mock object means any call to it will fail the test, so strict mocking automatically traps method calls you did not expect.

In a test, drop values that are not part of the behavior you are verifying (feed literal numbers) so the test stays focused on the interesting behavior; keep such values only when an expectation's calculation references them.

Distinguish allowances from expectations in a test: an 'allowing' clause says a call may happen but need not and represents supporting infrastructure or side effects you do not care about, whereas an expectation must occur; use the distinction to express what actually matters in the test.

Make assertions about an object's state-dependent behavior without breaking encapsulation by having the test listen to the notification events the object already sends to describe its state in its collaborators' terms, rather than exposing how the state is implemented.

Representing an object's state logically through its observable notifications, rather than its internal fields, lets you make radical changes to the object's implementation without changing its tests.

Aim for a test style in which the test's name closely matches the expectation it enforces, so the test expresses its essential intent; it is worth investing in the abstractions that make this possible.
Use empty or placeholder implementations to get code through the compiler when you are not ready to fill in the real code, so you can stay focused on the immediate task.

Consistency of representation is a guideline, not a rule: it is acceptable to use a simpler representation (such as a boolean) where a richer one (such as an enum) looks too complicated, especially when the field is private to a small class that is easy to change later and the code reads well.
exception: when a richer representation genuinely improves clarity, prefer it

statement: Grow a component such as a user interface one feature at a time rather than replacing the whole thing in one go, to avoid the risk of a big-bang rewrite.
Deferring effort on part of the system is fine, but catch up on the deferred structure at the point where upcoming requirements will need it, before it blocks progress.
Make the smallest change that gets a new structure into place (for example, replacing a label with a single-cell table) and then grow the additional functionality from there.
Earlier investment in clean structure pays off later, as new features fit into the existing structure and a change stays localized to the class that encapsulates the affected behavior.

Nothing shakes out a design like trying to implement it, and few people get their designs always right, so get into the critical areas of the code early and allow yourself to change your mind when you can do better, relying on small steps and tests to protect you.

Consolidate several special-purpose notification methods into a single state-change notification that carries an immutable snapshot value object; this simplifies the listener interface and often lets the implementation simplify too.

Extend a test's expectation language with small, descriptively named helper methods (such as custom matchers) that make expectations read well, effectively adding new vocabulary to an embedded testing DSL; design frameworks to be extensible in this way.

Model state transitions with immutable snapshot or value objects whose transition methods return new instances; this gives a clean mechanism for moving between states and packages field access, and even a partial state machine that does not enforce only legal transitions is a useful hint.

Push decision-making down into the value object or enum that owns the relevant knowledge (for example, letting the state decide what it becomes when the auction closes) so higher-level objects no longer need to know those details.
Do not treat any unit as too small to test; writing a test for a seemingly trivial class can reveal an unhandled case, such as an illegal repeated transition.

Prefer to make an illegal condition impossible by design; when you cannot yet do so, throw a dedicated exception (such as a 'Defect' exception) for conditions that could only be caused by a programming error rather than a runtime-environment failure.
Replace a noisy switch statement with polymorphic dispatch (for example, a method on an enum or type) to make the code more object-oriented and reduce the branching code to almost nothing.
Write a unit test even for code that seems unnecessary to test now, because it will protect you when you later change the code and forget to keep an associated mapping up to date.

As the design clarifies, remove now-unnecessary forwarding and translation calls; when a class collapses to a single remaining purpose (such as pushing updates onto the UI thread), refactor it into a Decorator and rename it to reflect its true role.
Introduce a small helper method to improve readability and to give tests access to derived values (such as display strings) without exposing constants across unrelated classes.

Move comparison and decision logic onto the object that owns the data (for example, let a snapshot decide whether it refers to the same item) rather than having a collaborator extract and compare its fields; this gives a clearer division of responsibilities, avoids the 'feature envy' code smell, and lets you change the implementation without changing the collaborator.

TDD is particularly helpful for tricky index and boundary logic, because writing the tests first clarifies the boundary conditions and then checks the implementation, avoiding hard-to-find off-by-one bugs buried in the code.

You can make development progress while user-interface and design details are still being worked out: build to the team's current understanding of the features and keep the code flexible to respond as the design firms up, rather than locking down the whole design before coding.

Keep the responsibilities of classes focused: when a user interaction implies an action outside the user interface, the user-interface class should delegate to a collaborating object rather than taking on concepts like connections itself.

Translate framework-internal events into domain events at the boundary: a user-interface class should convert a low-level framework event (such as a button action) into a domain event (such as a user request) and not concern itself with how the handling listener is implemented.
Introduce a listener or notification interface to decouple a source of requests (such as user actions) from whatever object handles them.

When you cannot write a simple synchronous unit test because of threading (for example, user-interface framework threads), use an integration test that waits until the tested code has stabilized before checking assertions.
Test asynchronous behavior with a polling probe that repeatedly checks for the desired state until it is satisfied or times out.
Step away from the keyboard and use informal techniques such as CRC cards to visualize and discuss the structure of the code at a design moment.
When changing user-interface state from outside the UI thread, marshal the call onto the UI thread rather than mutating shared UI state directly from another thread.

You can arrive at a good architecture (such as ports-and-adapters) incrementally, by repeatedly adding features and following design heuristics while keeping the code clean, rather than designing the whole structure up front.

Keep the core domain code free of any reference to external infrastructure, separating the system into components (core domain, communication/adapter, and display) with a single entry point that binds the domain model and infrastructure together.

Perform even significant refactorings incrementally: when you are unsure what to do next, scale down each individual change so you never stray more than a few minutes from working code, and backtrack to try another path if one does not work out.

Refactoring is a design activity that needs all your design skills continuously, so consider more than the static structure of classes and interfaces; also examine the dynamic structure of instances and threads, drawing an interaction diagram when needed.

When there is no obviously best fix, examine the circumstances and exercise judgment, and be wary that relying on an incidental side effect of the application to fix an issue can cause transient failures that are hard to track down.

Agile projects shift emphasis over time—from proving the concept, to implementing enough to deploy, to adding options for a wider range of users—and a flexible team responds to these changing sponsor needs, unlike a fixed-design approach that must approve structure before work begins or a code-and-fix approach that is not resilient to a changing role.

Extract a new class to gain a clearer separation of concerns when one class is implicitly responsible for two things (such as maintaining a record and displaying it), introducing a distinct role for each responsibility.
Introduce a role interface to accept a new responsibility and delegate to it, which keeps the top-level wiring code simple—little more than binding the components together.
Model a new distinct state explicitly when users need information about it (for example, a 'losing' state so users can still see the final price) rather than collapsing it into an existing state.
Use state or ordering assertions in a test to confirm that operations happen in the required order, such as joining an auction only after everything else is set up.
Catch failures at the boundary: when a framework silently drops exceptions thrown by handlers, make your handler catch everything so that failures are not lost.

Being precise about which exceptions to catch is usually preferable, but catching broadly is acceptable when the outcome is binary and the distinction does not matter (for example, either a message parses or it does not).
condition: when the specific exception type carries no actionable distinction

statement: Throw an exception when code tries to read a value that has not been set (for example a dedicated missing-value exception), so incomplete input is detected rather than silently processed with missing data.

Prefer giving each object a single responsibility even when it costs more lines of code: dividing a feature so each object does one thing well, with system behavior emerging from how objects are composed, keeps code maintainable because you do not have to cut through unrelated functionality to reach the piece you need.

Depend on a role (an interface) rather than a concrete implementation; mocking a real class defines a relationship with an implementation instead of a role and is a sign of being too precise about dependencies.
When adding a new concern (such as deciding what to do on failure or how to report it), invent a new collaborator to own it rather than piling more responsibilities onto an existing class.
Verify that failures are recorded by having an end-to-end test check the contents of a log file, so you confirm the organization can recover from those failures.

Running a test in memory instead of against a real resource such as a file is acceptable when that resource access is already covered by an end-to-end test and would introduce irrelevant dependencies or asynchrony, but write integration tests for more complex behavior.
condition: when the behavior is simple and file access is already covered elsewhere

statement: Mocking a concrete class rather than an interface is a rare, justified exception only when the class is a thin shim over a stable third-party API you do not own and introducing an extra layer of indirection is not worth it; do not do it for internal code you could give an interface, and extract a testable collaborator if the class grows in complexity.
exception: never for internal code, which you can describe with a role interface

statement: Keep code that cannot throw outside the try/catch block so that the catch handles only the operations that can actually fail.

Distinguish support logging (errors and info intended for support staff, administrators, and operators to diagnose failures or monitor a running system) from diagnostic logging (debug and trace messages that are programmer scaffolding and should not be on in production).

Test-drive support logging from someone's actual requirements (such as auditing or failure recovery) so every message has a clear purpose and downstream analysis tools are protected, whereas diagnostic logging is programmer scaffolding that probably need not be test-driven.

Prefer a notification to inline logging: replace logging statements (which mix domain logic with logging and break the single-responsibility principle) with a call to a support or reporting object whose concrete implementation—logger, message bus, or pop-up—is irrelevant at that level.

Encapsulating support reporting makes code express intent (helping the support people) rather than implementation (logging), centralizes reporting for consistency and reuse, and—because you write a test per report—avoids the 'log it and carry on' syndrome that causes log bloat and unhandled error conditions.

Needing to pass a logger through many domain objects is a test smell that signals an unclear design, such as confusing support with diagnostic logging, logging more than needed, or not yet finding the choke points where production logging belongs.
Excessive logging can harm a system—for instance when logs must be deleted before bugs can be diagnosed—so much so that logging nothing might have lost no useful information while running faster.

Mock concrete classes only as a last resort, because subclassing to mock leaves the relationship between the objects implicit, with nothing in the domain code to make the relationship visible or reusable.

Mocking a concrete class overspecifies the client by forcing it to depend on a whole class rather than the narrow interface it actually uses, violating the Interface Segregation Principle that clients should not depend on interfaces they do not use.

Extracting an interface forces you to name the relationship you have just discovered, which makes you think harder about the domain and teases out concepts you would otherwise miss, because once something has a name you can talk about it and find its other uses.

When forced to mock a class because of legacy code you cannot yet change or third-party code you cannot change at all, prefer writing a veneer over the library to mocking it directly, and treat any direct class-mocking as a temporary compromise to remove as soon as possible.

Never override a class's internal features in a test, because that locks the test to the current implementation; only override visible methods, never expose internals just to override them, and if you cannot reach the structure you need, break the class into smaller composable features.

Do not mock values, which should be immutable; just create an instance and use it. A class is likely a value (and not worth mocking) when it is immutable and you cannot think of a meaningful name for an interface and implementation pair; if a value is complex to set up, write a builder rather than mock it.

Fix a bloated constructor by looking for arguments that are always used together or share the same lifetime and packaging them into a new object that represents the implicit concept; being sensitive to complexity in the tests helps clarify the design.

A bloated constructor may instead signal a confused object with too many unrelated responsibilities pulling in many dependencies; such a class should be broken up, and if its test class slices into unrelated parts that share nothing, that is a sign to slice the object too.

A bloated constructor may signal that not all arguments are true dependencies: insist that dependencies be passed to the constructor, but initialize notifications and adjustments to safe defaults (such as a null object) and let them be reconfigured later; a final field is a hint that an argument is a genuine dependency.

Reduce the number of expectations in a test by distinguishing stubs (simulations of behavior, for side-effect-free queries, that just help the test pass) from expectations (assertions about how the object interacts with its neighbours, for calls with side effects); making everything an expectation hides what is actually significant.

Write few expectations in a unit test; needing more than a few means you are either testing too large a unit or locking down too many of the object's interactions, mirroring the guidance to avoid too many assertions.

A chain of calls to reach a distant object exposes dependencies that are not relevant to the caller; instead tell the nearest object to do the work for you, following 'Tell, Don't Ask' and the Law of Demeter.

Keep knowledge local to an object—either internal or passed in—so its implementation is independent of its context and it can be moved freely; needing 'magic' to create mocks signals knowledge leaking between components.
Emphasizing how objects communicate rather than what they are yields more, smaller abstractions defined in domain terms, which puts more domain vocabulary into the code.

Applying 'Tell, Don't Ask' consistently leads to passing behavior (as callbacks) into the system instead of pulling values up through the stack, giving better information hiding and clearer abstractions through more precise interfaces.

Keep tests and code clean as you go, because it is much easier to keep a codebase clean than to recover from a mess; once a codebase starts to rot, developers come under pressure to botch code and a team's good intentions quickly dissipate.

A unit test should focus on at most a few classes and should not need a large fixture or lots of preparation to reach the state where the feature can be exercised; very long tests (for example a thousand lines) are hard to understand and brittle because the objects are too tightly coupled.

TDD is unforgiving: poor-quality tests slow development to a crawl and poor internal quality of the system under test produces poor tests, so use the internal-quality feedback you get from writing tests to catch the problem early.

For TDD to be sustainable, tests must not only verify behavior but also express it clearly (be readable), because every time a developer has to puzzle through an unclear test there is less time for new features and team velocity drops.

Take as much care with test code as with production code, but in a different style: test code should be concrete about the example values it uses yet abstract about how the code works and read like a declarative description of what is being tested, whereas production code is abstract about values but concrete about how it does its job.

Watch for test readability smells: names that do not describe the point of the test, a single test exercising multiple features, tests with inconsistent structure that cannot be skim-read, setup and exception-handling code that buries the essential logic, and unexplained literal 'magic number' values.
Make the test's name the first clue to what is being tested and how the object should behave; avoid meaningless names and avoid naming a test merely after the method it exercises.

Name tests in terms of the features the object provides—what it does in different situations—rather than after the method it exercises, because naming a test after a method duplicates information available from the class and does not say what the method is for.

Use a sentence-style test-naming convention where the name reads like a sentence with the target class as the implicit subject, and make the name say something about the expected result, the action on the object, and the motivation for the scenario.

Treat tests as documentation for the code, and regularly read or generate and skim-read the documentation produced from test names to get a fresh perspective and catch unclear names you are too close to see.

Write tests in a standard canonical structure (setup, execute, verify, teardown, or the collapsed arrange-act-assert) so they can be skim-read; difficulty writing a test in the standard form is a hint that the code is too complicated or the idea is not yet clear.

Write a test 'backwards': first the name (to decide what you want to achieve), then the call to the target code, then the expectations and assertions, then the setup and teardown—reflecting how you think through the feature—then run it and watch it fail.

Do not insist on a single assertion per test (a useful training rule only); aim for one coherent feature per test, which may take a handful of assertions, and split a test that makes assertions about different features—the key criterion is whether a reader can tell what is significant.
Streamline test code to emphasize what it does over how, moving everything out of the test method that does not contribute to the description, in domain terms, of the feature being exercised.
Compose readable assertions from small, intention-revealing helper methods and matchers, prioritizing expressiveness over minimizing the number of source lines.

Extract common setup, teardown, and assertion behavior into shared, descriptively named methods, but do not make a test so abstract that you can no longer see what it does; refactor tests enough to reveal their flow, but not as hard as production code.

Catch an exception in a test only if you want to assert something about it; otherwise let it propagate for the test runner to catch (you may add exceptions to the test method signature since it is called only by reflection), which removes noise and preserves the stack trace.
Delegate to subordinate helper objects such as test drivers and fake servers so tests read in domain terms rather than in terms of infrastructure like UI toolkits and messaging.

Keep assertions and expectations as narrowly defined as possible, asserting only what matters (for example matching one property and using an 'any of type' matcher for irrelevant arguments), because asserting too much detail makes tests hard to read and brittle when things change.
Prefer explicit matchers (such as asserting 'not equal to') over a negated boolean assertion, because a negation is easy to misread and a matcher also reports the actual value in the failure message.

Allocate literal test values to well-named constants or variables that show the role each value plays and whether it is significant (for example just outside an allowed range) or merely an arbitrary placeholder.

Use test data builders—builder objects with chainable methods and a final build(), each field initialized to a safe default—to construct complex test data, so a test includes only the values relevant to the behavior; this copes with variation better than the Object Mother pattern, which needs a new factory method for every minor difference.

There are two approaches to creating subordinate test objects: write the test you want to see and then fill in the supporting objects, or write the code directly in the tests and then refactor out clusters of behavior.

The point of a test is not to pass but to fail: a failing test has succeeded at its job of detecting and reporting an error, and even an unexpected failure in an unrelated area is valuable because it reveals implicit relationships in the code.

Avoid the situation where you cannot diagnose a test failure without cracking open the debugger to step through the code; it signals that the tests do not express the requirements clearly enough and risks 'debug hell' and the temptation to delete the test and lose the safety net.

Synchronize with the source repository frequently, up to every few minutes, so that when a test fails unexpectedly it costs little to revert recent changes and try another approach, and do not be too inhibited about dropping code and restarting with a clear head.
Make tests fail informatively: a failing test that clearly explains what failed and why lets you diagnose and correct the code quickly and move on.
Keep each test small, focused, and well-named, because when a small test fails its name tells you most of what you need to know about what went wrong.
Add an explanatory message to an assertion identifying the value being asserted, so a failure describes the cause rather than just the symptom and makes clear which assertion failed.
Use matchers that describe the value that mismatched, so a failure report shows exactly what is different.

Build diagnostic detail into the values themselves ('self-describing values'): needing to add explanatory text to an assertion is, like a comment, a hint you could make the failure more obvious, for example by setting a test value to a self-describing string or giving a reference type a meaningful string representation.

Use obviously canned or improbable values (such as a negative number, a maximum value, or a date far outside the real range) so that a wrong value stands out as clearly not a production value, and adopt team conventions that make common special values conspicuous.

Use a tracer object—a dummy with no behavior except to describe its role when something fails—to check that an object is passed through the code and routed to the right collaborator, and name mock objects so failure reports are unambiguous.

A tracer object or empty marker interface can double as a design tool: use it to mark and name a domain concept and show how it is used in a collaboration, then fill in the interface with methods as the code grows.

When a test has both expectations and assertions, an ordinary assertion may fail before the expectations are checked and hide the real cause, so in those cases explicitly assert that all expectations were satisfied before the other assertions to get the right failure report.

Follow a four-step TDD cycle—fail, report, pass, refactor—checking that the failure reports clearly, because a good diagnostic is how you know you have understood the feature and that whoever changes it later will too; diagnostics are a first-class feature and test quality must be maintained like production code.

Use test 'states' with when/then clauses to enforce that an invocation happens only when the object is (or is not) in a particular state, so the test can reject events that would break the object's protocol.

States and sequences can be combined in a test, but needing such complexity is a hint that something should be broken into smaller, simpler pieces; it is most common when responding to external event feeds whose protocol you do not own.

When two expectations could match the same invocation, the one declared first wins, so declaration order can matter; in particular, if the first matching clause is an allowance a later expectation will never match and the test will fail.
Test 'states' can model all three participants in a test—the object under test, its peers, and the test itself—for example ignoring interactions while the test is still being set up.
Very liberal, dynamic expectation features move testing from a statically typed to a dynamically typed world, which brings both power and risk, so use these 'power tool' features with care.

Do not couple tests for generic adapter or marshalling code to application domain types, because it binds the application and adapter domains, makes tests brittle, risks misleadingly breaking tests when the domain model changes, and can leave tests that silently pass but no longer exercise the intended paths.

Test generic infrastructure such as a marshaller with dedicated 'guinea pig' objects that clearly represent the features being exercised (for example transient versus non-transient fields), unrelated to the real system, which also serve as self-describing values.

Some code crosses the boundary between feature-level and system-level design (for example multithreaded code, where behavior within a thread and interaction between threads are distinct concerns); such code is hard to test when you are not clear which aspect you are addressing, and lumping everything together produces confusing, brittle tests, whereas listening to the test smells leads to a clearer separation of responsibilities.

When testing an abstraction built over a persistence or ORM API, verify that it sends correct queries, configures mappings correctly, uses a compatible SQL dialect, respects the database's integrity constraints, interacts correctly with the transaction manager, and releases resources, while accepting that (as with any third-party API) these tests give integration confidence, not design feedback.
Isolate tests that affect persistent state: because persistent data survives from one test to the next, the test fixture must ensure each test starts with its persistent resources in a known state.

Clean up persistent data at the start of a test rather than at the end, so that a test run individually leaves data behind for diagnosing failures while a suite run still isolates tests from each other.
Capture the order in which tables or entities must be cleaned in a single place, such as a dedicated cleaner object, because that order must be kept up to date as the database schema evolves.

Make test transaction boundaries explicit rather than rolling back at the end of each test, because rolling back never tests what happens on commit (the ORM flush and the database's integrity checks), cannot test interactions between distinct transactions, and discards data useful for diagnosing failures.

Extract transaction management into a subordinate 'transactor' object that runs a unit of work within a transaction, and make the transaction boundaries stand out so they are easy to see when reading the test.

Bypassing an object's public API in a test (for example using reflection to reach its private state) is justified only when you are testing the configuration of a tool such as an ORM that itself uses that technique, not when you are test-driving the object's own design.
condition: only when verifying a tool that legitimately uses the same bypassing technique

statement: In persistence tests, ensure referential integrity by persisting referenced entities before saving the entity that refers to them, for example by wrapping a builder in a decorator that persists its result first.

Tests against realistic infrastructure such as a database are much slower than in-memory unit tests, so unit-test your code against a clean persistence interface defined in your domain terms with a mock, and verify the real implementation with fine-grained integration tests, rather than bringing up the whole system to test the technical layers.

Organize tests into a chain of phases—fast in-memory unit tests, slower integration tests that reach outside the process through third-party APIs, and end-to-end tests against a system deployed into a production-like environment—to get rapid feedback on core logic and incremental feedback on integration at increasingly coarse granularity.

Concurrency complicates test-driven development: unit tests give less confidence because synchronization is a system-wide concern, and failures are harder to diagnose because exceptions may be swallowed by background threads or tests may just time out.

Decide a broad-brush concurrency architecture and its principles ahead of time rather than in fine detail; it is often prescribed by the frameworks or libraries the application uses, and formal modeling tools can prove a design free of deadlock, livelock, or starvation.

Once the concurrency architecture is designed, test-drive the objects that fit into it: unit tests give confidence that an object meets its synchronization responsibilities, and coarser system tests give confidence that the whole system manages concurrency correctly.

Separate functional concerns from concurrency policy by passing in a task runner or executor, so you can unit-test the functional behavior on the test thread, and the object's API no longer hides its concurrency policy—an application of the context-independence principle.

Treat concurrency as a system-wide concern controlled outside the objects that run concurrent tasks; injecting an executor lets the application adapt an object's threading policy (for example adding a thread pool) without changing the object's implementation.

In a unit test, run tasks on the test thread using a deterministic executor so that assertion failures are caught and reported by the test runner and you do not have to synchronize with background threads.

Drive out synchronization with stress tests: specify one of the object's observable invariants with respect to concurrency, write a stress test that exercises the object many times from many threads, watch it fail and tune it until it fails reliably on every run, then add synchronization to make it pass.

Watch a stress test fail and understand its failure message, because it is easy to write a stress test that passes even though the object has a synchronization hole; if it does not fail reliably, raise the number of threads or iterations until you can trust it.

Write both the functional unit test and the synchronization stress test before writing the code, make sure both fail, then make both pass, to avoid checking in code that passes its functional tests but still contains concurrency errors.

Without precise control over the thread scheduler you cannot guarantee that a test will find synchronization errors; the best you can do is run the code enough times on enough threads to make detection likely.

To stress-test a passive object that has multiple threads pass through it and mutate its state, have the test start its own threads, and after they all finish the object's state should equal what it would have been had the calls happened in sequence.

Prefer synchronizing the test thread with background threads on a state condition (with a timeout on the test) rather than a fixed sleep, because fixed sleeps do not scale, slow the whole suite, and have to be tuned per environment; keep the unit-test suite fast enough that you never hesitate to run it.

Keep separate tests for functional behavior and for synchronization behavior, so that when one fails you can tell whether the fault is in the logic or the synchronization; race conditions are very hard to diagnose with a debugger because observing them (stepping or adding print statements) alters the thread scheduling that causes them.

Stress tests offer only a degree of reassurance that code is thread-safe, not a guarantee, because scheduling varies across operating systems, processors, and other running processes; the best you can do is run them frequently across a range of environments—locally before committing and on multiple build servers afterward.

Take a defence-in-depth ('belt and braces') approach to concurrency: unit tests to check an object correctly synchronizes threads, end-to-end tests to check unit-level synchronization policies integrate across the whole system, formal modeling tools where the architecture is not imposed by frameworks, and static-analysis tools in the automated build.

Asynchronous tests differ fundamentally from ordinary tests because control returns to the test before the triggered activity is complete, so returning from the call to the target code does not mean the result is ready to be checked.
An asynchronous test must be carefully coordinated with the system it tests, or it becomes unreliable—failing intermittently when the system is working or, worse, passing when the system is broken.
An asynchronous test must wait for success and use a timeout to detect failure, rather than checking the outcome immediately after triggering the activity.
Every tested activity must have an observable effect, because if an activity has no observable effect there is nothing for the test to wait for and no way for the test to synchronize with the system.

A test can observe the system either by sampling its observable state or by listening for events it emits; sampling is often the only option because many systems send no monitoring events, and a test may use both techniques for different ends of the system.

Beware flickering (intermittently failing) tests: they can mask real defects, and even a few of them break the team's culture of quality and habit of paying attention to feedback; tolerate a flicker only reluctantly and with a plan for when it will be fixed.
Make asynchronous tests succeed fast—detect success as quickly as possible so a succeeding test finishes as soon as the code responds, while only failing tests wait out the full timeout.

Listening for events is the quickest observation strategy because the test thread can block until an event wakes it, whereas sampling means polling with a delay that must be tuned to balance fast response against the load it puts on the target system, since too-fast polling can slow the system enough to make tests unreliable.
Define timeout values in a single place so the team can easily find and tune the balance between speed and reliability as the system grows and across different environments.

Do not scatter ad hoc sleeps and timeouts through tests; factor synchronization and assertion behavior into subordinate objects, which removes duplication, keeps the tests understandable, and lets you get this tricky code right once.

Prefer composition and dependency injection over adding getter methods that exist only to facilitate testing; injecting a collaborator through the constructor yields more object-oriented code than exposing internal state through getters.
Mock objects work best when they emphasize the roles that objects play for each other, asserting the messages sent between objects rather than merely the parameter values ('mock roles, not objects').
Use mock objects as a design tool to drive the design of the interfaces between objects, not merely as a technique for speeding up unit tests.
Express expectations through constraint or matcher objects that can describe what went wrong, because they make tests more expressive and produce better failure diagnostics.
When writing a custom matcher, name its factory method so the assertion or expectation that uses it reads clearly, considering how it will look at the call site.

Write a matcher's description so that it completes the sentence 'expected <description> but <mismatch-description>', so the matcher fits seamlessly into the failure messages that the test frameworks generate.
